definition: A loose sleeveless outer garment made from aba cloth; worn by Arabs.
etymology: Borrowed from Arabic عَبَاءَة (ʕabāʔa). Compare abaya.

definition: The act of giving something up.
example: Since he left her, she's suing him for divorce on grounds of abandonment.
etymology: Borrowed from French abandonnement, from abandonner (“to abandon, relinquish”). abandonner was originally equivalent to mettre à bandon (“to leave to the jurisdiction, i.e.

definition: The superior of an abbey of monks.
The cavity containing the major viscera; in mammals it is separated from the thorax by the diaphragm.
The criminal act of capturing and carrying away by force a family member; if a man's wife is abducted it is a crime against the family relationship and against the wife.
example: The abduction of a child.
etymology: From Latin abductiō(n) (“a robbing; an abduction”), from abdūcō (“to take or lead away”), from ab (“away”) + dūcō (“to lead”). By surface analysis, abduct + -ion or abduce + -tion.

definition: Lasting a long time.
example: An abiding belief.
etymology: Present participle or participial adjective from abide (verb) + -ing; or, from Middle English participle form of abiden, abyden (“to abide”).

definition: Having a strong healthy body.
example: Every able-bodied young man served in the army.
etymology: From able body + -ed.

definition: Do away with.
example: Slavery was abolished in the mid-19th century in America and in Russia.

definition: Terminate before completion.
example: Abort the mission.
etymology: From Middle English, from Latin abortus, perfect active participle of aborior (“miscarry”), formed from ab + orior (“to come into being”). Doublet of abortus.

definition: Be abundant or plentiful; exist in large quantities.
example: Wild animals abound wherever man does not stake his claim.
etymology: * First attested around 1325.

definition: Exist in large quantity.
Marked by sudden changes in subject and sharp transitions.
example: Abrupt prose.
etymology: First attested in 1583. Borrowed from Latin abruptus (“broken off”), perfect passive participle of abrumpō (“break off”), formed from ab (“from, away from”) + rumpō (“to break”).

definition: In statistics, the absolute difference between an element of a data set and a given point.
example: This average absolute deviation gives the average distance of any data item from the mean and thus is a good measure of spread.

definition: An indicator used in reactions that involve precipitation.
A bottomless gulf or pit; any unfathomable (or apparently unfathomable) cavity or chasm or void extending below (often used figuratively).
example: They fell into the abyss of drug addiction.
etymology: From Middle English abissus, from Late Latin abyssus (“a bottomless gulf”), from Ancient Greek ἄβυσσος (ábussos, “bottomless”, from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + βυσσός (bussós, “deep place”)), from βυθός (buthós, “deep place”).

definition: A gown worn by academics or judges.
A coagulation factor.
A process of increasing by addition (as to a collection or group).
example: The art collection grew through accession.
etymology: Ultimately from Latin accessiō(n), from accēdō (English accede). Cognate to French accession. First attested in 1646.

definition: Praise vociferously.
example: A highly-acclaimed novel.
etymology: * First attested in the early 14th century. * (to applaud): First attested in the 1630s. * Borrowed from Latin acclāmō (“raise a cry at; applaud”), formed from ad- + clāmō (“cry out, shout”).

definition: Helpful in bringing about a harmonious adaptation.
example: The warden was always accommodating in allowing visitors in.
etymology: From accommodate + -ing.

definition: Reflex changes in the eyes that enable an object to be focused on the retina.
A liability account showing how much is owed for goods and services purchased on credit.
A debtor's accounts of money they owe; normally arise from the purchase of products or services.
Get or gather together.
example: I am accumulating evidence for the man's unfaithfulness to his wife.
etymology: First attested c. 1487;

definition: Causing a dull and steady pain.
example: My aching head.

definition: Being or containing an acid; of a solution having an excess of hydrogen atoms (having a pH of less than 7).
example: An acidic solution.
etymology: From acid + -ic. Doublet of acidy.

definition: A hydrogen atom in an acid that forms a positive ion when the acid dissociates.
The state or quality of being recognized or acknowledged.
example: She seems to avoid much in the way of recognition or acknowledgement of feminist work prior to her own.

definition: (acoustics) A material, structure or object absorbing sound energy when sound waves collide with it, as opposed to reflecting the energy.
A modem that converts electrical signals to telephone tones and back again.
An acquired response that is under the control of (conditional on the occurrence of) a stimulus.
Declared not guilty of a specific offense or crime; legally blameless.
example: He stands acquitted on all charges.

definition: A word formed from the initial letters of the several words in the name and pronounced as one word.
example: The word ‘scuba’ is an acronym for s(elf)-c(ontained) u(nderwater) b(reathing) a(pparatus).
etymology: Borrowed from German Akronym (from Ancient Greek ἄκρον (ákron, “end; peak”) + ὄνυμα (ónuma, “name”)), modelled after Homonym and Synonym, first attested in German in the early 1900s and in English in 1940.

definition: Polymerized from acrylonitrile.
example: When it comes to painting, I prefer using acrylics as my medium.
etymology: From acryl + -ic, from acrolein, from Latin acer (“sharp”) + olere (“to smell”).

definition: An unsaturated liquid carboxylic acid used in the manufacture of acrylic resins.
Polymerized from acrylonitrile.
Used especially by artists.
Powdered or granular carbon used for purifying by adsorption; given orally (as a slurry) it is an antidote for some kinds of poisons.
Causing motion or action or change.
(mineral extraction) a surface-active chemical used in flotation process to increase the attraction to a specific mineral.
A placebo used in experimental tests of a drug that has noticeable side effects.
example: An active placebo mimics the side effects of the experimental drug.

definition: The physical ouster of a tenant from the leased premises; the tenant is relieved of any further duty to pay rent.
Rapidly progressing leukemia.
Often improvised or impromptu.
example: An ad hoc committee meeting.
etymology: Learned borrowing from New Latin ad hoc (“to this, for this”).

definition: Impervious to pleas, persuasion, requests, reason.
example: He is adamant in his refusal to change his mind.
etymology: From Middle English adamant, adamaunt, from Latin adamantem, accusative singular form of adamās (“hard as steel”), from Ancient Greek ἀδάμαντ- (adámant-, “invincible”), oblique stem of ἀδάμας (adámas). Doublet of diamond.

definition: Having or showing knowledge and skill and aptitude.
example: Adept in handicrafts.
etymology: Borrowed from French adepte, from Latin adeptus (“who has achieved”), the past participle of adipisci (“to attain”).

definition: Faithful support for a cause or political party or religion.
example: Adherence to a fat-free diet.
etymology: From Middle French adhérence, from Latin adhærentia.

definition: Tending to adhere.
example: Adhesive material.
etymology: From French adhésif, from Medieval Latin adhaesivus, from adhaereō (supine adhaesum); see adhere.

definition: A substance that unites or bonds surfaces together.
A substance that unites or bonds surfaces together.
Tape coated with adhesive.
Of or relating to or functioning as an adjective.
example: Adjectival syntax.
etymology: From Middle English adjectif, adjective, from Old French adjectif, from Latin adiectivus, from adiciō + -īvus, from ad- (“to, towards, at”) + iaciō (“throw”).

definition: A hotel room that shares a wall with another hotel room.
Something added to another thing but not an essential part of it.
etymology: From Latin adiunctus, perfect passive participle of adiungō (“join to”), from ad + iungō (“join”). Doublet of adjoint.

definition: Inspiring admiration or approval.
example: Among her many admirable qualities are generosity and graciousness.
etymology: From Middle English admyrable, partly from Middle French admirable and partly from its etymon, Latin admirābilis. By surface analysis, admire + -able.

definition: The department in charge of the navy (as in Great Britain).
etymology: From French amirauté, for an older amiralté (“office of admiral”), from Late Latin admīrālitās. See admiral. Analyzable as admiral + -ty.

definition: The branch of international law that deals with territorial and international waters or with shipping or with ocean fishery etc.
Sun-dried brick; used in hot dry climates.
California herb with pinkish purple flowers.
The time period between the beginning of puberty and adulthood.
example: During adolescence, the body and mind go through many complex changes, some of which are difficult to deal with.
etymology: From Middle English adolescence, from Old French adolescence, from Latin adolēscentia, from adolēscēns (“young”); see adolescent.

definition: Regarded with deep or rapturous love (especially as if for a god).
example: Adored grandchildren.

definition: Provided with something intended to increase its beauty or distinction.
Giving an advantage.
example: A contract advantageous to our country.
etymology: From advantage + -ous or from Middle French avantageus (French avantageux). See advantage.

definition: Willing to undertake or seeking out new and daring enterprises.
example: Adventurous pioneers.
etymology: From Middle English aventurous, aunterous, auntrous, from Old French aventuros (whence French aventureux). By surface analysis, adventure + -ous.

definition: Someone who offers opposition.
example: He prepared to fight his adversary.
etymology: From Middle English adversarie, from Anglo-Norman aversaire (in Wace's Life of Saint Margaret) and Old French aversier, aversaire (French adversaire), from Latin adversārius, from adversus (“turned toward”).

definition: In an adverse manner.
example: She was adversely affected by the new regulations.
etymology: From adverse + -ly.

definition: Give heed (to).
example: To meditate, one must advert the mind toward the breath.
etymology: Clipping of advertisement.

definition: Someone whose business is advertising.
etymology: From advertise + -er.

definition: Worthy of being recommended or suggested; prudent or wise.
example: Such action is neither necessary nor advisable.
etymology: From advise + -able.

definition: A torpedo designed to be launched from an airplane.
(old-fashioned) at or from or to a great distance; far.
example: We traveled afar.
etymology: From Middle English afer, equivalent to a- (“for, on, or of”) + far.

definition: Having or displaying warmth or affection.
example: Affectionate children.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin affectiōnātus. By surface analysis, affection + -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Doublet of aficionado.

definition: Written declaration made under oath; a written statement sworn to be true before someone legally authorized to administer an oath.
example: He submitted his affidavit rather than appearing to testify in court.
etymology: From Medieval Latin affidavit (“he has sworn”), the third person singular perfect tense of affido (“swear”), from fīdō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeydʰ- (“to command, to persuade, to trust”).

definition: Any defensive pleading that affirms facts rather than merely denying the facts alleged by the plaintiff.
Grievously affected especially by disease.
An affluent person; a person who is financially well off.
example: The so-called emerging affluents.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French affluent, borrowed in turn from Latin affluentem, accusative singular of affluēns, present active participle of affluō (“flow to or towards;

definition: Aimlessly drifting.
example: A rubber duck and other toys were afloat in the bath.
etymology: From a- + float.

definition: (nautical, aeronautical) situated at or toward the stern or tail.
etymology: From Old English æftan (“behind”); possibly originally superlative of of (“off”). See after.

definition: Acquiring desirable qualities by being left undisturbed for some time.
Made more severe or intense especially in law.
example: Aggravated assault.

definition: Several things grouped together or considered as a whole.
etymology: From Latin aggregātiō, from aggregō (“aggregate”).

definition: Moving quickly and lightly.
example: Sleek and agile as a gymnast.
etymology: From earlier agil, borrowed from Latin agilis (“agile, nimble”), from agō (“do, act; move”). See agent.

definition: The gracefulness of a person or animal that is quick and nimble.
example: His superior agility countered his lack of strength.
etymology: From late Middle English, borrowed from Middle French agilité, from Latin agilitās, from agilis (“nimble, fleet, quick”), equivalent to agile + -ity.

definition: Troubled emotionally and usually deeply.
example: Agitated parents.

definition: A female newspaper columnist who answers questions and offers advice on personal problems to people who write in.
example: You should write in to the agony aunt; she'll sort it out for you.
etymology: From the much earlier British term agony column, initially used for personal columns and then for advice columns, and the informal use of aunt for any older female fictive kin.

definition: The utterance of a sound similar to clearing the throat; intended to get attention, express hesitancy, fill a pause, hide embarrassment, warn a friend, etc.
etymology: Onomatopoeic.

definition: Belonging to or on behalf of a specified person (especially yourself); preceded by a possessive.
example: ‘ain’ is Scottish.
etymology: From (Scots) Middle English aȝen.

definition: A compressor that takes in air at atmospheric pressure and delivers it at a higher pressure.
An appliance designed to extract humidity from the air and thereby cool it.
example: We rarely turn on the air-conditioner.

definition: A woman steward on an airplane.
Reconnaissance either by visual observation from the air or through the use of airborne sensors.
Someone who travels by airplane.
An appliance designed to extract humidity from the air and thereby cool it.
example: We rarely turn on the air-conditioner.

definition: A subsonic jet airliner operated over short distances.
etymology: From air + bus.

definition: A place where planes take off and land.
etymology: From air + field.

definition: The space in the atmosphere immediately above the earth.
example: The legalisation of free radios caused a bitter fight for airspace.
etymology: From air + space.

definition: Experiencing a sudden sense of danger.
example: This door is alarmed.

definition: Soluble in alcohol.
A liquor or brew containing alcohol as the active agent.
example: Alcohol (or drink) ruined him.

definition: Excessive use of alcohol and alcoholic drinks.
A name that has been assumed.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin alias (“at another time; at another place, elsewhere, under other circumstances, otherwise”). Doublet of else and allo-. See also alien and alter.

definition: Socially disoriented.
example: We live in an age of rootless alienated people.

definition: Relating to or containing an alkali; having a pH greater than 7.
example: Alkaline soils derived from chalk or limestone.
etymology: First attested in 1677. From alkali + -ine, ultimately from Arabic اَلْقِلْي (al-qily, “alkali, ashes of the saltwort”), related to قَلَى (qalā, “to roast in a pan, fry”).

definition: Broad in scope or content.
example: An all-embracing definition.
etymology: From all- + encompassing.

definition: Used of a radio receiver that is adaptable to all voltages.
example: An all-mains set.

definition: A versatile person who is expert at many things.
example: She's the best all-rounder they've seen in years.
etymology: From earlier all-round (“versatile”) + -er, sense “versatile person” from 1875.

definition: Leather made from alligator's hide.
A clip with a spring that closes the metal jaws.
etymology: From its resemblance to an alligator's jaws.

definition: Prolific South American aquatic weed having grasslike leaves and short spikes of white flowers; clogs waterways with dense floating masses.
Prolific South American aquatic weed having grasslike leaves and short spikes of white flowers; clogs waterways with dense floating masses.
Distribute according to a plan or set apart for a special purpose.
example: I am allocating a loaf of bread to everyone on a daily basis.
etymology: From Latin allocātus, perfect passive participle of Latin allocō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ad- (“to”) + locō. Doublet of allow. By surface analysis, al- + locate.

definition: Given as a task.
example: Her allotted chores.

definition: Very rich cookie containing ground almonds; usually crescent-shaped.
Very rich cookie containing ground almonds; usually crescent-shaped.
Flavoring made from almonds macerated in alcohol.
Old World willow with light green leaves cultivated for use in basketry.
Having almond-shaped eyes.
Shaped like an almond.
etymology: From almond + shaped.

definition: An event that occurs when something passes from one state or phase to another.
example: The doctors don't see any alteration in the patient's condition.
etymology: From Old French alteracion (French altération), from Medieval Latin alterātiō. Morphologically alter + -ation.

definition: An electric current that reverses direction sinusoidally.
A white crystalline double sulfate of aluminum: the ammonium double sulfate of aluminum.
etymology: From Middle English alum, alym, alyme, from Anglo-Norman alum, alun, from Latin alūmen.

definition: Foil made of aluminum.
Any of various forms of aluminum oxide occurring naturally as corundum.
A chloride used as a wood preservative or catalyst.
An expression whose meaning cannot be determined from its context.
example: His speech was made with such great ambiguity that neither supporter nor opponent could be certain of his true position.
etymology: From Middle English ambiguite, from Old French ambiguite (French ambiguïté), from Latin ambiguitas, equivalent to ambiguous + -ity.

definition: A sum of money paid in compensation for loss or injury.
example: Amends were made for the damage and no charges were filed.
etymology: From French amendes, plural of amende. Compare with amende.

definition: A plastic (synthetic resin) made from amino compounds; used as an adhesive and as a coating for paper and textiles.
An independent ruler or chieftain (especially in Africa or Arabia).
etymology: From Arabic أَمِير (ʔamīr, “commander, prince”). Doublet of Amir, emir, admiral, and amira.

definition: A water solution of ammonia.
example: Never use ammonia to clean metal writing pens.
etymology: From Latin sal ammoniacus (“salt of Amun, ammonium chloride”), named so because it was found near the temple of (Jupiter) Ammon in Egypt. Ammon derives from Ancient Greek Ἄμμων (Ámmōn), from Egyptian jmn (i-mn:n-A4).

definition: An atomic clock based on vibrational frequency of the nitrogen atom in the ammonia molecule.
A water solution of ammonia.
Partial or total loss of memory.
example: A state of cultural amnesia.
etymology: From modified Latin amnesia, from Ancient Greek ἀμνησία (amnēsía, “forgetfulness”), a noun derivation from μιμνήσκω (mimnḗskō, “to remind, to remember”) prefixed with the alpha privative.

definition: Electronic equipment that increases strength of signals passing through it.
etymology: From amplify + -er.

definition: The level on a scale of amplitude.
An arcade featuring coin-operated game machines.
Similar or equivalent in some respects though otherwise dissimilar.
example: Brains and computers are often considered analogous.
etymology: From Latin analogus, from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓νᾰ́λογος (ănắlogos); Its English equivalent is analogue + -ous. The application to similar features of organisms is nearly as old as the general sense.

definition: Of a circuit or device having an output that is proportional to the input.
example: Analogue device.
etymology: Equivalent to ana- (“functionally similar”) + -logue. See analog.

definition: A computer that represents information by variable quantities (e.g., positions or voltages).
Consider in detail and subject to an analysis in order to discover essential features or meaning.
example: Analyze a sonnet by Shakespeare.

definition: Using or subjected to a methodology using algebra and calculus.
example: Analytic statics.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἀναλυτικός (analutikós).

definition: The abstract separation of a whole into its constituent parts in order to study the parts and their relations.
An advocate of anarchism.
etymology: From French anarchiste, from Ancient Greek ἀναρχία (anarkhía) from the roots ἀν- (an-, “without”) + ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “rule”), equivalent to anarchy + -ist.

definition: Someone from whom you are descended (but usually more remote than a grandparent).
example: This fossil animal is regarded as the ancestor of the horse.
etymology: From Middle English ancestre, auncestre, ancessour; the first forms from Old French ancestre (modern French ancêtre), from the Latin nominative antecessor (“one who goes before”);

definition: Worship of ancestors.
Inherited or inheritable by established rules (usually legal rules) of descent.
example: Ancestral home.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman ancestrel, from ancestre (“ancestor”), equivalent to ancestor + -al.

definition: A fee for anchoring.
example: Anchorage is five pounds a night outside the harbour.
etymology: From anchor + -age.

definition: Place for vessels to anchor.
Loss of bodily sensation with or without loss of consciousness.
etymology: Sense of “insensibility” attested since 1679, from New Latin anaesthēsia, from Ancient Greek ἀναισθησία (anaisthēsía, “without sensation”), from ἀν- (an-, “not”) and αἴσθησις (aísthēsis, “sensation”).

definition: Marked by extreme anger.
Forming or set at an angle.
example: Angled parking.

definition: With anger.
example: He angrily denied the accusation.
etymology: From Middle English angrily, equivalent to angry + -ly.

definition: An acute but unspecific feeling of anxiety; usually reserved for philosophical anxiety about the world or about personal freedom.
etymology: Borrowed from German Angst or Danish angst; attested since the 19th century in English translations of the works of Søren Kierkegaard.

definition: Extreme mental distress.
example: It took years to overcome the anguish from my wife's death.
etymology: From Middle English angwischen, anguis(s)en, from Old French angoissier, anguissier, from the noun (see Etymology 1).

definition: (physics) the rate of change of the angular velocity of a rotating body.
The terminal branch of the facial artery.
The angular separation between two objects as perceived by an observer.
example: He recorded angular distances between the stars.

definition: The product of the momentum of a rotating body and its distance from the axis of rotation.
example: Any rotating body has an angular momentum about its center of mass.

definition: A shape having one or more sharp angles.
A short vein formed by the supraorbital vein and the supratrochlear vein and continuing as the facial vein.
(physics) the rate of change of the angular position of a rotating body; usually expressed in radians per second or radians per minute.
Pigment occurring in animals.
One form in which body fuel is stored; stored primarily in the liver and broken down into glucose when needed by the body.
A toxin resembling bacterial toxins in its antigenic properties that is found in the fluids of certain animals.
Reports of the work of a society or learned body etc.
example: Annals of Science.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French annales, from Latin annālēs librī (“chronicles”), from annālis (“pertaining to a year”), from annus (“year”) + librī, plural of liber (“book”). Compare with annual.

definition: Cause annoyance in; disturb, especially by minor irritations.
example: Marc loved his sister, but when she annoyed him he wanted to switch her off.
etymology: From Middle English anoyen, from Old French anoier (“to bother, disturb”), from Late Latin inodiāre (“to make loathsome”), derived from Latin odium (“loathing, hatred”). Displaced native Old English dreċċan, gremman.

definition: The psychological state of being irritated or annoyed.
example: Having to wait 45 minutes for the bus is a real annoyance, but it's the only way to get to work.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English anoyaunce (rare form of noyaunce), from Old French anuiance, anoiance, from the verb anuier (“to cause problems”), equivalent to annoy + -ance. Compare French ennui.

definition: Small short-lived fern of Central and South America.
Income from capital investment paid in a series of regular payments.
example: His retirement fund was set up to be paid as an annuity.
etymology: From French annuité, from Medieval Latin annuitās, from Latin annuus (“annual”). Cf. annuality.

definition: Deviation from the normal or common order or form or rule.
example: He is an anomaly among his friends in that he's the only one who's unmarried.
etymology: From Latin anomalia, from Ancient Greek ἀνωμαλία (anōmalía, “irregularity, anomaly”), from ἀνώμαλος (anṓmalos, “irregular, uneven”), negating the meaning of ὁμαλός (homalós, “even”), from ὁμός (homós, “same”).

definition: At another time.
example: Ever and anon.
etymology: From Middle English anoon, anon, anan (literally “in one (moment)”), from on (“in”) + ān (“one”). See on and one.

definition: Without giving a name.
example: She wrote these letters anonymously.
etymology: From anonymous + -ly.

definition: Someone who offers opposition.
example: A flexor, which bends a part, is the antagonist of an extensor, which extends it.
etymology: From Latin antagonista, from Ancient Greek ἀνταγωνιστής (antagōnistḗs, “opponent”) (ἀντί (antí, “against”) + ἀγωνιστής (agōnistḗs, “a combatant, pleader, actor”)), from ἀνταγωνίζομαι (antagōnízomai, “to antagonize”).

definition: (poker) the initial contribution that each player makes to the pot.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin ante (“before”). Doublet of and.

definition: Cancel or discharge a debt.
One of the two roots of a spinal nerve that passes ventrally from the spinal cord and that consists of motor fibers.
One of the two roots of a spinal nerve that passes ventrally from the spinal cord and that consists of motor fibers.
A large subgenre of trance music, named for the feeling which listeners claim to get (often described as a ‘rush’).
A collection of selected literary passages.
A remedy that stops or controls the effects of a poison.
The historic period preceding the Middle Ages in Europe.
example: Cicero was an eloquent orator of antiquity.
etymology: From Middle English antiquyte, antiquite, antiquytee, a borrowing from Old French antiquité, antiquitet, from Latin antiquitas, from antiquus. Equivalent to antique + -ity. See antique, antic.

definition: Of laws and regulations; designed to protect trade and commerce from unfair business practices.
example: The regulators used antitrust laws to block the merger, believing it would eliminate competition.
etymology: From anti- + trust.

definition: A legal action brought against parties who are charged with limiting free competition in the market place.
Law intended to promote free competition in the market place by outlawing monopolies.
Law intended to promote free competition in the market place by outlawing monopolies.
A form of hysteria having features of both conversion disorder and anxiety neurosis.
Used to indicate that a statement explains or supports a previous statement.
example: Anyhow, he is dead now.
etymology: From any + how.

definition: Hypothetical organism formerly thought to be intermediate between apes and human beings.
A device that controls amount of light admitted.
example: An aperture in a wall.
etymology: From late Middle English, from Latin apertūra (“an opening”), from aperiō (“to uncover, make or lay bare”) + -tūra (“-ure”, action noun suffix). Doublet of overture and apertura.

definition: Prophetic of devastation or ultimate doom.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin apocalypticus, from Ancient Greek ἀποκαλυπτικός (apokaluptikós, “revelatory”), from ἀποκάλυψις (apokálupsis, “revelation”), from ἀποκαλύπτω (apokalúptō, “to reveal, uncover”).

definition: An ardent early supporter of a cause or reform.
example: An apostle of revolution.
etymology: From Middle English apostle, from Old French apostle, from Late Latin apostolus, from Ancient Greek ἀπόστολος (apóstolos, “one sent forth, apostle”). Merged with Old English apostol, borrowing from the same Latin source.

definition: Causing consternation.
example: Appalling conditions.
etymology: By surface analysis, appall + -ing.

definition: Of or relating to or taking account of appeals (usually legal appeals).
example: Appellate court.
etymology: From Latin appellātus.

definition: A court whose jurisdiction is to review decisions of lower courts or agencies.
Clap one's hands or shout after performances to indicate approval.
example: After the performance, the audience applauded for five minutes.
etymology: From Middle English applauden, from Latin applaudere (“to clap the hands together, applaud”), from ad (“to”) + plaudere (“to strike, clap”).

definition: A small open pie filled with sliced apples and sugar.
Smelling of apples.
A device or control that is very useful for a particular job.
example: Many house fires are caused by faulty appliances, such as refrigerators, washing machines and dryers.
etymology: Recorded since the 1560s. From the English apply + -ance.

definition: The classification of someone or something with respect to its worth.
etymology: From appraise + -al.

definition: The costs that are incurred in assessing that products/services conform to the requirements.
example: Some example component items of the total appraisal costs are: field testing, test and inspection equipment, and quality audits.

definition: Fully understood or grasped.
example: Dangers not yet appreciated.

definition: The position of apprentice.
etymology: From apprentice + -ship.

definition: Money set aside (as by a legislature) for a specific purpose.
etymology: From Middle English appropriacion, appropriacioun, from Medieval Latin appropriātiō. By surface analysis, appropriate + -ion.

definition: A legislative act proposing to authorize the expenditure of public funds for a specified purpose.
Expressing or manifesting praise or approval.
example: Approbative criticism.

definition: An approximate calculation of quantity or degree or worth.
etymology: From approximate + -ion.

definition: A garment of cloth or leather or plastic that is tied about the waist and worn to protect your clothing.
example: She tied an apron around her waist before cooking dinner.
etymology: Rebracketing of napron (a napron → an apron), from Middle English naperoun, napron, apron, from Old French napperon, diminutive of nappe (“tablecloth”), from Latin mappa (“napkin”).

definition: (usually used in the plural) a cord used to tie an apron at the waist.
example: Tied to someone's apron strings.

definition: A shade of blue tinged with green.
etymology: From Middle English aqua (“water”), borrowed from Latin aqua. Perhaps also a learned borrowing directly from Latin. Doublet of ea, Eau, eau, and yeo.

definition: Tree (as opposed to shrub).
etymology: From Middle English arbour, erbour, from Old French erbier (“field, meadow, kitchen garden”), from erbe (“grass, herb”), from Latin herba (“grass, herb”) (English herb).

definition: So extremely old as seeming to belong to an earlier period.
example: Archaic laws.

definition: A group of many islands in a large body of water.
example: The Gulag Archipelago.
etymology: The noun is borrowed from Italian arcipelago (“Aegean Sea;

definition: Of or relating to or contained in or serving as an archive.
example: Archival boxes archival paper.
etymology: The adjective is derived from archive (“place for storing earlier, and often historical, material; material so kept, considered as a whole”, noun) + -al (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives).

definition: Subarctic perennial poppy of both hemispheres having fragrant white or yellow to orange or peach flowers.
Characterized by intense emotion.
example: Ardent love.
etymology: First attested circa 14th century as Middle English ardaunt, borrowed from Anglo-Norman ardent and Old French ardant, from Latin ardentem, accusative of ardēns, present participle of ardeō (“to burn”).

definition: An elaborate song for solo voice.
etymology: From Italian aria, metathesis from Latin āerem, accusative of āēr, from Ancient Greek ἀήρ (aḗr, “air”). Doublet of air.

definition: Lacking sufficient water or rainfall.
example: An arid climate.
etymology: From French aride or directly from Latin āridus (“dry, arid, parched”), compare its synonymous contracted form ardus. Originally from the verb āreo (“to be dry, to be parched”), akin to ārdeō (“to be on fire, to burn”).

definition: Relating to or involving arithmetic.
example: Arithmetical computations.
etymology: From French arithmétique, from Latin arithmēticus, from Ancient Greek ἀριθμητῐκός (arithmētĭkós).

definition: The sum of the values of a random variable divided by the number of values.
A mathematical operation involving numbers.
(mathematics) a progression in which a constant is added to each term in order to obtain the next term.
example: 1-4-7-10-13- is the start of an arithmetic progression.

definition: Persuasion by the use of direct personal pressure.
example: Some gentle arm-twisting produced the desired result.
etymology: From arm + twisting.

definition: A squire carrying the armor of a knight.
Covered with heavy steel.
example: Armor-plated vehicles.

definition: Covered with heavy steel.
example: Armor-plated vehicles.
etymology: From armor + plated.

definition: Dinosaurs having bony armour.
Covered with heavy steel.
Covered with heavy steel.
Used of animals; provided with protective covering.
example: The armoured vehicles rolled into the city.

definition: An armor-plated truck with strong doors and locks used to transport money or valuables.
A vehicle that is protected by armor plate.
The child of a career officer of the United States Army.
(chemistry) of or relating to or containing one or more benzene rings.
example: An aromatic organic compound.
etymology: Late Middle English, from Middle French and Old French aromatique, from Late Latin aromaticus, from Ancient Greek ἄρωμα (árōma, “seasoning, spicy and/or fragrant smell”).

definition: A hydrocarbon containing one or more benzene rings that are characteristic of the benzene series of compounds.
Aroused to action.
example: The aroused opposition.

definition: Malicious burning to destroy property.
example: The British term for arson is ‘fire-raising’.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman and Old French arson, from the verb ardoir, from Latin ardeō (“to burn”). Compare ardent.

definition: A style of design that was popular in the 1920s and 1930s; marked by stylized forms and geometric designs adapted to mass production.
Of or involving or contained in the arteries.
example: Arterial disease.
etymology: From artery + -al.

definition: A major or main route.
Consisting of segments held together by joints.
A ladder consisting of segments (usually four) that are held together by joints that can lock in place.
An additive to food intended to improve its flavor or appearance or shelf-life.
Not according to nature; not by natural means.
example: Artificially induced conditions.
etymology: From artificial + -ly.

definition: Moving or going or growing upward.
example: The ascending plane.
etymology: From ascend + -ing.

definition: A movement upward; rise above the ground.
example: The ascension of the hot-air balloon gave us a better view.
etymology: From Middle English ascencioun, from Old French ascension, from Latin ascēnsiō, ascēnsiōnem (“ascent”). Displaced native Old English upfæreld.

definition: An upward slope or grade (as in a road).
example: He made a tedious ascent of Mont Blanc.
etymology: Formed from ascend on the model of descend/descent.

definition: Establish after a calculation, investigation, experiment, survey, or study.
example: As soon as we ascertain what the situation is, we can plan how to proceed.
etymology: From Middle English acerteynen, from Old French acertener, from a- (“to, towards”) + certener (“make sure of”), from the adjective certain, from Latin certus (“certain, fixed”). Compare to Spanish acertar.

definition: Plant whose succulent young shoots are cooked and eaten as a vegetable.
etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin asparagus, sparagus, from Ancient Greek ἀσπάραγος (aspáragos), variant of ἀσφάραγος (aspháragos). Displaced Old English eorþnafola. Later became an eggcorn in dialect as sparrowgrass.

definition: Any of several trees of the genus Populus having leaves on flattened stalks so that they flutter in the lightest wind.
example: Above a certain elevation, the aspens gave way to scrubby, gnarled pines.
etymology: From Middle English aspen, corresponding to asp + -en.

definition: A will to succeed.
example: Riley has an aspiration to become a doctor.
etymology: From aspire + -ation.

definition: Have an ambitious plan or a lofty goal.
example: To aspire to / for / after / to do something; to aspire that something happens.
etymology: From Middle English aspiren, from Old French aspirer, from Latin aspīrō (“breathe on; approach; desire”).

definition: The acetylated derivative of salicylic acid; used as an analgesic anti-inflammatory drug (trade names Bayer, Empirin, and St. Joseph) usually taken in tablet form; used as an antipyretic; slows clotting of the blood by poisoning platelets.
A powdered form of aspirin.
An appraisal of the state of affairs.
example: They made an assay of the contents.
etymology: From Middle English assay (noun) and assayen (verb), from Anglo-Norman assai (noun) and Anglo-Norman assaier (verb), from Old French essai. Doublet of essay.

definition: A mark on an article of trade to indicate its origin and authenticity.
The act of gathering something together.
Put oneself forward in an assertive and insistent manner.
Relating to the use of or having the nature of a declaration.
The act of distributing something to designated places or persons.
example: The first task is the assignment of an address to each datum.

definition: Consisting of a haphazard assortment of different kinds.
example: An arrangement of assorted spring flowers.

definition: A collection containing a variety of sorts of things.
example: A great assortment of cars was on display.
etymology: From assort + -ment.

definition: Filled with the emotional impact of overwhelming surprise or shock.
example: I stood enthralled, astonished by the vastness and majesty of the cathedral.

definition: Bewildering or striking dumb with wonder.
example: Astounding success an astounding spectacle.

definition: A pseudoscience claiming divination by the positions of the planets and sun and moon.
example: Followers of pseudosciences such as astrology often draw spurious parallels between their beliefs and established science.

definition: Relating or belonging to the science of astronomy.
example: Astronomic telescope.
etymology: Attested since at least 1550, from Middle French astronomique or directly from Latin astronomicus, from Ancient Greek ἀστρονομικός (astronomikós).

definition: Any telescope designed to collect and record electromagnetic radiation from cosmic sources.
The time for the earth to make one revolution around the sun, measured between two vernal equinoxes.
Not in accord.
example: Desires at variance with his duty.

definition: A lack of belief in the existence of God or gods.
etymology: 16th century Middle French athéisme, from athée (“atheist”), a loan from Ancient Greek ἄθεος (átheos, “godless”, from ἀ- (a-, “without”) + θεός (theós, “deity, god”)). First English attestation dates to 1587 (OED).

definition: A sock worn for athletic events.
Giant saturniid moth widespread in Asia; sometimes cultured for silk.
(often followed by ‘to’) giving care or attention.
example: Attentive to details.
etymology: From Middle English attentif, attentijf, from Old French attentif.

definition: Provide evidence for; stand as proof of; show by one's behavior, attitude, or external attributes.
example: His high fever attested to his illness.
etymology: PIE word *tréyes Borrowed from Middle French attester, from Latin attestor (“to witness to, bear witness”), from at-, combining form of ad (“to”) + testor (“to bear witness”), from testis (“a witness”).

definition: Clothing of a distinctive style or for a particular occasion.
example: Formal attire.
etymology: The verb is from Middle English atyren, atiren, from Old French atirier (“to equip”), from a- + tire (“rank”), akin to German Zier (“ornament”) and Old Norse tírr (“glory, renown”).

definition: Anything on your premises that might attract children into danger or harm.
example: Their swimming pool is an attractive nuisance; they should fence it in.

definition: The quality of arousing interest; being attractive or something that attracts.
example: Her personality held a strange attraction for him.
etymology: From attractive + -ness.

definition: Capable of being attributed.
example: The collapse of the movement was attributable to a lack of morale.
etymology: From attribute + -able.

definition: Assigning some quality or character to a person or thing.
example: The attribution of language to birds.
etymology: From Middle French attribution, from Latin attributio.

definition: Fearless daring.
example: The brash private had the audacity to criticize the general.
etymology: From Middle English audacite, from Medieval Latin audācitās (whence -acity), from Latin audāx (“bold”), from audeō (“to be bold, to dare”).

definition: Heard or perceptible by the ear.
example: He spoke in an audible whisper.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French audible, from Late Latin audibilis, from Latin audire (“to hear”).

definition: An amplifier that increases the amplitude of reproduced sound.
Someone who listens attentively.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman auditour, from Latin audītor (“hearer, auditor”).

definition: Of or relating to the process of hearing.
example: Auditory processing.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin audītōrius (“pertaining to a hearer or hearing”), from audiō (“to hear”) + -tōrius (“-tory”, adjectival suffix).

definition: The cortical area that receives auditory information from the medial geniculate body.
The part of the brain (in a fold of the cerebral cortex of the temporal lobe on both sides of the brain) that receives impulses from the ear by way of the auditory nerve.
The ability to hear; the auditory faculty.
The sensory system for hearing.
The sister of your father or mother; the wife of your uncle.
etymology: From aunt + -ie.

definition: The trait of great self-denial (especially refraining from worldly pleasures).
etymology: From Ancient Greek αὐστηρότης (austērótēs, “bitter, harsh”). Morphologically austere + -ity.

definition: Endowed with authority.
example: An authoritative communique.
etymology: From authorit(y) + -ative.

definition: Grant authorization or clearance for.
example: The rock star never authorized this slanderous biography.
etymology: See author about the orthography with ⟨h⟩. Doublet of octroy.

definition: An automatic mechanical device on a record player that causes new records to be played without manual intervention.
Something written by one's own hand.
example: Some autograph-hunters were pestering the players after the game.
etymology: From Latin autographum, in turn from Ancient Greek αὐτόγραφον (autógraphon, “a writing in one’s own hand”). Equivalent to auto- + -graph.

definition: An album for autographs.
A computer program for automatically moderating an online forum or discussion.
An unattended machine (outside some banks) that dispenses money when a personal coded card is used.
An unattended machine (outside some banks) that dispenses money when a personal coded card is used.
A toaster into which bread slices are inserted vertically into the slots and pop up after the toasting cycle is complete.
A home appliance for washing clothes and linens automatically.
Of plants that bloom during the autumn.
Of plants that bloom during the autumn.
(nautical) an extra boiler (as a ship's boiler that is used while the ship is in port).
A verb that combines with another verb in a verb phrase to help form tense, mood, voice, or condition of the verb it combines with.
A slide of large masses of snow and ice and mud down a mountain.
Perennial herb having large white flowers marked with orange; found near the snow line in the northwestern United States.
Take revenge for a perceived wrong.
example: He wants to avenge the murder of his brother.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English avengen, borrowed from Old French avengier, from a- + vengier.

definition: The average of the absolute deviations from a central point and a summary statistic of statistical dispersion or variability.
A feeling of intense dislike.
example: Due to her aversion to the outdoors she complained throughout the entire camping trip.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin āversiō, āversiōnem. Doublet of aversio.

definition: A pear-shaped tropical fruit with green or blackish skin and rich yellowish pulp enclosing a single large seed.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin American Spanish avocado, from the earlier aguacate, which comes from Classical Nahuatl āhuacatl (“avocado”). Doublet of abacate. Compare aguacatillo, avocadillo.

definition: Tropical American tree bearing large pulpy green fruits.
Cause to become awake or conscious.
example: Each morning he awakens with a smile on his face.
etymology: From Middle English awakenen or awaknen, from Old English awæcnan or awæcnian, from a- plus wæcnan or wæcnian.

definition: Aroused or activated.
example: An awakened interest in ballet.

definition: A grant made by a law court.
example: He criticized the awarding of compensation by the court.

definition: Used as intensifiers.
example: I'm awful sorry.
etymology: From awful + -ly.

definition: In an awkward manner.
example: He bent awkwardly.
etymology: From awkward + -ly.

definition: The handle of an ax.
The cutting head of an ax.
A shaft on which a wheel rotates.
example: The mechanic replaced the broken axle on the truck.
etymology: From Middle English axil, in turn a combination of Old English eax and Old Norse ǫxull.

definition: An iron bar that serves as an axletree.
A thick heavy grease used to lubricate axles.
Of a deep somewhat purplish blue color similar to that of a clear October sky.
etymology: From Middle English asure, from Old French azur, derived from Arabic لَازَوَرْد (lāzaward, “lapis lazuli”), dropping the l as if it were equivalent to the French article l'.

definition: A member of the baby boom generation in the 1950s.
example: They expanded the schools for a generation of baby boomers.
etymology: From baby + boomer, or from baby boom + -er, when there was a marked increase in birthrates throughout the Western world following the return of servicemen at the end of World War II.

definition: A small vehicle with four wheels in which a baby or child is pushed around.
A person born in the generation following the baby boom when the birth rate fell dramatically.
etymology: From baby bust + -er, following baby boomer.

definition: (phonetics) Any vowel sound produced in the back of the mouth.
example: Examples of back vowels include ‘u’ in ‘rule’ and ‘o’ in ‘pole’.

definition: The Cyrillic letter Ъ/ъ, which in modern languages serves to denote a hard (non-palatalized) consonant.
example: The final yer appears to be a back yer, but several corrections to this letter have been made.

definition: A film of mucus and bacteria deposited on the teeth that encourages the development of dental caries.
A check that is dishonored on presentation because of insufficient funds.
example: Issuing a bad check is a form of larceny.

definition: Annoy persistently.
example: He kept badgering her about her bad habits.
etymology: From Middle English bageard (“marked by a badge”), from bage (“badge”), referring to the animal's badge-like white blaze, equivalent to badge + -ard. Displaced earlier brock, from Old English brocc.

definition: Small long-bodied short-legged German breed of dog having a short sleek coat and long drooping ears; suited for following game into burrows.
etymology: From badger + dog, a calque of German Dachshund (from their use in hunting badgers).

definition: A game played on a court with light long-handled rackets used to volley a shuttlecock over a net.
etymology: Named after Badminton House, an estate in Gloucestershire owned by the Duke of Beaufort, where the game was first played in England. For the house name, see Badminton.

definition: The court on which badminton is played.
Equipment for playing the game of badminton.
Perplexed by many conflicting situations or statements; filled with bewilderment.
example: She looked completely baffled by the puzzle.

definition: An attendant who takes care of baggage.
A cheek-rouging cosmetic made by baking colored liquid on terra cotta tiles.
example: Baked blush is considered to give a more long-lasting and vibrant effect than a traditional pressed powder formula.

definition: Molds or pans used to make baked items that come in a variety of shapes and sizes.
Feathery fern of tropical Asia and Malaysia.
A narrative song with a recurrent refrain.
etymology: From French ballade, from Old Occitan ballada (“poem for a dance”), from Late Latin ballare. Doublet of balada and ballade.

definition: A composer of words or music for popular songs.
Relating to or characteristic of the motion of objects moving under their own momentum and the force of gravity.
example: Ballistic missile.

definition: A craft capable of traveling in outer space; technically, a satellite around the sun.
A missile that is guided in the first part of its flight but falls freely as it approaches target.
etymology: From ballistic + missile.

definition: A facility in which ball games are played (especially baseball games).
example: Take me out to the ballpark.
etymology: From ball + park. Sense 2 related to ballpark figure.

definition: Any of a variety of social dances performed by couples in a ballroom.
Any of various aromatic resinous substances used for healing and soothing.
example: Classical music is a sweet balm for our sorrows.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English bawme, borrowed from Anglo-Norman and Middle French baume, from Old French basme, from Latin balsamum, itself from Ancient Greek βάλσαμον (bálsamon). Spelling modified 16th c.

definition: A dark, very strong lager, fermented at cooler temperatures.
example: The late 1990s saw to the re-launch of Baltic porters by several German breweries.

definition: An ideological barrier around communist China especially in the 1950s and 1960s.
A popular trend that attracts growing support.
example: When they saw how things were going everybody jumped on the bandwagon.
etymology: From band + wagon.

definition: The phenomenon of a popular trend attracting even greater popularity.
example: In periods of high merger activity there is a bandwagon effect with more and more firms seeking to engage in takeover activity.
etymology: bandwagon + effect

definition: A metal pipe filled with explosive, used to detonate land mines or to clear a path through barbed wire.
A stringed instrument of the guitar family that has long neck and circular body.
etymology: From the pronunciation of African slaves, of unknown ultimate origin. Possibly a corruption of bandore (from Spanish bandurria), alternatively from a West African language such as Mandinka banjul, or Kimbundu mbanza.

definition: A robber of banks.
Light teasing repartee.
etymology: 1670s as verb, 1680s as noun. The origin is unknown, possibly from London street slang; ostensibly as *bant + -er (frequentative suffix).

definition: Having undergone the Christian ritual of baptism.
An aggressive remark directed at a person like a missile and intended to have a telling effect.
example: To trade barbs.
etymology: PIE word *bʰardʰéh₂ From Middle English barbe, from Middle French barbe, from Old French barbe (“beard, beard-like element”). Doublet of beard.

definition: Tropical American shrub bearing edible acid red fruit resembling cherries.
Without civilizing influences.
example: Barbarian invaders.

definition: An elongated, two-pronged fork used to lift and turn food while being cooked as in the case of barbecue.
Capable of wounding.
example: A barbed compliment.

definition: A lyric poet.
example: Shakespeare is known as the bard of Avon.
etymology: First use appears c. 1449. From Scottish Gaelic bàrd, from Old Irish bard, from Proto-Celtic *bardos (“bard, poet”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷerH- (“praise”), and reinforced by Latin bardus, borrowed from Celtic.

definition: Without shoes.
example: The barefoot boy.
etymology: From Middle English barefote, barfot, from Old English bærfōt (“barefoot”), from Proto-West Germanic *baʀafōt, from Proto-Germanic *bazafōts (“barefoot”) equivalent to bare + foot.

definition: A long pole used to propel or guide a barge.
example: I wouldn't touch it with a barge pole.

definition: Small beetle that bores tunnels in the bark and wood of trees; related to weevils.
Small Asian deer with small antlers and a cry like a bark.
Of southwest United States and Mexico; call is like a dog's bark.
A grain of barley.
A brittle transparent candy made by melting and cooling cane sugar.
European annual grass often found as a weed in waste ground especially along roadsides and hedgerows.
Broth used to feed infants.
A brittle transparent candy made by melting and cooling cane sugar.
A noblewoman who holds the rank of baron or who is the wife or widow of a baron.
etymology: From Middle English baronesse; equivalent to baron + -ess.

definition: Having elaborate symmetrical ornamentation.
example: The building … frantically baroque.
etymology: Via French baroque (which originally meant a pearl of irregular shape), from Portuguese barroco (“irregular pearl”);

definition: The rapid and continuous delivery of linguistic communication (spoken or written).
example: A barrage of questions.
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French barrage (“barrage, barrier”) c. 1859. Compare barrier.

definition: An elongated tethered balloon or blimp with cables or net suspended from it to deter enemy planes that are flying low.
The heavy fire of artillery to saturate an area rather than hit a specific target.
example: They laid down a barrage in front of the advancing troops.

definition: Jam an entire frequency spectrum.
example: During the Cold War, the Soviets routinely barrage jammed to interfere with transmissions from the West.

definition: A cactus of the genus Ferocactus: unbranched barrel-shaped cactus having deep ribs with numerous spines and usually large funnel-shaped flowers followed by dry fruits.
Providing no shelter or sustenance.
example: Barren lands.
etymology: From Middle English bareyne, from Anglo-Norman baraigne, baraing (“sterile; barren”), of obscure origin; probably from a Germanic language, perhaps Frankish *baʀ (“bare; barren”), from Proto-Germanic *bazaz (“bare”).

definition: The act of excluding someone by a negative vote or veto.
A British or Canadian lawyer who speaks in the higher courts of law on behalf of either the defense or prosecution.
etymology: From bar (a collective term for lawyers or the legal profession) and the suffix -ster.

definition: The quantity that a barrow will hold.
etymology: From Middle English barow, bareȝ, bareh, from Old English bearg, bearh (“boar”), from Proto-West Germanic *barug, *barah, from Proto-Germanic *barugaz, *barahaz.

definition: A male hawker of fruit and vegetables from a barrow.
A female hawker of fruit and vegetables from a barrow.
A male hawker of fruit and vegetables from a barrow.
A female hawker of fruit and vegetables from a barrow.
Juicy yellow pear.
Especially of leaves; located at the base of a plant or stem; especially arising directly from the root or rootstock or a root-like stem.
example: Basal placentation.
etymology: From base + -al.

definition: The amount of energy required to maintain the body of an individual in a resting state.
Body temperature in the morning before rising or moving about or eating anything.
A large vein passing along the medial surface of the temporal lobe and emptying into the great cerebral vein.
The handwear used by fielders in playing baseball.
etymology: From baseball + mitt.

definition: Perennial herb of the eastern United States having inconspicuous greenish flowers and narrow leaves that are very aromatic when bruised.
A cloth woven of two or more threads interlaced to suggest the weave of a basket.
Horizontal circular metal hoop supporting a net through which players try to throw the basketball.
Largest and lowest member of the violin family.
A group that defends a principle.
example: A bastion against corruption.
etymology: First attested in 1562. From French bastion, from Old French bastille (“fortress”).

definition: A fortification composed of many projecting triangular bastions (usually from five to eight), specifically designed to cover each other; first seen in the mid-15th century in Italy.
A mitt made of coarse fiber used to wash and scrub the body.
A preparation that softens or scents a bath.
A relatively large open container that you fill with water and use to wash the body.
A relatively large open container that you fill with water and use to wash the body.
example: I had a long, leisurely soak in the bathtub.
etymology: From bath + tub.

definition: Homemade gin especially that made illegally.
(baseball) a male ballplayer who is batting.
etymology: From bat + -s- + -man.

definition: Fried in batter.
Damaged by blows or hard usage.
example: A battered old car.
etymology: From batter + -ed.

definition: A glove worn by batters in baseball to give a firmer grip on the bat.
Scarred by battle.
Evergreen aromatic shrubby tree of southeastern United States having small hard berries thickly coated with white wax used for candles.
(antiquity) a wreath of laurel foliage worn on the head as an emblem of victory.
A shop where a variety of goods are sold.
etymology: From Middle French bazar or Italian bazar, from Ottoman Turkish بازار (bazar), from Persian بازار (bâzâr).

definition: A recreational vehicle with large tires used on beaches or sand dunes.
Small amphipod crustaceans that hop like fleas; common on ocean beaches.
Plant having hemispherical heads of wine-red flowers; found in coastal dunes from California to Mexico.
A small ball with a hole through the middle.
example: Holonym: prayer beads.

definition: Small tree of West Indies and northeastern Venezuela having large oblong pointed leaflets and panicles of purple flowers; seeds are black or scarlet with black spots.
etymology: Since its seeds are used as beads. Compare Unami manshapiàkw (literally “bead tree”).

definition: Beaklike mouth of animals other than birds (e.g., turtles).
example: Shut your beak!
etymology: Unknown; originally cant; first recorded in 17thC; probably related to obsolete cant beck "constable".

definition: Introduced into the United States from Mexico; feeds on the foliage of the bean plant.
A young bear.
Almond-flavored yeast-raised pastry shaped in an irregular semicircle resembling a bear's claw.
Having hair on the cheeks and chin.
example: Bearded mussel.
etymology: From Middle English berded, either from Old English ġebearded or formed anew in Middle English; by surface analysis, beard + -ed.

definition: Medium-sized greyish to yellow seal with bristles each side of muzzle; of the Arctic Ocean.
Someone whose employment involves carrying something.
A bond issued with detachable coupons that must be presented to the issuer for interest payments.
A stock that contains no ownership information and whose physical bearer is presumed to be the owner.
example: Bearer shares are banned in some countries, because of their potential for abuse.

definition: A stock that contains no ownership information and whose physical bearer is presumed to be the owner.
example: Bearer shares are banned in some countries, because of their potential for abuse.

definition: A rein designed to keep the horse's head in the desired position.
A shop where hairdressers and beauticians work.
The soft brown fur of the beaver.
Coverings that are used on a bed.
etymology: From Middle English bedding, beddyng, from Old English bedding (“bedding”), equivalent to bed + -ing.

definition: Material used to provide a bed for animals.
An ornamental plant suitable for planting in a flowerbed.
Solid unweathered rock lying beneath surface deposits of soil.
example: If culture is the bedrock of a society, then language is the cornerstone of culture.
etymology: From bed (“a layer on top of which something else rests.”) + rock.

definition: Manner or conduct of a physician in the presence of a patient.
etymology: From bedside + manner, from the fact that doctors and nurses usually stand or sit at the bedsides of their patients when speaking to them.

definition: European beetle; infests beehives.
Colorful chiefly tropical Old World bird having a strong graceful flight; feeds on especially bees.
Moth whose larvae live in and feed on bee honeycombs.
Any of several large deciduous trees with rounded spreading crowns and smooth grey bark and small sweet edible triangular nuts enclosed in burs; north temperate regions.
etymology: From Middle English beche, from Old English bēċe, from Proto-West Germanic *bōkijā (“beech”). Doublet of buky. Related to English book.

definition: Chiefly monoecious trees and shrubs: beeches, chestnuts, oaks; genera Castanea, Castanopsis, Chrysolepis, Fagus, Lithocarpus, Nothofagus, Quercus.
Any of several large deciduous trees with rounded spreading crowns and smooth grey bark and small sweet edible triangular nuts enclosed in burs; north temperate regions.
A stock made with beef.
A stew made with beef.
Make a strident noise.
example: The motorists in the traffic jam were getting more and more frustrated and started beeping their horns.
etymology: Onomatopoeic.

definition: Of or relating to behavior.
example: Behavioral sciences.
etymology: From behaviour + -al.

definition: Of a light greyish-brown color.
Capable of being believed.
example: Believable answer.
etymology: From Middle English bilevable, beleevable, equivalent to believe + -able.

definition: A foundry where bells are cast.
(used in the plural) trousers with legs that flare; worn by sailors; absurdly wide hems were fashionable in the 1960s.
A dive in which the abdomen bears the main force of impact with the water.
Dive so that one hits the water with one's belly.
The buckle used to fasten a belt.
A clamp used to hold work in place on a workbench.
Diagonal line traversing a shield from the upper right corner to the lower left.
A mark of bastardy; lines from top right to bottom left.
Pain resulting from rapid change in pressure.
The recipient of funds or other benefits.
etymology: From Latin beneficiarius (“enjoying a favor, granted a privilege”) from beneficium (“benefit”), perhaps via or influenced by French bénéficiaire (“beneficiary”).

definition: Intending or showing kindness.
example: A benevolent society.
etymology: From Old French benevolent, borrowed from Latin benevolēns ("benevolent"). Displaced native Old English welwillende (literally well-wishing).

definition: A tumor that is not cancerous.
A large mass of ice floating at sea; usually broken off of a polar glacier.
etymology: Clipping of iceberg.

definition: A job in an organization.
etymology: The noun is derived from Late Middle English birth (“(nautical) bearing away or off, clearance, berth”).

definition: Surrounded by hostile forces.
example: The besieged town.

definition: A book that has had a large and rapid sale.
Reveal unintentionally.
example: Her smile betrayed her true feelings.
etymology: From Middle English betrayen, bitrayen (“to commit an act of treason against”), equivalent to be- + tray (“to betray”).

definition: (formerly) a title of respect for a man in Turkey or Egypt.
example: He introduced me to Ahmet Bey.
etymology: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish بك (bey, “gentleman, chief”), from Old Anatolian Turkish بك (beg, “ruler”), from Proto-Turkic *bēg (“lord”). See there for more.

definition: Someone who makes an offer.
example: The highest bidder shall get the house.
etymology: From Middle English bidder, biddere, equivalent to bid + -er. Cognate with Saterland Frisian Bidder, German Bitter.

definition: Having a life cycle lasting two seasons.
example: A biennial life cycle.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin bienni(um) (“two-year period”) [from bis, bi- (“twice”) + annus (“year”)] + -al (suffix forming adjectives). By surface analysis, bi- + -ennial.

definition: The intolerance and prejudice of a bigot.
etymology: From French bigoterie, from bigot. By surface analysis, bigot + -ry.

definition: A person who rides a bicycle.
etymology: From bike + -er.

definition: Originally a British youth subculture that evolved out of the teddy boys in the 1960s; wore black leather jackets and jeans and boots; had greased hair and rode motorcycles and listened to rock'n'roll; were largely unskilled manual laborers.
The property of being symmetrical about a vertical plane.
A dictionary giving equivalent words in two languages.
Any notation that uses 2 characters (usually 0 and 1).
A machine that cuts grain and binds it in sheaves.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English byndere. By surface analysis, bind + -er.

definition: A cardboard used by bookbinders to make covers for books.
The organic chemistry of compounds and processes occurring in organisms; the effort to understand biology within the context of chemistry.
example: My aunt has a degree in biochemistry.
etymology: From bio- + chemistry.

definition: Of or relating to or being biography.
example: Biographical data.
etymology: From biography + -ical.

definition: (biology) a scientist who studies living organisms.
etymology: From biology + -ist.

definition: Plant materials and animal waste used as fuel.
etymology: From bio- (prefix denoting organic life) + mass (“matter, material”).

definition: Relating to the activities and applications of science to clinical medicine.
example: Biomedical research laboratory.
etymology: From bio- + medical.

definition: The application of the principles of the natural sciences to medicine.
Examination of tissues or liquids from the living body to determine the existence or cause of a disease.
example: We will need to perform a biopsy to determine whether the tumour is malignant or benign.
etymology: From French biopsie, from bi- + -opsy.

definition: The branch of molecular biology that studies the use of microorganisms to perform specific industrial processes.
example: Biotechnology produced genetically altered bacteria that solved the problem.
etymology: From bio- + technology.

definition: Supported by both sides.
example: A bipartisan bill.
etymology: From bi- + partisan.

definition: A canoe made with the bark of a birch tree.
Carbonated drink containing an extract from bark of birch trees.
A liquid ester with a strong odor of wintergreen; applied externally for minor muscle and joint pain.
A switch consisting of a twig or a bundle of twigs from a birch tree; used to hit people as punishment.
example: My father never spared the birch.

definition: Any betulaceous tree or shrub of the genus Betula having a thin peeling bark.
etymology: From birch + tree.

definition: An outdoor device that supplies food for wild birds.
etymology: From bird + feeder.

definition: (golf) a score of one stroke under par on a hole.
example: Aw, that's a cute little birdie. Is it a budgie?
etymology: From bird + -ie.

definition: The place where someone was born.
example: Portsmouth was Charles Dickens’ birthplace.
etymology: From birth + place.

definition: Small round bread leavened with baking-powder or soda.
etymology: PIE word *dwóh₁ Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ ▲ Proto-Indo-European *trísinflu.

definition: Almond trees having white blossoms and poisonous nuts yielding an oil used for flavoring and for medicinal purposes.
Any of several spiny shrubs of the genus Daviesia having yellow flowers and triangular seeds; Australia.
Hydrated magnesium sulfate that is taken orally to treat heartburn and constipation and injected to prevent seizures.
With bitterness; in a resentful manner.
example: She complained bitterly.
etymology: From Middle English bitterli, biterli, biterliche, from Old English biterlīċe, bitterlīċe (“bitterly”), equivalent to bitter + -ly.

definition: A feeling of deep and bitter anger and ill-will.
example: The bitterness of his words.
etymology: From Middle English bitternesse, biternesse, from Old English biternes (“bitterness; grief”), equivalent to bitter + -ness.

definition: Your occupation or line of work.
example: She's in show biz.

definition: Erect shrub with small if any spines having racemes of white to yellow flowers followed by curved pointed pods and black shiny seeds; West Indies and Florida.
New Zealand forest tree.
A mixture of calomel and limewater that is used on syphilitic sores.
Blackish racer of the eastern United States that grows to six feet.
Small spruce of boggy areas of northeastern North America having spreading branches with dense foliage; inferior wood.
Garden plant whose capsule discloses when ripe a mass of seeds resembling a blackberry.
Exert pressure on someone through threats.
example: He blackmailed a businesswoman by threatening to expose an alleged fraud.
etymology: From black + mail (“a piece of money”). Compare Middle English blak rente (“a type of blackmail levied by Irish chieftains”).

definition: A smith who forges and shapes iron with a hammer and anvil.
etymology: From black (color of forged iron) + smith (related to smite).

definition: Encysted saclike larva of the tapeworm.
A diet of foods that are not irritating.
example: He ate a bland diet because of his colitis.

definition: A check that has been signed but with the amount payable left blank.
A revolver that makes the sound of gunfire but does not fire bullets.
Blasphemous language (expressing disrespect for God or for something sacred).
example: That imam said that drawing the prophet Muhammad was a form of blasphemy.
etymology: From Middle English blasfemie, from Old French blasfemie, from Ecclesiastical Latin blasphēmia, from Ancient Greek βλασφημία (blasphēmía, “profanity”), from βλασφημέω (blasphēméō, “to slander”).

definition: Expletives used informally as intensifiers.
example: He's a blasted idiot.

definition: Without any attempt at concealment; completely obvious.
example: Blatant disregard of the law.
etymology: Coined by Edmund Spenser in 1596 in "blatant beast". Probably a variation of *blatand (Scots blaitand (“bleating”)), present participle of blate, a variation of bleat, equivalent to blate + -ant. See bleat.

definition: Shining intensely.
example: The blazing sun.

definition: Biennial of southwestern United States having white stems and toothed leaves that is grown for its large pale yellow flowers that open in early morning.
A solution containing bleaching agents that is used to bleach textiles or paper pulp.
Offering little or no hope.
example: Prospects were bleak.
etymology: From Middle English bleke (“small river fish, bleak, blay”), perhaps an alteration (due to Old English blǣc (“bright”) or Old Norse bleikja) of Old English blǣġe (“bleak, blay, gudgeon”);

definition: Mixture of two or more whiskeys or of a whiskey and neutral spirits.
Mixture of two or more whiskeys or of a whiskey and neutral spirits.
An electrically powered mixer with whirling blades that mix or chop or liquefy foods.
etymology: From blend + -er.

definition: The act of blending components together thoroughly.
example: Blendings of old and new.
etymology: From Middle English blendinge, equivalent to blend + -ing.

definition: An axle which turns but does not communicate motion.
Deprived of sight.
example: Blinded by perinatal vertical transmission of gonorrhea.

definition: Without seeing or looking.
example: He felt around his desk blindly.
etymology: From Middle English blindly, blyndly, from Old English blindlīċe (“in a blind manner; blindly; rashly”), equivalent to blind + -ly. Cognate with Swedish blindligt (“blindly”), Icelandic blindlega (“blindly”).

definition: Closing the eyes intermittently and rapidly.
example: He stood blinking in the bright sunlight.

definition: Abnormally distended especially by fluids or gas.
example: Hungry children with bloated stomachs.

definition: Anesthesia of an area supplied by a nerve; produced by an anesthetic agent applied to the nerve.
A ship that runs through or around a naval blockade.
A large bomb used to demolish extensive areas (as a city block).
example: He was watching the blockbuster film series Harry Potter.
etymology: From block + buster, referring originally to aerial bombs capable of destroying a whole block of buildings.

definition: Informal intensifiers.
etymology: By surface analysis, bloom + -ing.

definition: A top worn by women.
A device that produces a current of air.
example: Get on the blower and call headquarters right away!
etymology: From Middle English blowere, blower, from Old English blāwere; equivalent to blow + -er.

definition: A large catfish of the Mississippi valley.
Any of several plants of the genus Trichostema having whorls of small blue flowers.
Famous orchid of northern India having large pale to deep lilac-blue flowers.
Bluish-green blacksnake found from Ohio to Texas.
Widely distributed European titmouse with bright cobalt blue wings and tail and crown of the head.
Rare form of dichromacy characterized by a lowered sensitivity to blue light resulting in an inability to distinguish blue and yellow.
Belonging to or characteristic of the nobility or aristocracy.
example: The blue-blooded aristocracy.
etymology: From blue blood + -ed.

definition: Any of numerous shrubs of the genus Vaccinium bearing blueberries.
etymology: From blue + berry.

definition: Any of numerous shrubs of the genus Vaccinium bearing blueberries.
Pie containing blueberries and sugar.
Tall herb of eastern North America and Asia having blue berrylike fruit and a thick knotty rootstock formerly used medicinally.
Something intended as a guide for making something else.
example: A blueprint for a house.
etymology: From blue + print. Introduced by Sir John Herschel in 1842.

definition: Sensitized paper used to make blueprints.
Indistinct or hazy in outline.
example: A landscape of blurred outlines.
etymology: From blur + -ed.

definition: Indistinct or hazy in outline.
example: A landscape of blurred outlines.
etymology: From blur + -y.

definition: Old World wild swine having a narrow body and prominent tusks from which most domestic swine come; introduced in United States.
etymology: From Middle English bor, boor, from Old English bār, from Proto-West Germanic *bair.

definition: A walkway made of wooden boards; usually at seaside.
etymology: From board + walk.

definition: Speaking of yourself in superlatives.
A short light oar used without an oarlock to propel a canoe or small boat.
Water travel for pleasure.
etymology: From boat + -ing.

definition: Proof that a boater has taken and passed an approved boater education course.
example: A boating license or boater education card is required in most states in order to operate a motorized vessel.

definition: Having a body or a body of a specified kind; often used in combination.
example: Strong-bodied.
etymology: From body + -ed.

definition: (anatomy) a natural hollow or sinus within the body.
Lotion applied to the body after bathing.
Malodorousness resulting from a failure to bathe.
A one-piece tight-fitting undergarment for women that covers the torso (and may have sleeves and legs).
Someone who escorts and protects a prominent person.
etymology: From body + guard.

definition: Cause to slow down or get stuck.
example: The vote would bog down the house.
etymology: Uncertain, although possibly related to bug in its original senses of "big" and "puffed up".

definition: Get stuck while doing something.
example: She bogged down many times while she wrote her dissertation.

definition: A semiaquatic plant that grows in soft wet land; most are monocots: sedge, sphagnum, grasses, cattails, etc.; possibly heath.
A bog orchid with usually a solitary fragrant magenta pink blossom with a wide gaping corolla; Canada.
Poorly drained soils on top of peat and under marsh or swamp vegetation.
Plant having ovate leaves in a basal rosette and white starlike flowers netted with green.
Fraudulent; having a misleading appearance.
example: He was arrested for trying to cash a bogus check at the bank.
etymology: First attested as an underworld term for an apparatus for creating counterfeit coins, then the coins themselves. Later, the word was applied to anything of poor quality.

definition: A loose protective coverall or smock worn over ordinary clothing for dirty work.
With boldness, in a bold manner.
example: We must tackle these tasks boldly.
etymology: From Middle English boldely, boldeliche, baldeliche, from Old English bealdlīċe (“boldly, earnestly”), equivalent to bold + -ly.

definition: Large smooth-textured smoked sausage of beef and veal and pork.
etymology: From the Italian city of Bologna.

definition: Support and strengthen.
example: Bolster morale.
etymology: From Middle English bolster, bolstre, from Old English bolster (“pillow”), from Proto-West Germanic *bolstr, from Proto-Germanic *bulstraz (“pillow, cushion”).

definition: Support and strengthen.
example: Bolster morale.

definition: The rapid and continuous delivery of linguistic communication (spoken or written).
example: A bombardment of mail complaining about his mistake.
etymology: From bombard + -ment.

definition: An organized expression of goodwill at the start of a trip or new venture.
etymology: Borrowed from French bon voyage (“bon voyage, (have a) good journey”), from bon (“good”) + voyage (“journey”).

definition: Black substance containing char in the form of carbonized bone; used as a black pigment.
The fatty network of connective tissue that fills the cavities of bones.
A large outdoor fire that is lighted as a signal or in celebration.
etymology: PIE word *péh₂wr̥ From Middle English bonnefyre (“a fire in which bones are burnt, bonfire”) [and other forms], by surface analysis, bone + fire.

definition: A hat tied under the chin.
Indian macaque with a bonnet-like tuft of hair.
Small harmless hammerhead having a spade-shaped head; abundant in bays and estuaries.
Being very thin.
example: Pale bony hands.
etymology: From Middle English bony, equivalent to bone + -y.

definition: Minute arachnid sometimes found in old papers.
A shop where books are sold.
etymology: From book + store.

definition: Very lively and profitable.
example: The power of China's booming economy continues to stun the world.

definition: Very close and convivial.
example: Boon companions.
