etymology: From Middle English boon (“prayer”), from Old Norse bón (“prayer, petition”), from Proto-Germanic *bōniz (“supplication”), influenced by boon (“good, favorable”, adjective). Doublet of ben; see there for more.

definition: An additional dose that makes sure the first dose was effective.
The first stage of a multistage rocket.
Of questionable or minimal quality.
example: Borderline grades.
etymology: From border + line.

definition: The feeling of being bored by something tedious.
example: See more citations at boredoms.
etymology: From bore + -dom.

definition: Someone who receives something on the promise to return it or its equivalent.
example: A library borrower’s card.
etymology: From Middle English borower, borewer, borwere, equivalent to borrow + -er (agent suffix).

definition: Of or relating to plants or botany.
example: Botanical garden.
etymology: From botany + -ical.

definition: A facility where trees and shrubs are cultivated for exhibition.
The use of plants or plant extracts for medicinal purposes (especially plants that are not part of the normal diet).
All the plant life in a particular region or period.
example: The botany of China.
etymology: First attested in 1696: Back-formation from botanic.

definition: Hydrocarbon gases, usually propane or butane, kept under pressure.
Drinking water (often spring water) that is put into bottles and offered for sale.
A slow kind of alcoholic fermentation at a temperature low enough that the yeast cells can sink to the bottom of the fermenting liquid; used in the production of lager.
A scavenger that feeds low on the food chain.
An antipersonnel land mine.
An interval that includes its endpoints.
An arrangement of flowers that is usually given as a present.
example: For my birthday I received two bouquets.
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French bouquet, from Old French bochet, from bois, from Early Medieval Latin boscus (“grove”), borrowed from Frankish *busk, from Proto-Germanic *buskaz. Doublet of bosket.

definition: An archaic term for a boundary.
etymology: From Middle French borne, from Old French bodne, from Medieval Latin bodina, a word of unknown ultimate origin, but possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bʰudʰmḗn (“bottom, base”), see also Proto-Celtic *bundos.

definition: Of a stringed instrument; sounded by stroking with a bow.
example: A bowed instrument.

definition: Heavily burdened with work or cares.
example: Bowed down with troubles.

definition: A meat chopping machine used for food processing, including mixing, particle reduction and emulsifying.
A cricketer who delivers the ball to the batsman in cricket.
etymology: From bowl + -er.

definition: A felt hat that is round and hard with a narrow brim.
etymology: From the name of the hatmakers Thomas and William Bowler, associated with early production.

definition: A male person who is expert in the use of a bow and arrow.
etymology: From Middle English boweman, bouman, boughman, equivalent to bow + -man.

definition: Chiefly terrestrial turtle of North America; shell can be closed tightly.
A wrench with a closed loop (a socket) that fits over a nut or bolt head.
Enclosed in or set off by a border or box.
example: Boxed sections of the report.

definition: Enclosed in or as if in a box.
example: Boxed cigars.

definition: Enclosed in or as if in a box.
example: Boxed cigars.

definition: Underpants worn by men.
An appliance that corrects dental irregularities.
example: Susy has to go to the dentist to see if she needs braces.

definition: A woody fungus that forms shelflike sporophores on tree trunks and wood structures.
Exceptionally good.
example: His brag cornfield.
etymology: From Middle English braggen (“to make a loud noise; to speak boastfully”) of uncertain origin. Possibly related to the Middle English adjective brag (“prideful; spirited”), which is probably of Celtic origin;

definition: Exhibiting self-importance.
A tumor in the brain.
Exhaustion that affects mental keenness.
A difficult problem.
Subjected to intensive forced indoctrination resulting in the rejection of old beliefs and acceptance of new ones.
example: Brainwashed prisoners of war.

definition: Foot pedal that moves a piston in the master brake cylinder.
Broken husks of the seeds of cereal grains that are separated from the flour by sifting.
etymology: From a Celtic source; compare Welsh brân and Cornish bran.

definition: Conspicuously new.
A globular glass with a small top; used for serving brandy.
Enlargement of the nose with dilation of follicles and redness and prominent vascularity of the skin; often associated with excessive consumption of alcohol.
In a courageous manner.
example: Bravely he went into the burning house.
etymology: From brave + -ly.

definition: Braying characteristic of donkeys.
example: Whenever I walked by, that donkey brayed at me.
etymology: The verb is derived from Middle English brayen, brai, bray, braye (“of a person or animal: to vocalize loudly; of the weather: to make a loud sound, howl, roar”), from Old French brai, braire (“of an animal: to bray;

definition: The capacity to understand a broad range of topics.
example: A teacher must have a breadth of knowledge of the subject.
etymology: From Middle English bredthe, alteration (due to nouns ending in -th: length, strength, wrength, etc.) of brede ("breadth"; see bread). Equivalent to broad + -th (abstract nominal suffix).

definition: Ratio (in percent) of the maximum breadth to the maximum length of a skull.
Waves breaking on the shore.
etymology: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

definition: An escape from jail.
example: The breakout was carefully planned.
etymology: Deverbal from break out. The video game genre is named after Breakout, the first game of this kind, released in 1976 by Atari.

definition: Small dark geese that breed in the north and migrate southward.
etymology: The first word is perhaps from branded, meaning brindled.

definition: The practice of offering something (usually money) in order to gain an illicit advantage.
example: Accept bribery.
etymology: From bribe + -ery.

definition: A gown worn by the bride at a wedding.
(used in the plural) short tight-fitting underpants (trade name Jockey shorts).
Two-masted sailing vessel square-rigged on both masts.
etymology: Abbreviated from brigantine, from Italian brigantino; in sense “jail”, from the use of such ships as prisons.

definition: A general officer ranking below a major general.
etymology: Borrowed from French brigadier. Equivalent to brigade + -ier.

definition: A general officer ranking below a major general.
Make more cheerful through the use of color.
example: The paint will brighten the room.
etymology: From bright + -en.

definition: With brightness.
example: The windows glowed jewel bright.
etymology: From Middle English brightliche, from Old English beorhtlice, equivalent to bright + -ly.

definition: Having a bright color.
Having a bright color.
A light within the field of vision that is brighter than the brightness to which the eyes are adapted.
example: What brilliance it took from Harry Kane to control the cross and place the ball into the top corner.
etymology: From brilliant + -ance. Compare French brillance.

definition: A code name for a small computerized heat-seeking missile that was supposed to intercept and destroy enemy missiles.
With brightness.
example: The stars shone brilliantly.
etymology: From brilliant + -ly.

definition: Having little elasticity; hence easily cracked or fractured or snapped.
example: Brittle bones.
etymology: From Middle English britel, brutel, brotel (“brittle”), from Old English *brytel, *bryttol (“brittle, fragile”, literally “prone to or tending to break”); equivalent to brit + -le.

definition: Fragrant rounded shrub of southwestern United States and adjacent Mexico having brittle stems and small crowded blue-green leaves and yellow flowers; produces a resin used in incense and varnish and in folk medicine.
An animal resembling a starfish with fragile whiplike arms radiating from a small central disc.
etymology: From brittle + star.

definition: An animal resembling a starfish with fragile whiplike arms radiating from a small central disc.
Make broader.
example: Broaden the road.
etymology: From broad + -en (verbal suffix).

definition: A small book usually having a paper cover.
example: Have a look in the Acme brochure for a new vacuum cleaner.
etymology: 1748, from French brochure (“stitched work”), from brocher (“to stitch”), from Old French brochier (“to pierce”), from broche (“awl”), from Vulgar Latin brocca, from Latin broccus (“pointy-toothed”). Doublet of broach.

definition: A stock broker's business; charges a fee to act as intermediary between buyer and seller.
etymology: From broker + -age.

definition: A fund that a customer has entrusted to a securities brokerage.
example: You can't get a brokerage account unless you have $20,000.

definition: A stock broker's business; charges a fee to act as intermediary between buyer and seller.
Place where a broker conducts their business.
Think moodily or anxiously about something.
example: In some species of birds, both the mother and father brood the eggs.
etymology: From Middle English brood, brod, from Old English brōd (“brood; foetus; breeding, hatching”), from Proto-Germanic *brōduz (“heat, breeding”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreh₁- (“breath, mist, vapour, steam”).

definition: A delicious freshwater food fish.
A cleaning implement for sweeping; bundle of straws or twigs attached to a long handle.
A small room for storing brooms and other cleaning equipment.
etymology: By analogy with closet, and due to the association of witchcraft with brooms.

definition: Any of several grasses of the genus Andropogon; used in broom making.
The handle of a broom.
Small palm of southern Florida and West Indies closely resembling the silvertop palmetto.
Prickly yellow-flowered shrub of the moors of New England and Europe.
Annual of southwestern United States having rigid woody branches with sticky foliage and yellow flowers.
Cooking to a brown crispiness over a fire or on a grill.
example: Proper toasting should brown both sides of a piece of bread.

definition: Combination of breakfast and lunch; usually served in late morning.
etymology: Blend of breakfast + lunch. Attested from 1895 in British English and from 1930 in the United States.

definition: A woman's short housecoat or wrapper.
Marked by dark or relatively dark pigmentation of hair or skin or eyes.
example: A brunette beauty.
etymology: Borrowed from French brunette, the feminine form of brunet, from brun (“brown”). Doublet of burnet.

definition: Any of various small or medium-sized kangaroos; often brightly colored.
A textile machine that is used in the finishing process to improve the appearance of fabric.
A cruelly rapacious person.
example: One of them was a hulking brute of a man, heavily tattooed and with a hardened face that practically screamed "I just got out of jail.".
etymology: From Middle French brut, from Old French brut, from Latin brūtus (“dull, stupid, insensible”), an Oscan loanword, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷréh₂us (“heavy”).

definition: Beginning to develop.
example: A budding genius.

definition: Having a buff color.
Having a buff color.
Low-growing annual herb of southwestern United States (Texas) having silky foliage and blue flowers; a leading cause of livestock poisoning in the southwestern United States.
Informal or slang terms for mentally irregular.
example: This software is so buggy that I don't know how anyone can use it!
etymology: From bug + -y.

definition: The act of building up an accumulation.
example: I envied his rapid buildup of assets.

definition: Of large size for its weight.
etymology: From Middle English bulki, boulky, equivalent to bulk + -y.

definition: Largest and lowest member of the violin family.
Attack viciously and ferociously.
etymology: From bull + dog, in reference to bullbaiting.

definition: Any of the large fierce Australian ants of the genus Myrmecia.
A clip with a spring that closes the metal jaws.
etymology: Possibly a reference to the tenacity of a bulldog’s bite. Regarding sense 1 (“binder clip with rigid handles”), Bulldog was originally a trademark registered to Brandsley Limited in the United Kingdom in 1944.

definition: Without flaws or loopholes.
example: A bulletproof argument.
etymology: From bullet + -proof.

definition: Young bull.
etymology: From Middle English bullok, from Old English bulluc, from Proto-West Germanic *bulluk, corresponding to bull + -ock (diminutive suffix). Compare Old Dutch bullok (“bullock”).

definition: A pulley-block at the head of a topmast.
Small tropical American tree bearing a bristly heart-shaped acid tropical fruit.
A place on a baseball field where relief pitchers can warm up during a game.
example: Magnus and Big Dick are over in the bullpen, ready for tonight's rodeo.
etymology: From bull + pen.

definition: Dressed warmly.
example: Bundled-up sailors and soldiers.

definition: A small house with a single story.
A long trough for feeding cattle.
example: Jane sleeps in the top bunk, and her little sister Lauren takes the bottom bunk.
etymology: Sense of sleeping berth possibly from Scottish Scottish English bunker (“seat, bench”), the origin of which is uncertain but possibly Scandinavian (North Germanic);

definition: Beds built one above the other.
example: He had dibs on the top bunk bed.
etymology: From bunk + bed.

definition: Go to bed.
example: We can bunk down in that room.

definition: Play truant from work or school.
Defensiveness resulting from repeated attacks.
example: After so many suicide bombings the Israelis have to resist developing a bunker mentality.

definition: The fleshy part of the human body that you sit on.
Of or relating to or resembling a bureaucrat or bureaucracy.
example: His bureaucratic behavior annoyed his colleagues.
etymology: Borrowed from French bureaucratique, from bureaucrate (“bureaucrat”) or bureaucratie (“bureaucracy”) + -ique (“-ic”), equivalent to bureaucrat + -ic or bureau + -cratic.

definition: Needlessly time-consuming procedure.
A thief who enters a building with intent to steal.
example: The burglar made off with a large diamond from the museum.

definition: A loud warning signal produced by a burglar alarm.
example: They could hear the burglar alarm a mile away.

definition: Entering a building unlawfully with intent to commit a felony or to steal valuable property.
etymology: From New Latin burglaria. By surface analysis, burglar + -y. Displaced native Old English hūsbryċe (literally “house-breach”).

definition: A dark purplish-red to blackish-red color.
etymology: 1881, from attributive use of Burgundy (“wine from Burgundy”) from Burgundy wine, from Burgundy (“region of France”) + wine.

definition: (archeology) a heap of earth placed over prehistoric tombs.
Seed vessel having hooks or prickles.
example: You left a bunch of burrs on those parts yesterday. You've already been told not to miss the deburring operation.
etymology: From Middle English burre, perhaps related to Old English byrst (“bristle”). Cognate with Danish burre, borre (“burdock, burr”), Swedish borre (“sea-urchin”).

definition: A high speed drill that dentists use to cut into teeth.
Medium to large deciduous oak of central and eastern North America with ovoid acorns deeply immersed in large fringed cups; yields tough close-grained wood.
Having a head of straight hair cut very short (hence bristly).
A quantity of explosive to be set off at one time.
A high explosive that is used to damage the target that is under attack.
Concealing something under the ground.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English biryinge, buryinge; by surface analysis, bury + ing.

definition: A tract of land used for burials.
Shrubby or herbaceous plants widely used for forage, soil improvement, and especially hay in southern United States.
Any of various plants of the genus Thermopsis having trifoliate leaves and yellow or purple racemose flowers.
Active grey titmice of western North America.
Tax write-off for expenses of doing business.
An informal form of address for a man.
example: Hey buster, what's up?
etymology: Originally a dialectal variant of burster; later influenced by bust + -er.

definition: Used of men; markedly masculine in appearance or manner.
etymology: Originally, it was probably used as an abbreviation of butcher. Later, in the 1940s, the sense of “masculine lesbian” developed.

definition: A hinge mortised flush into the edge of the door and jamb.
A butt joint that is welded.
Creating a butt joint by welding.
A butt joint that is welded.
Creating a butt joint by welding.
Vine of tropical Asia having pinnate leaves and bright blue flowers with yellow centers.
Fern of New Zealand and Australia having trailing fronds with dark green buttonlike leaflets.
A push button at an outer door that gives a ringing or buzzing signal when pushed.
In an experimental fashion.
White butterfly whose larvae (cabbageworms) feed on cabbage.
Low-growing fan-leaved palm of coastal southern United States having edible leaf buds.
example: It isn't bad when we come back; we notice little similarities to our dreaming places. The cabbage palms, the fire pit, the family.

definition: A large motorboat that has a cabin and plumbing and other conveniences necessary for living on board.
Any succulent plant of the family Cactaceae native chiefly to arid regions of the New World and usually having spines.
Constituting the order Opuntiales.
Burrowing mouse of desert areas of southwestern United States.
Someone who is morally reprehensible.
etymology: Short for caddie, from Scots, from French cadet, from Occitan capdet (“chief, captain”), from Latin capitellum, diminutive of caput (“head”).

definition: A military trainee (as at a military academy).
example: A cadet branch of the family.
etymology: Borrowed from French cadet, from Gascon capdet, from Late Latin capitellum (“small head”). Attested in English from 1634. Doublet of caddie, cadeau, cadel, capital, capitellum, and caudillo.

definition: Small cup of strong black coffee without milk or cream.
Black coffee with Cognac and lemon peel and sugar.
A restaurant where you serve yourself and pay a cashier.
etymology: Borrowed from Mexican Spanish cafetería (“coffeehouse”), from cafetera (“coffee maker”), from French cafetière, from café, from Ottoman Turkish قهوه (kahve) (Turkish kahve), from Arabic قَهْوَة (qahwa, “coffee”).

definition: (usually plural) facilities for providing food for employees or visitors.
A tray for carrying your food in a cafeteria.
Someone addicted to caffeine.
Molds or pans used to make baked items that come in a variety of shapes and sizes.
A deliquescent salt; used in de-icing and as a drying agent.
A white crystalline oxide used in the production of calcium hydroxide.
A phosphate of calcium; a main constituent of animal bones.
The act of checking or adjusting (by comparison with a standard) the accuracy of a measuring instrument.
example: The thermometer needed calibration.
etymology: From calibrate + -ion. First attested in 1852.

definition: The act of appeasing (as by acceding to the demands of).
A camel cavalry used in the early modern era by Arab, Afghan, Persian, and Indian armies.
A viral disease caused by MERS-CoV that is typically transmitted from camels.
Engraving or carving in low relief on a stone (as in a brooch or ring).
etymology: Borrowed from Italian cammeo, from Medieval Latin camaeus, of unknown origin. The movie sense is short for “cameo role” referring to a famous person who was playing no character, but him or herself.

definition: A male photographer who operates a movie camera.
A jay of northern North America with black-capped head and no crest; noted for boldness in thievery.
Someone acting as an informer or decoy for the police.
etymology: From French canarie, from Spanish canario, from the Latin Canariae insulae (“Canary Islands”) (Spanish Islas Canarias);

definition: Any of several small Old World finches.
Canary Islands grass; seeds used as feed for caged birds.
A mixture of seeds used to feed caged birds.
A moderate yellow with a greenish tinge.
Having the color of a canary; of a light to moderate yellow.
Characterized by directness in manner or speech; without subtlety or evasion.
example: I gave them my candid opinion.

definition: A miniature camera with a fast lens.
etymology: Although used as its name, the term predates the long-running American television program Candid Camera (first broadcast in 1948).

definition: The campaign of a candidate to be elected.
etymology: From candid(ate) + -acy.

definition: Smelling of candy.
Of or relating to a pointed conical tooth.
etymology: From Latin canīnus (“of dogs, doglike, dogtooth”), from canis (“dog”). Compare French canin.

definition: One of the four pointed conical teeth (two in each jaw) located between the incisors and the premolars.
etymology: Calque of Latin dens canīnus (“doglike tooth”), from canis (“dog”), from their prominence in dogs and wolves. Compare dogtooth.

definition: A large firecracker.
Soldiers who are regarded as expendable in the face of artillery fire.
etymology: Mid-19th century, from cannon (“artillery piece”) + fodder (“food”), a calque of German Kanonenfutter, itself possibly a calque of English food for powder. See the German for more.

definition: Large valuable arborvitae of northwestern United States.
Appearing in a biblical canon.
example: A canonical book of the Christian New Testament.
etymology: From Middle English canonycal, from Medieval Latin canōnicālis. By surface analysis, canon + -ical.

definition: (Roman Catholic Church) one of seven specified times for prayer.
Draw advantages from.
example: He is capitalizing on her mistake.
etymology: From capital + -ize, the first element ultimately from Latin capitālis (“of the head”).

definition: Firm chewy candy made from caramelized sugar and butter and milk.
etymology: Borrowed from French caramel, from Spanish caramelo, from Portuguese caramelo, dissimilated from Late Latin calamellus, diminutive of calamus (“reed”) (and a doublet of chalumeau and shawm).

definition: An apple that is covered with a candy-like substance (usually caramelized sugar).
etymology: Compound of caramel + apple.

definition: Having the color of caramel; of a moderate yellow-brown.
An inn in some eastern countries with a large courtyard that provides accommodation for caravans.
An odorless very poisonous gas that is a product of incomplete combustion of carbon.
example: Carbon monoxide poisoning.

definition: A custodian who is hired to take care of something (property or a person).
example: Her dad was a cemetery caretaker for many years. There was a lot of landscaping work. The gravedigging itself was done with backhoes.
etymology: From care + taker.

definition: Small beetle whose larvae are household pests feeding on woolen fabrics.
A loom for weaving carpeting.
Larvae feed on carpets and other woolens.
A tack used to nail down carpets.
Creating carpets, both machine-made and hand-woven.
A wrench designed for use with carriage bolts.
Pudding made with grated carrots.
Tough elastic tissue; mostly converted to bone in adults.
etymology: Borrowed from French cartilage, from Latin cartilāgō. Partially displaced native gristle, from Old English gristel.

definition: An alloy of copper and zinc (containing about 30% zinc) that is wrought into cartridges or tubing.
Any font that is contained in a cartridge that can be plugged into a computer printer.
A fuse cased in a tube.
Form by carving.
example: Carve a flower from the ice.
etymology: From Middle English kerven, from Old English ceorfan, from Proto-West Germanic *kerban, from Proto-Germanic *kerbaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gerbʰ- (“to scratch”).

definition: Establish or create through painstaking effort.
example: She carved out a reputation among her male colleagues.

definition: Separate into parts or portions.
example: The British carved up the Ottoman Empire after World War I.

definition: Makes decorative wooden panels.
etymology: From Middle English carver, karvere, kerver, kervere, equivalent to carve + -er. Cognate with Scots kerver, carver, carvour (“carver”).

definition: A large fork used in carving cooked meat.
A large knife used to carve cooked meat.
A small waterfall or series of small waterfalls.
example: The bride carried a cascade of roses and baby's breath.
etymology: From French cascade, from Italian cascata, from cascare (“to fall”), from Vulgar Latin *cāsicāre, derived from Latin cadere, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱh₂d-.

definition: Rush down in big quantities, like a cascade.
The housing or outer covering of something.
example: Some people like to split the casing of a sausage before cooking so it doesn’t burst.

definition: A container that holds a magnetic tape used for recording or playing sound or video.
A tape deck for playing and recording cassette tapes.
Electronic equipment for playing cassettes.
A cassette that contains magnetic tape.
Tropical American thorny shrub or small tree; fragrant yellow flowers used in making perfumery.
etymology: From French cassie. Doublet of acacia.

definition: A burglar who unlawfully breaks into and enters another person's house.
example: The police were baffled by the exploits of a cat burglar who only stole from the upper floors of high-rise apartments.
etymology: From cat + burglar.

definition: A chemical reactor for converting oils with high boiling points into fuels with lower boiling points in the presence of a catalyst.
Flea that breeds chiefly on cats and dogs and rats.
Having concealed difficulty.
example: A catchy question.
etymology: From catch + -y.

definition: Arranged into categories.
example: All of my records are categorized.

definition: A wormlike and often brightly colored and hairy or spiny larva of a butterfly or moth.
example: The bird just ate that green caterpillar.
etymology: From Middle English catirpel, catirpeller, probably from Old Northern French catepeluse (Modern French chatte + pileuse (“hairy cat”)), from Late Latin catta + pilōsa.

definition: An endless metal belt on which tracked vehicles move over the ground.
Having caterpillar treads or tracks on the wheels.
example: A caterpillar-tracked earthmover.

definition: Flesh of scaleless food fish of the southern United States; often farmed.
etymology: From cat + fish. Likely so named for its prominent barbels like a cat's whiskers. Compare West Frisian katfisk (“catfish”), Dutch katvis (“catfish”). Compare also German Seekatze (“catfish”, literally “sea-cat”).

definition: Involving or constituting a cause; causing.
example: A causal relationship between scarcity and higher prices.
etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin causalis, from Latin causa (“cause”), equivalent to cause + -al, see cause.

definition: Any entity that produces an effect or is responsible for events or results.
Any entity that produces an effect or is responsible for events or results.
A determining or causal element or factor.
As if with kid gloves; with caution or prudence or tact.
example: She ventured cautiously downstairs.
etymology: From cautious + -ly.

definition: Widely cultivated herb with aromatic leaf stalks that are eaten raw or cooked.
etymology: From French céleri, from Lombard selleri, a plural of Latin selīnum, from Ancient Greek σέλῑνον (sélīnon). Displaced English march (“celery, smallage”) and smallage (“wild celery”).

definition: Australasian evergreen conifer having a graceful head of foliage resembling celery that is composed of phyllodes borne in the axils of scalelike leaves.
Grown for its thickened edible aromatic root.
Ground celery seed and salt.
Seed of the celery plant used as seasoning.
Celery stalks cut into small sticks.
A globe that is a spherical model of the heavens.
A method of controlling the flight of a missile or spacecraft by reference to the positions of celestial bodies.
The collective body of angels.
The great circle on the celestial sphere whose plane passes through the sensible horizon and the center of the Earth.
(astronomy) the angular distance of a celestial body north or to the south of the celestial equator; expressed in degrees; used with right ascension to specify positions on the celestial sphere.
The branch of astronomy concerned with the application of Newton's laws of motion to the motions of heavenly bodies.
Navigating according to the positions of the stars.
The (usually elliptical) path described by one celestial body in its revolution about another.
One of two points of intersection of the Earth's axis and the celestial sphere.
The apparent surface of the imaginary sphere on which celestial bodies appear to be projected.
A large stringed instrument; seated player holds it upright while playing.
etymology: Shortening of cellophane.

definition: A machine with a large revolving drum in which cement is mixed with other materials to make concrete.
Someone who censures or condemns.
example: I tried using a dirty word as my user name for the online game, but the censor rejected it.
etymology: The noun is borrowed from Latin cēnsor (“magistrate; critic”), from cēnseō (“to give an opinion, judge; to assess, reckon; to decree, determine”) + -sor (variant of -tor (suffix forming masculine agent nouns)).

definition: Suppressed or subject to censorship.
example: The censored press in some countries.

definition: A system where the votes cast by those eligible to vote are not equal, but are weighed differently according to the person's rank in the census (e.g., people with high income have more votes than those with a small income).
Of or relating to or completing a period of 100 years.
example: Centennial celebration.
etymology: From Latin centēnārius (“containing 100; local official overseeing a hundred”), either directly or through French centenaire from centēnī (“100 each”) + -ārius (-ary), from centum (“hundred”).

definition: Of or relating to or completing a period of 100 years.
example: Centennial celebration.
etymology: From Late Latin centennium (“period of 100 years, century”) + English -al (suffix forming adjectives and nouns).

definition: (linguistics) any vowel sound in which the tongue is positioned halfway between a front vowel and a back vowel.
example: In practice, unrounded central vowels tend to be further forward and rounded central vowels further back.

definition: Drawn toward a center or brought under the control of a central authority.
example: Centralized control of emergency relief efforts.

definition: In or near or toward a center or according to a central role or function.
example: The theater is centrally located.
etymology: From central + -ly.

definition: Having or situated at or near a center.
etymology: From Ancient Greek κεντρικός (kentrikós), equivalent to centre + -ic.

definition: Utensils made from ceramic material.
The art of making and decorating pottery.
etymology: From ceramic + -ics.

definition: Any of the arteries supplying blood to the cerebral cortex.
The layer of unmyelinated neurons (the grey matter) forming the cortex of the cerebrum.
Either half of the cerebrum.
The layer of unmyelinated neurons (the grey matter) forming the cortex of the cerebrum.
Any of several veins serving the cerebral hemispheres of the brain.
Marked by pomp or ceremony or formality.
example: A ceremonial occasion.
etymology: From Middle English cerymonial, from Latin caerimōniālis. Morphologically ceremony + -al or -ial.

definition: A dance that is part of a religious ritual.
A formal event performed on a special occasion.
example: A ceremony commemorating Pearl Harbor.

definition: A check containing certification that the person who issued the check has sufficient funds on deposit to cover payment.
Of or relating to the cervix of the uterus.
example: Cervical cancer.
etymology: Borrowing from French cervical, from New Latin cervīcālis, from cervīx (“the neck, nape”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix). By surface analysis, cervic- + -al.

definition: A contraceptive device consisting of a small thimble-shaped cup that is placed over the uterine cervix to prevent the entrance of spermatozoa.
Any of eight pairs of spinal nerves emerging from the cervical section of the spinal cord.
A vein that accompanies an artery of the same name.
A stopping.
example: A cessation of the thunder.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French cessation, itself a borrowing from Latin cessātiō. By surface analysis, cease + -ation. Compare cession < cede.

definition: A modern ballroom dance from Latin America; small steps and swaying movements of the hips.
etymology: From Cuban/Latin American Spanish cha-cha, imitative of the music.

definition: A fern of the genus Woodwardia having the sori in chainlike rows.
Another name for chain tongs.
A heavy smoker (usually of cigarettes) who lights one off of another.
Bound with chains.
example: Enchained demons strained in anger to gnaw on his bones.

definition: A tall narrow wineglass.
A person who changes something.
example: An inveterate changer of the menu.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English chaungere, chaungeour (“moneychanger”); equivalent to change + -er.

definition: Freshwater food fish common throughout central United States.
A clergyman ministering to some institution.
etymology: From Middle English chapeleyn, from Old French chapelain, from Medieval Latin, Late Latin cappellānus, from cappella. Doublet of capelin. Displaced Old English handprēost.

definition: A charred substance.
example: Among other native delicacies, they give you fresh char.
etymology: Back-formation from charcoal.

definition: Describe or portray the character or the qualities or peculiarities of.
example: You can characterize his behavior as that of an egotist.
etymology: From Medieval Latin charactērizō, from Ancient Greek χαρακτηρίζω (kharaktērízō, “to designate by a characteristic mark”), from χαρακτήρ (kharaktḗr, “a mark, character”). By surface analysis, character + -ize.

definition: A worker whose job is to make charcoal.
example: Here in Canada very few people gather charcoal burners for food, as it is tricky to identify.

definition: A pile of wooden billets, covered with turf or moistened clay, used to produce wood charcoal.
example: Professional charcoal burners often lived alone in small huts in order to tend their charcoal piles.

definition: A light four-wheel horse-drawn ceremonial carriage.
example: The warriors rode into battle on a horse-drawn chariot.
etymology: From Middle English chariot, from Old French chariot, from char (“cart”), from Latin carrus (“wagon”), itself borrowed from Gaulish *karros, from Proto-Celtic *karros (“wagon”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱr̥sós.

definition: A race between ancient chariots.
A personal attractiveness or interestingness that enables you to influence others.
Possessing an extraordinary ability to attract.
example: A charismatic leader.
etymology: From Ancient Greek χάρισμα (khárisma, “grace, favour, gift”) + -ic.

definition: A muscular cramp (especially in the thigh or calf) following vigorous exercise.
A muscular cramp (especially in the thigh or calf) following vigorous exercise.
Strongly attracted.
example: You are very gracious; I am charmed by your personality.

definition: A British or Canadian accountant who is a member of a professional body that has a royal charter.
An impressive country house (or castle) in France.
Click repeatedly or uncontrollably.
example: Chattering teeth.
etymology: From Middle English chateren, from earlier cheteren, chiteren (“to twitter, chatter, jabber”), of imitative origin.

definition: Marks on a glaciated rock caused by the movement of a glacier.
In a stingy manner.
etymology: From cheap + -ly.

definition: A list of items (names or tasks etc.) to be checked or consulted.
example: A checklist of the plants of the Guiana Shield.
etymology: From check + list.

definition: A place (as at a frontier) where travellers are stopped for inspection and clearance.
example: The travellers were stopped at the checkpoint.
etymology: From check + point.

definition: Hard smooth-textured cheese; originally made in Cheddar in southwestern England.
etymology: From Cheddar cheese. The slang use meaning "money, currency" may be derived from association with cheese (“wealth”), probably from Persian چیز (čiz, “thing”).

definition: Hard smooth-textured cheese; originally made in Cheddar in southwestern England.
Mat-forming perennial of central Europe with large fragrant pink or red flowers.
A membranous pouch inside the mouth of many rodents (as a gopher).
An enthusiastic and vocal supporter.
example: He has become a cheerleader for therapeutic cloning.
etymology: From cheer + leader.

definition: A laboratory for research in chemistry.
A notation used by chemists to express technical facts in chemistry.
A written order directing a bank to pay money.
etymology: From check, possibly influenced by exchequer. First attested in the 1790s.

definition: Characterized by feeling or showing fond affection for.
example: A cherished friend.

definition: Common birch of the eastern United States having spicy brown bark yielding a volatile oil and hard dark wood used for furniture.
Small Asiatic tree bearing edible red or yellow fruit.
Wood of any of various chestnut trees of the genus Castanea.
etymology: The noun is a contraction of chest(en) (“(obsolete) chestnut tree; fruit of this tree, chestnut”) + nut.

definition: An oak having leaves resembling those of chestnut trees.
Any of several attractive deciduous trees yellow-brown in autumn; yield a hard wood and edible nuts in a prickly bur.
(of hair or feathers) of brown tinged with chestnut.
Having the brown color of chestnuts.
Having the brown color of chestnuts.
V-shaped sleeve badge indicating military rank and service.
A preparation (usually made of sweetened chicle) for chewing.
A stock made with chicken.
A farm building for housing poultry.
etymology: From chicken + coop.

definition: A stew made with chicken.
For the most part.
example: Their relationship is chiefly professional.
etymology: From Middle English chefly; equivalent to chief + -ly (adverbial suffix).

definition: The parturition process in human beings; having a baby; the process of giving birth to a child.
etymology: From Middle English childbyrth [and other forms], perhaps a partial calque of Old Norse barnburðr (“childbearing, childbirth”, literally “bairn birth”); equivalent to child + birth.

definition: A service involving care for other people's children.
etymology: From child + care.

definition: Fiery vinegar flavored with chili peppers.
Very hot and finely tapering pepper of special pungency.
Walls that project out from the wall of a room and surround the chimney base.
American swift that nests in e.g. unused chimneys.
American swift that nests in e.g. unused chimneys.
Any compound containing a chlorine atom.
etymology: From chlor(ine) + -ide, coined by British chemist Humphry Davy in 1812.

definition: A common nonmetallic element belonging to the halogens; best known as a heavy yellow irritating toxic gas; used to purify water and as a bleaching agent and disinfectant; occurs naturally only as a salt (as in sea water).
etymology: Coined by British chemist Humphry Davy in 1810 from Ancient Greek χλωρός (khlōrós, “pale green”) + -ine.

definition: An explosive gas (ClO2) used chiefly in bleaching paper or starch or soap or flour and in water purification.
An aqueous solution of chlorine used as a bleaching agent.
Fudge made with chocolate or cocoa.
A gallery in a church occupied by the choir.
A coil of low resistance and high inductance used in electrical circuits to pass direct current and attenuate alternating current.
A coil of low resistance and high inductance used in electrical circuits to pass direct current and attenuate alternating current.
An acute intestinal infection caused by ingestion of contaminated water or food.
With speed.
etymology: From Chinese Pidgin English, from Cantonese 速速 (cuk1 cuk1, “quick”). Recorded in English since the 1830s (see citations for adverb). Recorded as a Chinese term in 1795.

definition: A grounder that bounces high in the air.
etymology: From chop + -er.

definition: A considerably big knife used for chopping or mincing meat, vegetables, etc.
A steady wooden block on which food can be cut or diced or wood can be split.
example: Jim really put his head on the chopping block when he started flirting with the boss's daughter.

definition: A wooden board where meats or vegetables can be cut.
A considerably big knife used for chopping or mincing meat, vegetables, etc.
A show involving artistic dancing.
example: She has staged many successful ballets, so her choreography skills must be excellent.
etymology: Reshaping of earlier choregraphy, a borrowing from French chorégraphie, from Ancient Greek χορεία (khoreía, “dance”) + -γραφίᾱ (-graphíā, “written form (of a word, etc.), spelling”).

definition: An electronic device that creates the effect of more than one sound from a single source by combining a short delay with slight deviations in pitch.
Informal terms for a meal.
example: I'm going to pick up some chow for dinner.
etymology: Shortened from chow-chow, from Chinese Pidgin English chow-chow. Compare Macanese chau-cháu. See also English chow fun, chow mein, etc.

definition: A queue of people waiting for food to be served (especially at a military camp).
(genetics) the process of locating genes on a chromosome.
Slowly progressing leukemia.
Relating to or arranged according to temporal order.
example: Chronological age.
etymology: From chrono- + -logical or chronology + -ical.

definition: Age measured by the time (years and months) that something or someone has existed.
example: His chronological age was 71 years.

definition: A chronological account of events in successive years.
A following of one thing after another in time.
Sufficiently fat so as to have a pleasing fullness of figure.
example: A chubby child.
etymology: Recorded since 1611, from chub (“short, thick fish species used as bait";

definition: Like or containing small sticky lumps.
example: The dumplings were chunky pieces of uncooked dough.
etymology: From chunk + -y.

definition: Small to medium-sized tree of Tasmania.
example: An hour passes before the first sign of any prior trip appears […] . Then, not far on, a black blaze on a cider gum trunk.

definition: Mill that extracts juice from apples to make apple cider.
Vinegar made from cider.
Small part of a cigar that is left after smoking.
An implement for cutting the tip off of a cigar.
A lighter for cigars or cigarettes.
A smoker of cigarettes.
Aromatic bark of Saigon cinnamon used medicinally as a carminative.
Rolled dough spread with cinnamon and sugar (and raisins) then sliced before baking.
Rolled dough spread with cinnamon and sugar (and raisins) then sliced before baking.
Hardy Chinese vine naturalized in United States and cultivated as an ornamental climber for its glossy heart-shaped cinnamon-scented leaves and in the tropics for its edible tubers.
Knitted in tubular form.
example: Circular-knit sweaters without seams.

definition: Cold-water fish caught in Lake Superior and northward.
etymology: From French ciscoette (“siscowet”), from Ojibwe siscowet (“cooks itself”).

definition: A stronghold into which people could go for shelter during a battle.
etymology: From French citadelle, from Italian cittadella, diminutive of città (“city”), from Latin cīvitās.

definition: A group's refusal to obey a law because they believe the law is immoral (as in protest against discrimination).
example: Thoreau wrote a famous essay justifying civil disobedience.

definition: The social process whereby societies achieve an advanced stage of development and organization.
etymology: Borrowed from French civilisation, equivalent to civilise + -ation or civil + -isation.

definition: Fasten or fix with a clamp.
example: Clamp the chair together until the glue has hardened.
etymology: From Middle Dutch clamp, klampe (“a clamp, hook”), from Proto-Germanic *klampō (“clamp, clasp, cramp”), related to Proto-West Germanic *klammjan.

definition: Repress or suppress (something regarded as undesirable).
example: The police clamped down on illegal drugs.

definition: A demonstration of approval by clapping the hands together.
etymology: From Middle English clappynge; equivalent to clap + -ing.

definition: Butter made clear by heating and removing the sediment of milk solids.
etymology: From clarified + butter, from Middle English clarifien and buter. Earliest attestation of clarified in this sense from the 14th century.

definition: Arrange or order by classes or categories.
example: How would you classify these pottery shards — are they prehistoric?
etymology: From French classifier. By surface analysis, class + -ify.

definition: An acquaintance that you go to school with.
A hammer with a cleft at one end for pulling nails.
etymology: From claw + hammer, descriptive of the shape of the tool's head.

definition: Shop where dry cleaning is done.
The habit of keeping free of superficial imperfections.
etymology: From cleanly + -ness.

definition: Clean one's body or parts thereof, as by washing.
example: Clean up before you see your grandparents.
etymology: From Middle English clensen, from Old English clǣnsian, from Proto-West Germanic *klainisōn, from Proto-West Germanic *klainī (“clean”).

definition: A very large profit.
example: The cost of environmental cleanup after an oil spill.
etymology: A deverbal from clean up.

definition: (baseball) the fourth position in the batting order (usually filled by the best batter on the team).
(baseball) the fourth position in the batting order (usually filled by the best batter on the team).
(of weather or climate) physically mild.
example: Clement weather.
etymology: From Old French, from Latin clēmēns (“merciful”). Equivalent to clīnō + participial suffix -menos. https://www.etymonline.com/word/clemency

definition: A clergyman or other person in religious orders.
etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin clēricus, from Ancient Greek κληρικός (klērikós), from κλῆρος (klêros, “a casting lots, drawing lots”).

definition: Of or relating to clerks.
example: Clerical work.
etymology: From Late Latin clēricālis (“clerical”), from clēricus (“clergyman, priest”).

definition: A stiff white collar with no opening in the front; a distinctive symbol of the clergy.
Secure or fasten by flattening the ends of nails or bolts.
example: The girder was clinched into the wall.
etymology: 16th-century alteration of clench.

definition: Come or be in close contact with; stick or hold together and resist separation.
example: The dress clings to her body.
etymology: From Middle English clingen, from Old English clingan (“to adhere”), from Proto-West Germanic *klingan, from Proto-Germanic *klinganą. Cognate with Danish klynge (“to cluster, to crowd”). Compare clump.

definition: A thin plastic film made of saran (trade name Saran Wrap) that sticks to itself; used for wrapping food.
Hold firmly, usually with one's hands.
In a clinical manner.
example: She is clinically qualified.
etymology: From clinical + -ly.

definition: Cut or trimmed by clipping.
example: A handsome man with a clipped moustache.

definition: Thickened or coalesced in soft thick lumps (such as clogs or clots).
example: Seeds clogged together.

definition: A vowel sound made with your tongue near the top of your mouth.
example: The vowel in seat is a close vowel and that in sat a fairly open vowel.

definition: Having the sails trimmed for sailing as close to the wind as possible.
A syllable that ends with a consonant.
example: The vowel in a closed syllable is short.

definition: Wearing or provided with clothing; sometimes used in combination.
example: Clothed and in his right mind.
etymology: From clothe + -ed.

definition: A hamper that holds dirty clothes to be washed or wet clothes to be dried.
Any of several small yellowish or buff-colored moths whose larvae eat organic matter e.g. woolens.
Wood or plastic fastener; for holding clothes on a clothesline.
A plant of the genus Trifolium.
Hairy Eurasian plant with small yellow flowers and an astringent root formerly used medicinally.
A building that is occupied by a social club.
example: The clubhouse needed a new roof.
etymology: From club + house.

definition: Lacking grace in movement or posture.
example: Clumsy fingers.
etymology: Possibly from an alteration of clumsed (“benumbed”) or from clumse (“a stupid fellow; lout”) + -y. More at clumse.

definition: A person with poor motor coordination.
A pedal or lever that engages or disengages a rotating shaft and a driving mechanism.
example: He smoothly released the clutch with one foot and stepped on the gas with the other.

definition: One of two or more beneficiaries of the same benefit.
A seam of coal.
A hand shovel for shoveling coal.
Of textures that are rough to the touch or substances consisting of relatively large particles.
example: Coarse meal.
etymology: Adjectival use of course that diverged in spelling in the 18th century. The sense developed from '(following) the usual course' (cf.

definition: A child's four-wheeled toy cart sometimes used for coasting.
A hard ferromagnetic silver-white bivalent or trivalent metallic element; a trace element in plant and animal nutrition.
A reddish mineral consisting of hydrated cobalt arsenate in monoclinic crystalline form and used in coloring glass; usually found in veins bearing cobalt and arsenic.
A shade of blue tinged with green.
A machine used in the treatment of cancer with the use of gamma rays from cobalt-60 radioisotopes.
example: Because the cobalt machines were expensive and required specialist support, they were often housed in cobalt units.

definition: (nautical) a large locker under the cockpit seating.
Overly self-confident or self-assertive.
example: A very cocky young man.
etymology: From cock (“male domestic chicken”) + -y (suffix forming adjectives with the sense of ‘having the quality of’).

definition: Tall palm tree bearing coconuts as fruits; widely planted throughout the tropics.
etymology: From Portuguese/Spanish coco (“grinning face”) (due to the three holes in the shell resembling a human face). Doublet of coque.

definition: Tall palm tree bearing coconuts as fruits; widely planted throughout the tropics.
Seed of the cacao tree; ground roasted beans are source of chocolate.
Small tropical American tree bearing edible plumlike fruit.
A constant number that serves as a measure of some property or characteristic.
etymology: From French coefficient. Coined by French mathematician François Viète.

definition: The act of compelling by force of authority.
Evergreen fern of California and Baja California.
A mill that grinds roasted coffee beans.
The psychological result of perception and learning and reasoning.
example: Human cognition.

definition: The branch of neuroscience that studies the biological foundations of mental phenomena.
The branch of semantics that studies the cognitive aspects of meaning.
Causing cohesion.
example: A cohesive agent.
etymology: From Latin cohaesus, past participle of cohaereō, + -ive.

definition: A company of companions or supporters.
example: The 18–24 cohort shows a sharp increase in automobile fatalities over the proximate age groupings.
etymology: From Latin cohors (stem cohort-); borrowed into Old English as coorta, but reintroduced into Middle English as cōhort and chōors via Old French cohorte. Doublet of court.

definition: A notebook with a coil binding.
Go with, fall together.
example: The two squares coincide nicely.
etymology: From French coïncider, from Medieval Latin coincidere, from con- + incidere, from in- (“into, to”) + cadere (“to fall, fall down, drop”).

definition: Without compunction or human feeling.
example: Cold-blooded killing.
etymology: From cold blood + -ed.

definition: The colder parts of temperate waters.
A paste-up made by sticking together pieces of paper or photographs to form an artistic image.
example: He used his computer to make a collage of pictures superimposed on a map.
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French collage. Doublet of collagen, colloid, and protocol.

definition: A movie that juxtaposes different kinds of footage.
A fibrous scleroprotein in bone and cartilage and tendon and other connective tissue; yields gelatin on boiling.
etymology: From French collagène, coined from Ancient Greek κόλλα (kólla, “glue”) and -γενής (-genḗs, “-forming”) (see -gen); it is the main substance that animal glues are derived from.

definition: An Irish girl.
etymology: Borrowed from Irish cailín.

definition: Of or resembling or typical of a college or college students.
example: Collegiate living.
etymology: From Middle English collegiate, from Medieval Latin collēgiātus (“colleague”), from collēgium (“community, group”).

definition: An abridged dictionary of a size convenient to hold in the hand.
Be incompatible; be or come into conflict.
example: When a body collides with another, then momentum is conserved.
etymology: From Latin collīdō (“to clash, strike, dash, beat, or press together”), from con- (“together”) + laedō (“to strike, collide, hurt”) (whence col- (“assimilated form of com-”)).

definition: Hit against; come into sudden contact with.
Someone who works in a coal mine.
etymology: From Middle English colier, colyer, alteration of earlier coler, collere (“one who makes or sells charcoal”), from Old English *colere (“collier”), equivalent to coal + -ier.

definition: Secret agreement.
etymology: Dated from the 14th century C.E. as Middle English collusioun, collusion; from Old French collusion, from Latin collusio (“act of colluding”).

definition: The soldier who carries the standard of the unit in military parades or in battle.
Genetic inability to distinguish differences in hue.
example: Despite the fact that race is embedded in American social life, "color blindness" has recently emerged as the dominant ideology of race.
etymology: From color blind + -ness or color + blindness.

definition: So great in size or force or extent as to elicit awe.
example: Colossal crumbling ruins of an ancient temple.
etymology: From French colossal, formed from Latin colossus, from Ancient Greek κολοσσός (kolossós, “giant statue”).

definition: Genetic inability to distinguish differences in hue.
Biradially symmetrical hermaphroditic solitary marine animals resembling jellyfishes having for locomotion eight rows of cilia arranged like teeth in a comb.
etymology: From their prominent bands of cilia, and their jelly-like texture and resemblance to jellyfish.

definition: A locomotor organ consisting of a row of strong cilia whose bases are fused.
Things that make you comfortable and at ease.
example: All the comforts of home.

definition: A punctuation mark (‘,’) used to indicate the separation of elements within the grammatical structure of a sentence.
etymology: From Latin comma, from Ancient Greek κόμμα (kómma), from κόπτω (kóptō, “to cut”).

definition: A member of a military unit trained as shock troops for hit-and-run raids.
etymology: From Afrikaans kommando, from Portuguese comando (“command”), from Late Latin *commandare, from Latin commendare.

definition: Celebrate by some ceremony or observation.
example: On November 11th we commemorate the fallen with a march.
etymology: First attested in 1599; borrowed from Latin commemorātus, perfect passive participle of commemorō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

definition: A ceremony to honor the memory of someone or something.
example: Commemoration ceremony.
etymology: First attested in 1384, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English commemoracioun, from Old French commemoration (French commémoration), from Latin commemorātiō. By surface analysis, commemorate + -ion

definition: The time at which something is supposed to begin.
example: The time of Henry VII nearly coincides with the commencement of what is termed modern history.
etymology: From French commencement; analyzable as commence + -ment.

definition: An academic exercise in which diplomas are conferred.
The day on which university degrees are conferred.
An academic exercise in which diplomas are conferred.
Express approbation of.
example: The schoolboy was commended for raising the alarm about the burning building.
etymology: From Middle English commenden, from Old French comender, from Latin commendō (“commend, entrust to, commit, recommend”), from com- + mandō (“to commit, intrust, enjoin”), from manus (“hand”) + dō (“to put”).

definition: Bribery of a purchasing agent in order to induce the agent to enter into a transaction.
A salesman who travels to call on customers.
The act of granting authority to undertake certain functions.
example: The destroyer's commissioning will be held on February 1st.

definition: A brokerage firm dealing in commodities.
A commissioned naval officer who ranks above a captain and below a rear admiral; the lowest grade of admiral.
An ax with a long handle and a head that has one cutting edge and one blunt side.
Grass yielding grain used for breakfast food and animal feed and in malt beverages.
Large European beech with minutely-toothed leaves; widely planted as an ornamental in North America.
European birch with silvery white peeling bark and markedly drooping branches.
Deciduous erect spreading broom native to western Europe; widely cultivated for its rich yellow flowers.
Native to the Canary Islands and Azores; popular usually yellow cage bird noted for its song.
European twining plant whose flowers are used chiefly to flavor malt liquors; cultivated in America.
European shrub with white or rosy flowers followed by black berries.
A nuisance that unreasonably interferes with a right that is common to the general public.
North American raccoon.
Annual sunflower grown for silage and for its seeds which are a source of oil; common throughout United States and much of North America.
Small terrestrial viper common in northern Eurasia.
A variety of vespid wasp.
Of the plains of central and eastern Africa.
Completely ordinary and unremarkable.
example: Air travel has now become commonplace.
etymology: A calque of Latin locus commūnis, referring to a generally applicable literary passage, itself a calque of Ancient Greek κοινὸς τόπος (koinòs tópos).

definition: A notebook in which you enter memorabilia.
The smallest administrative district of several European countries.
etymology: From Middle English commune, comune, from Old French comune, commune, from Medieval Latin commūnia, from Latin commūne (“community, state”), from commūnis (“common”). Doublet of comune.

definition: Any of three arteries in the brain that make up the circle of Willis.
A passenger train that is ridden primarily by passengers who travel regularly from one place to another.
example: He takes the commuter to headquarters at least once a week.
etymology: The sense of "one who travels to work" derives via commutation ticket, an early form of season ticket.

definition: Traffic created by people going to or returning from work.
A passenger train that is ridden primarily by passengers who travel regularly from one place to another.
The travel of a commuter.
(law) negligence allocated between the plaintiff and the defendant with a corresponding reduction in damages paid to the plaintiff.
Force somebody to do something.
example: We compel all students to fill out this form.
etymology: From Middle English compellen, borrowed from Middle French compellir, from Latin compellere, itself from com- (“together”) + pellere (“to drive”). Displaced native Old English nīedan.

definition: The quality of being adequately or well qualified physically and intellectually.
etymology: From Late Latin competentia. Doublet of competence.

definition: An aggressive willingness to compete.
etymology: From competitive + -ness.

definition: The act of compiling (as into a single book or file or list).
example: The job of compiling the inventory took several hours.

definition: (computer science) a program that decodes instructions written in a higher order language and produces an assembly language program.
Two angles whose sum is a right angle.
example: Let angle A = 30° and angle B = 10°, so that their complementary angles are A′ = 60° and B′ = 80°, respectively.
etymology: Complementary in the sense of completing, i.e. they form a complete right angle.

definition: The coloring of a person's face.
example: A rugged complexion.

definition: Inclined to comply.
example: Children compliant with the parental will.
etymology: From comply + -ant.

definition: Make more complicated.
example: There was a new development that complicated the matter.
etymology: First attested in the early 17th century;

definition: The act or process of complicating.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French complication, from Latin complicatio, complicationem. Morphologically complicate + -ion.

definition: Conveying or resembling a compliment.
example: A complimentary remark.
etymology: From compliment (noun) + -ary. Piecewise doublet of complementary.

definition: Form the substance of.
example: Greed and ambition composed his personality.

definition: The spatial property resulting from the arrangement of parts in relation to each other and to the whole.
example: Harmonious composition is essential in a serious work of art.

definition: Light microscope that has two converging lens systems: the objective and the eyepiece.
The part of grammar that deals with combinations of simple words into compound words.
Combined into or constituting a chemical compound.
Fracture in which the bone collapses (especially in short bones such as vertebrae).
A mechanical device that compresses gasses.
etymology: From compress + -or, or from New Latin compressor.

definition: Making or willing to make concessions.
example: Loneliness tore through him … whenever he thought of … even the compromising Louis du Tillet.

definition: Caused by or suggestive of psychological compulsion.
example: Compulsive drinking.
etymology: Borrowed from French compulsif, formed from Latin compulsus, past participle of compellere (“to compel”), from com- (“together”) + pellere (“to drive”).

definition: The procedure of calculating; determining something by mathematical or logical methods.
etymology: From late Middle English computacioun, from Middle French computation, from Latin computatiō, from computare (“sum up, reckon, compute”); see compute. Morphologically compute + -ation.

definition: Make a mathematical calculation or computation.
example: Can anyone here compute the square root of 10201?
etymology: 17th century. Borrowed from French computer, from Latin computō (“calculate, compute”). Doublet of count.

definition: Suitable for feeding directly into a computer.
Admit (to a wrongdoing).
example: I have to concede the argument.
etymology: From Middle English [Term?], from Old French conceder, from Latin concēdō (“give way, yield”), from con- (“wholly”) + cēdō (“to yield, give way, to go, grant”), from Proto-Indo-European *ked- (“to go, yield”).

definition: Have the idea for.
example: He conceived of a robot that would help paralyzed patients.
etymology: From Middle English conceyven, from Old French concevoir, conceveir, from Latin concipiō, concipere (“to devise, to conceive”).

definition: Form a mental image of something that is not present or that is not the case.
example: Can you conceive of him as the president?

definition: A gradient in concentration of a solute as a function of distance through a solution.
example: The movement of a solute down its concentration gradient is called diffusion.

definition: Involving the joint activity of two or more.
example: Concerted action.

definition: Music arranged in parts for several voices or instruments.
A composition for orchestra and a soloist.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian concerto, deverbal from concertare. Doublet of concert.

definition: Expressing much in few words.
example: A concise explanation.
etymology: From Latin concīsus (“cut short”), from concīdere (“cut to pieces”), from caedēre (“to cut, to strike down”).

definition: Forming an end or termination; especially putting an end to doubt or question.
example: Conclusive proof.
etymology: From French conclusif, from Late Latin conclusivus, from Latin conclūsīvē (“conclusively”), from past participle of concludere.

definition: Go together.
example: Their ideas concorded.
etymology: From French concorde, Latin concordia, from concors (“of the same mind, agreeing”); con- + cor, cordis (“heart”). See heart, and compare accord.

definition: A machine with a large revolving drum in which cement is mixed with other materials to make concrete.
Occurring or operating at the same time.
example: The concurrent jurisdiction of courts.
etymology: From Middle English concurrent, from Old French concurrent, from Latin concurrēns, present active participle of concurrō (“happen at the same time”), from con- (“with”) + currō (“run”).

definition: (law) negligence of two of more persons acting independently; the plaintiff may sue both together or separately.
Two or more operations performed at the same time (or within a given interval).
Overlapping in duration.
example: Concurrently with the conference an exhibition of things associated with Rutherford was held.
etymology: From concurrent + -ly.

definition: Containing or imposing condemnation or censure.
example: A condemnatory decree.

definition: Sweetened evaporated milk.
A conditioned response that anticipates the occurrence of an aversive stimulus.
The stimulus that is the occasion for a conditioned response.
Exercise that conditions the body.
example: Farm work can be a good conditioner.
etymology: From condition + -er.

definition: A passage (a pipe or tunnel) through which water or electric wires can pass.
example: The computers were connected through a system of conduits.
etymology: From Middle English conduyt, condit, from Old French conduit, from Latin conductus. Doublet of conduct.

definition: Evergreen Chinese woody climber with shiny dark green leaves and intensely fragrant white flowers.
With confidence; in a confident manner.
example: We have to do what is right confidently.
etymology: From confident + -ly.

definition: Concluding state of pregnancy; from the onset of contractions to the birth of a child.
etymology: Borrowed from French confinement. By surface analysis, confine + -ment.

definition: Present at birth but not necessarily hereditary; acquired during fetal development.
etymology: From Latin congenitus + -al, equivalent to con- + genital.

definition: A disease or disorder that is inherited genetically.
A defect that is present at birth.
A composite rock made up of particles of varying size.
etymology: First attested in the second part of the 16ᵗʰ century;

definition: A hypothesis that has been formed by speculating or conjecturing (usually with little hard evidence).
example: He dismissed it as mere conjecture.
etymology: From Old French, from Latin coniectūra (“a guess”), from coniectus, perfect passive participle of cōniciō (“throw or cast together; guess”), from con- (“together”) + iaciō (“throw, hurl”); see jet.

definition: Conduct or direct the steering of a ship or plane.
example: The pilot conned the ship safely into the harbor.
etymology: Variant of cond, from Middle English conduen, condien, from Anglo-Norman conduire, from Latin condūcō (“lead, bring or draw together”), from con- (“with, together”) + dūcō (“lead”). Doublet of conduce.

definition: An instrumentality that connects.
example: He soldered the connection.
etymology: From connect + -or.

definition: The act of conquering.
etymology: From conquer + -ing.

definition: A political or theological orientation advocating the preservation of the best in society and opposing radical changes.
etymology: Either irregularly from conservative + -ism or from conservate + -ism; ultimately from Latin cōnservāre (“to conserve; to keep, guard, observe”).

definition: The faculty and students of a school specializing in one of the fine arts.
etymology: From Medieval Latin cōnservātōrium directly and via French conservatoire and Italian conservatorio, from cōnservātus (“conserved, preserved”) + -ōrium (“-ory: forming related nouns”).

definition: Keep constant through physical or chemical reactions or evolutionary change.
example: Energy is conserved in this process.
etymology: From Middle English conserven, from Old French conserver, from Latin conservare (“to keep, preserve”), from com- (intensive prefix) + servo (“keep watch, maintain”). See also observe.

definition: Showing concern for the rights and feelings of others.
example: Friends considerate enough to leave us alone.

definition: Unite into one.
example: The companies consolidated.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin consolidātus, from the verb consolidō, from solidus (“solid”). By surface analysis, con- + solid + -ate.

definition: Obvious to the eye or mind.
example: A tower conspicuous at a great distance.
etymology: From Latin conspicuus (“visible, striking”), from cōnspicere (“to notice”), from con- (“with, together”) + specere (“to look at”).

definition: Lacking spontaneity; not natural.
example: A constrained smile.

definition: Action by a landlord that compels a tenant to leave the premises (as by rendering the premises unfit for occupancy); no physical expulsion or legal process is involved.
Of or relating to anabolism.
Having to do with a consul or their office or duties.
example: If this is a consular ship, where is the ambassador?
etymology: From Middle English consular, from Latin cōnsulāris. By surface analysis, consul + -ar.

definition: The practice of giving expert advice within a particular field.
example: A business management consultancy.
etymology: From consultant + -cy or consult + -ancy.

definition: A policy of creating strategic alliances in order to check the expansion of a hostile power or ideology or to force it to negotiate peacefully.
example: Containment of communist expansion was a central principle of United States' foreign policy from 1947 to the 1975.
etymology: From contain + -ment.

definition: Look at thoughtfully; observe deep in thought.
example: Contemplate one's navel.
etymology: First attested in the 1590s; borrowed from Latin contemplātus, the perfect active participle of contemplor (“to observe, survey, gaze (at), contemplate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). See also template.

definition: All the people living at the same time or of approximately the same age.
Inclined or showing an inclination to dispute or disagree, even to engage in law suits.
example: A style described as abrasive and contentious.
etymology: From Middle French contentieux, from Latin contentiōsus (“quarrelsome, perverse”), from contentiō (“contention”), from contendere, past participle contentus (“to contend”). Equivalent to English contention + -ous.

definition: A person who participates in competitions.
etymology: From French contestant, present participle of contester.

definition: A glacier that spreads out from a central mass of ice.
A possible event or occurrence or result.
A fee that is payable only if the outcome is successful (as for an attorney's services).
An alternative to the normal procedure; triggered if an unusual but anticipated situation arises.
Recurring regularly or frequently in a prolonged and closely spaced series.
example: The continual banging of the shutters.
etymology: From Middle English continuel, from Old French continuel, formed from Latin continuus (“continuous”) with the suffix -el, equivalent to continue + -al.

definition: A continuous nonspatial whole or extent or succession in which no part or portion is distinct or distinguishable from adjacent parts.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin continuum, neuter form of continuus, from contineō (“contain, enclose”).

definition: A line drawn on a map connecting points of equal height.
example: The low drag contour of a modern automobile.
etymology: Borrowed from French contour, from contourner, equivalent to con- + tour.

definition: A tone language that uses pitch changes.
A line drawn on a map connecting points of equal height.
A map having contour lines through points of equal elevation.
A sheet (usually with elastic edges) tailored to fit a particular mattress.
Birth control by the use of devices (diaphragm or intrauterine device or condom) or drugs or surgery.
(physiology) a shortening or tensing of a part or organ (especially of a muscle or muscle fiber).
example: Our contraction of debt in this quarter has reduced our ability to attract investors.
etymology: PIE word *ḱóm From Late Middle English contraccioun, contraxion (“spasm, contraction; constriction, shrinking;

definition: Relating to or part of a binding legal agreement.
example: Contractual obligations.
etymology: Morphologically contract + -ual, from Latin contractus + -al.

definition: Be in contradiction with.
example: His testimony contradicts hers.
etymology: Derived from Latin contrādictus (“contradicted”), the past participle of contrādīcō (“speak against”) (originally two words).

definition: Opposition between two conflicting forces or ideas.
example: His contradiction of the proposal was very interesting.
etymology: From Middle English contradiccioun, contradiction, from Old French contradiction, from Latin contrādictiō, from contrādīcō (“speak against”).

definition: Of words or propositions so related that both cannot be true and both cannot be false.
example: ‘perfect’ and ‘imperfect’ are contradictory terms.
etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin contradictorius, from Latin contradico. Equivalent to contradict + -ory.

definition: Strikingly different; tending to contrast.
example: Contrasting (or contrastive) colors.
etymology: From contrast + -ing.

definition: A religious residence especially for nuns.
etymology: From Middle English convent, variant of covent, from Old French covent, from Latin conventus, perfect participle of the verb convenio (whence ultimately convene), see con- + venio. Doublet of coven.

definition: The occurrence of two or more things coming together.
example: We built a homestead at the convergence of two rivers.
etymology: From converge + -ence (after Latin convergentia).

definition: Of words so related that one reverses the relation denoted by the other.
example: ‘parental’ and ‘filial’ are converse terms.
etymology: From Old French converser, from Latin conversor (“live, have dealings with”).

definition: A mental disorder characterized by the conversion of mental conflict into somatic forms (into paralysis or anesthesia having no apparent cause).
A device for changing one substance or form or state into another.
etymology: From convert + -er.

definition: Curving or bulging outward.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French convexe, from Latin convexus (“arched”).

definition: A shape that curves or bulges outward.
A person who conveys (carries or transmits).
example: The conveyer of good tidings.

definition: A moving belt that transports objects (as in a factory).
etymology: From conveyor + belt.

definition: Speak softly or lovingly.
example: The mother who held her baby was cooing softly.
etymology: Onomatopoeic. Compare Dutch koeren.

definition: A book of recipes and cooking directions.
example: They inherited an interesting nineteenth-century cookbook from their grandparents. It tells how to render lard.

Assign a name or title to.
