etymology: Borrowed from Latin dēsignātus, perfect passive participle of designō, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of design.

definition: A ballplayer who is designated to bat in place of the pitcher.
Morally reprehensible.
example: Would do something as despicable as murder.
etymology: From Late Latin dēspicābilis, from Latin dēspicor, a variant of dēspiciō (“to despise”), from de (“down”) + speciō (“to look at, behold”). First attested in the 1550s. Equivalent to despise + -able.

definition: Warship smaller than a destroyer; designed to escort fleets or convoys.
Of or relating to catabolism.
Visual impairment resulting from the retina becoming separated from the choroid in the back of the eye; treated by photocoagulation.
Avoiding emotional involvement.
etymology: From French détachement. By surface analysis, detach + -ment.

definition: Try to prevent; show opposition to.
example: Their boss deterred them from both taking holidays at the same time, claiming he couldn't manage it all on his own.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin dēterreō (“deter, discourage”), from de (“from”) + terreō (“to frighten”).

definition: A symptom of reduced quality or strength.
etymology: Borrowed from French détérioration; morphologically deteriorate + -ion.

definition: Tending to deter.
example: The deterrent effects of high prices.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin dēterrēns, dēterrentem.

definition: Punishment intended as a warning to others.
The hospital ward or clinic in which patients are detoxified.
etymology: Clipping of detoxification.

definition: A damage or loss.
etymology: From Old French detriement, from Latin detrimentum (“loss, damage, literally a rubbing off”), from dēterere (“to rub off, wear”), from dē- (“down, away”) + terere (“to rub”).

definition: A variation that deviates from the standard or norm.
example: The deviation from the mean.
etymology: From Middle French deviation, from Medieval Latin deviatio. Morphologically deviate + -ion.

definition: Completely wanting or lacking.
example: The sentence was devoid of meaning.
etymology: From obsolete Middle English verb devoiden, from Old French desvuidier (“to empty out”) (compare French dévider).

definition: Deeply religious.
example: Devout sighs; devout eyes; a devout posture.
etymology: From Middle English devout, devot, from Old French devot (French dévot), from Latin dēvōtus, perfect passive participle of dēvōveō. Doublet of devote.

definition: Terrestrial worm that burrows into and helps aerate soil; often surfaces when the ground is cool or wet; used as bait by anglers.
Of or relating to or causing diabetes.
example: Diabetic complications.
etymology: From diabetes + -ic. Doublet of diabatic.

definition: Coma that can develop in inadequately treated cases of diabetes mellitus.
A diet designed to help control the symptoms of diabetes.
Determine or distinguish the nature of a problem or an illness through a diagnostic analysis.
example: Flu was diagnosed.
etymology: Back-formation from diagnosis. Compare also sclerose (verb).

definition: (geometry) a straight line connecting any two vertices of a polygon that are not adjacent.
etymology: From Middle French diagonal, from Latin diagōnālis, from Ancient Greek διαγώνιος (diagṓnios, “from angle to angle”), from διά (diá, “across”) + γωνία (gōnía, “angle”).

definition: A square matrix with all elements not on the main diagonal equal to zero.
An atlas showing the distribution of distinctive linguistic features.
The study of the geographical distribution of linguistic features.
A conversation between two persons.
etymology: Variant of dialogue. Equivalent to dia- + -log or di- + -alog.

definition: (computer science) a small temporary window in a graphical user interface that appears in order to request information from the user; after the information has been provided the user dismisses the box with ‘okay’ or ‘cancel’.
etymology: Compound of dialog + box.

definition: Separation of substances in solution by means of their unequal diffusion through semipermeable membranes.
etymology: From Latin dialysis, from Ancient Greek διάλυσις (diálusis). By surface analysis, dia- + -lysis. First use appears c. 1550.

definition: A medical instrument for separating substances in solution by unequal diffusion through semipermeable membranes.
An anniversary celebrating the passage of 60 years.
The body of Jews (or Jewish communities) outside Palestine or modern Israel.
Determined or decided upon as by an authority.
example: The dictated terms of surrender.

definition: A locomotive driven by a diesel engine.
The part of calculus that deals with the variation of a function with respect to changes in the independent variable (or variables) by means of the concepts of derivative and differential.
Made different (especially in the course of development) or shown to be different.
example: The differentiated markings of butterflies.

definition: A discrimination between things as different and distinct on the basis of their characteristics or attributes.
etymology: From differentiate + -ion, from different + -iate, from differ + -ent, from Middle English differen, from Old French differer, from Latin differō (“carry apart, put off, defer;

definition: Spread out; not concentrated in one place.
example: A large diffuse organization.
etymology: From Middle French diffuser, from Latin diffūsus, past participle of diffundere, from dis- + fundere.

definition: Vacuum pump used to obtain a high vacuum.
Relating to or having the power to cause or promote digestion.
example: Digestive juices.
etymology: From Old French digestif, from Late Latin dīgestīvus. Doublet of digestif.

definition: Secretions that aid digestion.
Secretions that aid digestion.
The system that makes food absorbable into the body.
example: All the food that you eat goes through your digestive system and is digested.

definition: Arteries in the hand and foot that supply the fingers and toes.
By means of the fingers.
example: The exam was carried out digitally.
etymology: From digital + -ly.

definition: Having or expressing dignity; especially formality or stateliness in bearing or appearance.
example: Her dignified demeanor.

definition: An excavation for ore or precious stones or for archaeology.
etymology: Clipping of diggings.

definition: Reduced in strength or concentration or quality or purity.
example: Diluted alcohol.

definition: Having greatly reduced vision.
Decrease in size, extent, or range.
etymology: Formed under the influence of both diminue (from Old French diminuer, from Latin dīminuo) and minish.

definition: Becoming smaller or less or appearing to do so.
example: Diminishing returns.

definition: Have supper; eat dinner.
example: We often dine with friends in this restaurant.

definition: Eat at home.
Eat at a restaurant or at somebody else's home.
A person eating a meal (especially in a restaurant).
etymology: From dine + -er.

definition: The noise made by a bell.
etymology: Mid 16th century, imitative of the alternate chimes of a bell. For sense of penis, compare Saterland Frisian Ding (“penis”), German Low German Dings (“penis”), English thing.

definition: A mail pouch that is sealed shut and that is used to carry communications between a legation and its home office.
A report of the exact words used in a discourse.
Radio; determines the direction of incoming radio waves.
Relating to or indicating directions in space.
example: A directional microphone.
etymology: From direction + -al.

definition: A microphone that is designed to receive sound from a particular direction.
A group of persons chosen to govern the affairs of a corporation or other large institution.
etymology: From director + -ate.

definition: A relatively long dagger with a straight blade.
example: The word dick itself serves as model for two variants which are probably Midwestern, dirk and dork, also meaning "penis"...
etymology: Etymology unknown, apparently from Scots dirk. First attested in 1602 as dork, in the later 17th century as durk. The spelling dirk is due to Johnson's Dictionary of 1755.

definition: Marked by deprivation especially of the necessities of life or healthful environmental influences.
A feeling of disliking something or what someone is doing.
example: Everyone glared in disapproval at the man talking loudly on the phone.
etymology: From disapprove + -al.

definition: Doubt about the truth of something.
example: She cried out in disbelief on hearing that terrorists had crashed an airplane into the World Trade Center in New York City.
etymology: From dis- + belief.

definition: A person who announces and plays popular recorded music.
example: The disc jockey played brilliant music at the party.
etymology: Disc refers to the flat, circular shape of the traditional medium for recorded music.

definition: Comment on music to be played.
Anything that is cast aside or discarded.
etymology: From dis- + card. Compare Spanish descartar.

definition: Someone who believes and helps to spread the doctrine of another.
etymology: From Middle English disciple, discipul, from Old English discipul (“disciple, scholar”), from Latin discipulus (“pupil, learner”). Later influenced or superseded in Middle English by Old French deciple.

definition: (law) a voluntary repudiation of a person's legal claim to something.
etymology: Partly from Middle English discleymer, from Anglo-Norman desclamer; and partly from disclaim + -er.

definition: Street names for methylenedioxymethamphetamine.
Pull the plug of (electrical appliances) and render inoperable.
example: My wi-fi got disconnected.
etymology: From dis- + connect.

definition: Showing or experiencing dissatisfaction or restless longing.
example: Saw many discontent faces in the room.
etymology: From dis- + content.

definition: Lack of agreement or harmony.
etymology: Circa 1230, Middle English descorde, discorde; from Anglo-Norman, Old French descort (derivative of descorder), descorde (“disagreement”);

definition: Cause to be distrusted or disbelieved.
example: The paper discredited the politician with its nasty commentary.
etymology: From dis- + credit.

definition: Marked by prudence or modesty and wise self-restraint.
example: His trusted discreet aide.
etymology: From Middle English discrete, from Old French discret, from Latin discrētus, from past participle of discernere. Doublet of discrete.

definition: A difference between conflicting facts or claims or opinions.
example: They found a discrepancy between the first set of test results and the second, and they're still trying to figure out why.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin discrepantia, from discrepans, from discrepō, from crepō. By surface analysis, discrepant + -cy. See also discrepant.

definition: Having or using the ability to act or decide according to your own discretion or judgment.
example: The commission has discretionary power to award extra funds.
etymology: From discretion + -ary (“pertaining to”). Compare French discrétionnaire.

definition: A trust that gives the trustee discretion to pay the beneficiary as much of the trust income as the trustee believes appropriate.
Being biased or having a belief or attitude formed beforehand.
example: Discriminatory attitude.
etymology: From discriminate + -ory.

definition: Lack of respect accompanied by a feeling of intense dislike.
example: The cat viewed the cheap supermarket catfood with disdain and stalked away.
etymology: From Middle English disdeynen, from Old French desdeignier (modern French dédaigner).

definition: Giving offense to moral sensibilities and injurious to reputation.
etymology: From disgrace + -ful.

definition: A machine for washing dishes.
A machine for washing dishes.
example: Load the dishwasher.
etymology: From Middle English dysche wescheare, equivalent to dish + washer.

definition: A cache that stores copies of frequently used disk sectors in random access memory (RAM) so they can be read without accessing the slower disk.
A person who announces and plays popular recorded music.
Comment on music to be played.
example: He has a job disk-jockeying on the weekend.

definition: Regarded with aversion.
example: He was intensely disliked.

definition: Causing dejection.
example: The first dismal dispiriting days of November.
etymology: From Middle English dismal, dismale, from Anglo-Norman dismal, from Old French (li) dis mals (“(the) bad days”), from Medieval Latin diēs malī (“bad days”).

definition: Torn down and broken up.
The feeling of despair in the face of obstacles.
example: He looked in dismay at the destruction of the town caused by the hurricane.

definition: The failure to obey.
example: The teacher complained of the child's disobedience.
etymology: From Middle English disobedience, dysobediaunce, from Old French desobedience. By surface analysis, dis- + obedience. Displaced native Old English unhīersumnes.

definition: Fundamentally different or distinct in quality or kind.
example: Such disparate attractions as grand opera and game fishing.
etymology: First attested in 1586;

definition: Inequality or difference in some respect.
etymology: From Middle French disparité, from Latin disparitātem, accusative of disparitās, from dispār + -tās, from dis- + pār. By surface analysis, dis- + parity.

definition: Distribute loosely.
example: The Jews are dispersed among all nations.
etymology: From Middle French disperser, from Latin dispersus, past participle of dispergō (“to scatter abroad, disperse”), from dis- (“apart”) + spargō (“to scatter”); see sparse.

definition: (of colloids) a substance in the colloidal state.
(of colloids) a substance in the colloidal state.
Fracture in which the two ends of the broken bone are separated from one another.
Your usual mood.
example: He has a happy disposition.
etymology: From Middle English disposicioun, from Middle French disposition, from Latin dispositiōnem, accusative singular of dispositiō, from dispōnō. By surface analysis, dispose + -ition. Doublet of dispositio.

definition: Out of proportion.
example: Grossly disproportionate.
etymology: From dis- + proportionate.

definition: In a manner which is out of proportion.
example: This wall is disproportionately long.
etymology: From disproportionate + -ly.

definition: Disqualified by law or rule or provision.
Marked by breaks or gaps.
example: Many routes are unsafe or disrupted.

definition: Characterized by unrest or disorder or insubordination.
example: Effects of the struggle will be violent and disruptive.

definition: The feeling of being displeased and discontent.
example: He was never slow to express his dissatisfaction with the service he received.
etymology: From dis- + satisfaction.

definition: In a state of sulky dissatisfaction.
example: We offer refunds to dissatisfied customers.
etymology: From dis- + satisfied.

definition: The opening of a subject to widespread discussion and debate.
etymology: From Latin dissēminātiō, from dissēmināre [from dis- (“in all directions”) + sēmināre (“to plant or propagate”) (itself from sēmen (“seed”))] + -tiō. By surface analysis, disseminate + -tion.

definition: Grow less and less substantial until it disappears.
example: The ruling party or coalition sometimes dissolves parliament early when the polls are favorable, hoping to reconvene with a larger majority.
etymology: Recorded since c.

definition: Situated farthest from point of attachment or origin, as of a limb or bone.
example: The distal end of a bone or muscle.
etymology: From distant + -al.

definition: Water that has been purified by distillation.
A pair of jean trousers ripped and bleached on purpose or by extended wear.
Doubt about someone's honesty.
example: Many people have developed a cynical distrust of politicians.
etymology: From dis- + trust, alteration of the earlier term wantrust.

definition: A mark used to indicate the word above it should be repeated.
example: Please run off twenty-four dittos of this assignment for my students.
etymology: First attested in 1625. From regional Italian ditto, variant of detto, past participle of dire (“to say”), from Latin dīcō (“to say, to speak”). Not related to English dittography.

definition: A mark used to indicate the word above it should be repeated.
Someone who works underwater.
etymology: From dive + -er.

definition: Diverging from another or from a standard.
example: A divergent opinion.
etymology: From Latin dis- (“apart”) + vergere (“to turn”) + the adjectival suffix -ent.

definition: Thinking that moves away in diverging directions so as to involve a variety of aspects and which sometimes lead to novel ideas and solutions; associated with creativity.
etymology: Coined by Joy Paul Guilford in 1956.

definition: Having variety of character or form or components; or having increased variety.
example: A diversified musical program ranging from classical to modern.

definition: Turn aside; turn away from.
example: The workers diverted the stream away from the road.
etymology: From Middle English diverten, Old French divertir (“to turn or go different ways, part, separate, divert”), from Latin di- (“apart”) + vertere (“to turn”); see verse.

definition: Pleasantly occupied.
Any supernatural being worshipped as controlling some part of the world or some aspect of life or who is the personification of a force.
example: I studied divinity at Harvard Divinity School.
etymology: From Old French divinité, from Latin divinitas. Composed of divine + -ity. Displaced native Old English godcundnes.

definition: Of or relating to a military division.
example: Divisional artillery.
etymology: From division + -al.

definition: Dissenting (especially dissenting with the majority opinion).
example: Rather than fostering unity, he becomes divisive.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin dīvīsīvus.

definition: A large metal pot (12 gallon camp kettle) for cooking; used in military camps.
etymology: From Hindi देगची (degcī, “a kettle, a metallic cooking pot”), from Classical Persian دیگچه (degča, “a pot, small cauldron”), from دیگ (deg, “pot”) + ـچه (-ča).

definition: Having or causing a whirling sensation; liable to falling.
example: Had a dizzy spell.
etymology: From Middle English dysy, desy, dusi, from Old English dysiġ (“stupid, foolish”), from Proto-West Germanic *dusīg (“stunned; dazed”).

definition: The act of securing an arriving vessel with ropes.
etymology: From dock + -ing.

definition: Landing in a harbor next to a pier where ships are loaded and unloaded or repaired; may have gates to let water in or out.
A fee charged for a vessel to use a dock.
A lengthy, formal treatise written by a candidate for the doctoral degree at a university.
example: The term graduate thesis is sometimes used to refer to both master's theses and doctoral dissertations.

definition: One of the highest earned academic degrees conferred by a university.
etymology: From Latin doctōrātus.

definition: A shifty deceptive person.
etymology: From dodge + -er.

definition: Nonperformance of something distasteful (as by deceit or trickery) that you are supposed to do.
example: Twistings and dodgings.

definition: Of uncertain outcome; especially fraught with risk.
example: Asked why, a spokesman gave a dodgy answer about legal ramifications.
etymology: From dodge (verb) + -y. First used in mid-19th century England.

definition: A hard biscuit for dogs.
Flea that attacks dogs and cats.
An elementary swimming stroke imitating a swimming dog.
A wrench with a handle shaped like a crank.
Informal terms for dogs.
example: That's such a cute little doggy, Keira!
etymology: From dog + -y (diminutive suffix).

definition: A bag for food that a customer did not eat at a restaurant; the transparent pretense is that the food is taken home to feed the customer's dog.
etymology: From doggy + bag. In the food sense, this refers to the idea that the food is to be taken home for the diner's dog.

definition: A religious doctrine that is proclaimed as true without proof.
etymology: From Latin dogma (“philosophical tenet”), from Ancient Greek δόγμα (dógma, “opinion, tenet”), from δοκέω (dokéō, “to seem good, think”). Treated in the 17th and 18th century as Greek, with plural dogmata. Compare decent.

definition: A share of money or food or clothing that has been charitably given.
example: C. 1650s, John Cleveland, Upon Phillis Walking in a Morning before Sun-rising At her general dole, / Each receives his ancient soul.
etymology: From Middle English dol, from Old English dāl (“portion, share, division, allotment”), from Proto-Germanic *dailą (“part, deal”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰayl- (“part, watershed”).

definition: Administer or bestow, as in small portions.
example: Dole out some money.

definition: Spar under the bowsprit of a sailboat.
With respect to the internal affairs of a government.
example: Domestically, the president proposes a more moderate economic policy.
etymology: From domestic + -ally.

definition: (nautical) an extra boiler (as a ship's boiler that is used while the ship is in port).
A cart with an underslung axle and two seats.
A small ring-shaped friedcake.
etymology: Alteration of doughnut, from dough + nut. Attested 1900.

definition: A machine used to fry large quantities of doughnuts at once.
An aimless drawing.
example: Mrs. Sneak. Why doodle! jackanapes! harkee, who am I? Sneak. Come, don't go to call names: am I? vhy my vife, and I am your master.
etymology: Originally dialectal, from Low German dudeldopp (“simpleton”). Influenced by dawdle. Compare also German dudeln (“to play (the bagpipe)”).

definition: Spring-loaded doorlock that can only be opened from the outside with a key.

A monoamine neurotransmitter found in the brain and essential for the normal functioning of the central nervous system; as a drug (trade names Dopastat and Intropin) it is used to treat shock and hypotension.
In a condition of biological rest or suspended animation.
example: Dormant buds.
etymology: From Middle English, from Old French, from Latin dormiēns, present participle of dormiō (“to sleep”).

definition: A savings account showing no activity (other than posting interest) for some specified period.
example: The dormant account reverted to the state under escheat laws.

definition: Belonging to or on or near the back or upper surface of an animal or organ or part.
example: The dorsal fin is the vertical fin on the back of a fish and certain marine mammals.
etymology: From Late Middle English dorsal/dorsale, borrowing from Medieval Latin dorsālis (“of or relating to the back”), from dorsum (“the back”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix); equivalent to dorsum + -al.

definition: Unpaired median fin on the backs of fishes and some other aquatic vertebrates that help to maintain balance.
One of two roots of a spinal nerve that passes dorsally from the spinal cord and that consists of sensory fibers.
One of two roots of a spinal nerve that passes dorsally from the spinal cord and that consists of sensory fibers.
A collection of papers containing detailed information about a particular person or subject (usually a person's record).
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French dossier.

definition: Having a pattern of dots.
example: Please print your name and address clearly on the dotted line.
etymology: From dot + -ed.

definition: A line made up of dots or dashes; often used to indicate where you are supposed to sign a contract (or other documents).
example: Just sign on the dotted line.

definition: Shoot two strokes under par.
A clinch with two loops.
A chemical reaction between two compounds in which parts of each are interchanged to form two new compounds (AB+CD=AD+CB).
Two incomes received from the same source (as by holding a government job and receiving a government pension).
A pair of parallel helices intertwined about a common axis.
example: The shape of the DNA molecule is a double helix.

definition: A vehicle carrying many passengers; used for public transport.
etymology: From double + deck + -er.

definition: Without qualification; used informally as (often pejorative) intensifiers.
example: A double-dyed villain.

definition: Provide with two sheets of glass.
A large wine bottle (holds 4/5 of a gallon).
(of type or print) having a blank line between lines of type.
example: Manuscripts must be double-spaced.

definition: Typing that leaves alternate lines blank.
Marked by or given to doubt.
Strong durable timber of a douglas fir.
Lofty douglas fir of northwestern North America having short needles and egg-shaped cones.
Characterized by plain blunt honesty.
example: A downright answer.
etymology: The adverb is derived from Middle English dounright, dounriȝt (“right down, straight down; face down; vertically;

definition: The ratio of the drag on a body moving through air to the product of the velocity and the surface area of the body.
A dealer in fabrics and sewing materials (and sometimes in clothing and drygoods).
etymology: From Middle English draper, from Anglo-Norman draper, from Old French drapier, from drap + -ier.

definition: Control and direct with or as if by reins.
Underpants worn by men.
etymology: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

definition: Causing fear or dread or terror.
example: The dread presence of the headmaster.

definition: An early subgenre of trance music that peaked prominently on the international dance scene between 1995 and 1998.
Someone who is dreaming.
etymology: From Middle English dremer, dremere, dremare, equivalent to dream + -er.

definition: Furniture with drawers for keeping clothes.
example: He's a very snappy dresser.
etymology: From Middle English dressure, dressor, dressour, a borrowing from Old French drecëur, drecëure, from the verb dresser.

definition: A small mat placed under a glass to protect a surface from condensation.
(architecture) a projection from a cornice or sill designed to protect the area below from rainwater (as over a window or doorway).
A liquid (as water) that flows in drops (as from the eaves of house).
example: Lying in bed, I could hear drippings from the leaky roof.

definition: Pan for catching drippings under roasting meat.
The axle of a self-propelled vehicle that provides the driving power.
Biscuit made from dough with enough milk that it can be dropped from a spoon.
Shop where dry cleaning is done.
Masonry without mortar.
A dry swab for dusting floors.
Inflammation in the socket of a tooth; sometimes occurs after a tooth is extracted and a blood clot fails to form.
Fraught with uncertainty or doubt.
example: Dubious about agreeing to go.
etymology: From Latin dubius; like doubt, from Latin duo (cognate to English two), implying “two alternatives” (yes or no, true or false, etc.).

definition: Two items of the same kind.
etymology: PIE word *dwóh₁ From Italian duetto (“short musical composition for two voices”), diminutive of due (“two”).

definition: A stiff flour pudding steamed or boiled usually and containing e.g. currants and raisins and citron.
etymology: Representing a northern England and Scots pronunciation of dough.

definition: In accordance with what is appropriate or suitable for the circumstances.
example: I met the junior senator from Illinois and I was duly impressed.
etymology: From Middle English duely, dewly, dulyche, dueliche, duweliche (“rightly, properly”), equivalent to due + -ly.

definition: An informal expression for a mildly depressed state.
example: In the dumps.

definition: Treat cruelly.
example: Now, ya dun it!
etymology: Unknown; perhaps a variant of din. Several sources suggest origin from Joe Dun, the name of a bailiff known for arresting debtors, but this is controversial.

definition: Having a dun color.
A ridge of sand created by the wind; found in deserts or near lakes and oceans.
etymology: Partly from a dialectal form of down; and partly from Dutch duin (from Middle Dutch dune) or from Middle Low German dûne; all ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *dūn, *dūnā, of uncertain origin;

definition: Permanence by virtue of the power to resist stress or force.
example: They advertised the durability of their products.
etymology: From Middle English durabilite, from Old French durabilité, from Latin dūrābilitās (“durability”). Corresponding to durable + -ity.

definition: The time of day immediately following sunset.
example: Witnessing the dusk gives a feeling of solace.
etymology: From Middle English dosk, dusk(e) (“dusky”, adj.), from Old English dox (“dark, swarthy”), from Proto-Germanic *duskaz (“dark, smoky”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰwes-, related to *dʰewh₂- (“smoke, mist, haze”).

definition: A dry swab for dusting floors.
Creeping European clover having white to pink flowers and bright green leaves; naturalized in United States; widely grown for forage.
Shrubby chestnut tree of southeastern United States having small edible nuts.
Tiny grey woolly tufted annual with small golden-yellow flower heads; southeastern California to northwestern Arizona and southwestern Utah; sometimes placed in genus Eriophyllum.
Low-growing spring-flowering American iris with bright blue-lilac flowers.
Widely distributed boreal shrubby willow with partially underground creeping stems and bright green glossy leaves.
(used of color) artificially produced; not natural.
Someone whose job is to dye cloth.
etymology: From dye + -er.

definition: Impaired in function; especially of a bodily system or organ.
example: Live dysfunctional, likely die dysfunctional; live eufunctional, likely die eufunctional.
etymology: From dysfunction + -al.

definition: An alert and energetic person.
With eagerness; in an eager manner.
example: The news was eagerly awaited.
etymology: From Middle English egrely, egerly; equivalent to eager + -ly.

definition: A non-pierced earring of varying size (i.e. small wrap or hook big enough to hang over the whole ear and dangle) worn on the rim of the ear.
Widely distributed edible fungus shaped like a human ear and growing on decaying wood.
The fleshy pendulous part of the external human ear.
Of plants that bloom during the spring.
Of or belonging to or characteristic of this earth as distinguished from heaven.
example: Earthly beings.
etymology: From Middle English erthely, erthlich, ierðlich, from Old English eorþlīċ, corresponding to earth + -ly. Cognate with Old Norse jarðligr (“earthly”).

definition: The concerns of this life as distinguished from heaven and the afterlife.
(of pain or sorrow) made easier to bear.
A change for the better.
Medium-sized spruce of eastern North America; chief lumber spruce of the area; source of pulpwood.
Someone who consumes food for nourishment.
example: A very fussy eater.
etymology: From Middle English eter, etere, etter, from Old English etere; equivalent to eat + -er (agent noun suffix) or + -er (patient suffix) (food suitable for eating).

definition: A very dark black.
Fruit and timber trees of tropical and warm regions including ebony and persimmon.
Tropical tree of southern Asia having hard dark-colored heartwood used in cabinetwork.

(of sounds) repeating by reflection.

Mobilization of the economy.
Feeling great rapture or delight.

Suggestive of the supernatural; mysterious.

Coming next after the seventeenth in position.

definition: Use of physical or mental energy; hard work.
A man whose advice is highly respected.
Subject to popular election.

Freshwater catfish of the Nile and tropical central Africa having an electric organ.

A socket into which a lightbulb can be inserted.
A toothbrush with an electric motor in the handle that vibrates the head of the brush.
A typewriter powered by an electric motor.
Converter that converts alternating current into direct current or vice versa.
A person who installs or repairs electrical or telephone lines.

Collider that consists of an accelerator that collides electrons and positrons.

The branch of electronics that deals with beams of electrons and their focusing and deflection by magnetic fields.
(telecommunication) converter for converting a signal from one frequency to another.
Deliberate radiation or reflection of electromagnetic energy for the purpose of disrupting enemy use of electronic devices or systems.
By electronic means.

definition: A refined quality of gracefulness and good taste.

definition: The latest possible moment.

Any of various trees of the genus Ulmus: important timber or shade trees.

Drawn out or made longer spatially.

definition: Possessing or existing in bodily form.

definition: (botany) a minute rudimentary plant contained within a seed or an archegonium.
etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin embryō, from Ancient Greek ἔμβρυον (émbruon, “fetus”), from ἐν (en, “in-”) + βρύω (brúō, “to grow, swell”).

definition: Honorably retired from assigned duties and retaining your title along with the additional title ‘emeritus’ as in ‘professor emeritus’.

Migration from a place (especially migration from your native country in order to settle in another).

etymology: From Ancient Greek ἐν (en, “in”) + δῆμος (dêmos, “people”) + -ic. Possibly via Ancient Greek ἔνδημος (éndēmos, “among one's people, at home, native”) and/or French endémique. By surface analysis, en- + demic.

definition: A disease that is constantly present to a greater or lesser degree in people of a certain class or in people living in a particular location.

Arouse or elicit a feeling.

definition: A journey taken for pleasure.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin excursiō (“a running out, an inroad, invasion, a setting out, beginning of a speech”), from excurrere (“to run out”), from ex (“out”) + currere (“to run”). By surface analysis, excurse + -ion.

definition: A reduced rate for a round-trip ticket.
Granted exemption.

definition: Worthy of imitation.

Put to use.

A series derived from the expansion of an exponential expression.
In an exponential manner.

Performing gestures or possessing qualities or features that suggest a certain state of being or emotion.
