Presiding officer of a school.
etymology: From head + master.

definition: Electro-acoustic transducer for converting electric signals into sounds; it is held over or inserted into the ear.
A person skilled in a particular type of therapy.
example: Faith healer.
etymology: From Middle English helere, the agent noun of heal; analysed as heal + -er. Cognate with Dutch heler (“healer”), German Heiler (“healer”), Icelandic heilari (“healer”).

definition: A large number or amount.
Full of sorrow.
example: When he told me he didn't want to see me anymore, I was heartbroken.
etymology: From heart + broken.

definition: Sincerely earnest.
example: Heartfelt condolences.
etymology: From heart + felt.

definition: The central region of a country or continent; especially a region that is important to a country or to a culture.
example: The home counties are the Conservative heartland.
etymology: From heart (“(figuratively) centre, core, essence”) + land.

definition: Lacking in feeling or pity or warmth.
example: His heartless actions and cold manner left her saddened and feeling alone.
etymology: From Middle English hertles, herteles, from Old English heortlēas (“without courage; listless”), equivalent to heart + -less. Cognate with German herzlos.

definition: Showing warm and heartfelt friendliness.
example: A hearty welcome.
etymology: Equivalent to heart + -y.

definition: A condition marked by dizziness and nausea and weakness caused by depletion of body fluids and electrolytes.
(of a chemical reaction or compound) occurring or formed with absorption of heat.
Extinct prairie chicken.
European herb bearing small tubers used for food and in Scotland to flavor whiskey.
An influential person who works hard to promote the causes they are interested in.
A syllable with a branching nucleus or a branching rime.
example: A heavy syllable consists of a long vowel or a diphthong, or a short vowel followed by one or more consonants in the same syllable.

definition: (of movement) lacking ease or lightness.
example: His tired heavy-footed walk.

definition: Marked by intense agitation or emotion.
example: The city center is so hectic at 8 in the morning that I go to work an hour beforehand to avoid the crowds.

definition: Shrubby Eurasian maple often used as a hedge.
Stiffly branching Old World annual with pale yellow flowers; widely naturalized in North America; formerly used medicinally.
Small brownish European songbird.
South African shrub having forked spines and plumlike fruit; frequently used as hedging.
Common European violet that grows in woods and hedgerows.
Paying particular notice (as to children or helpless people).
example: He spends without heed to the consequences.

definition: (of a person) possessing physical strength and weight; rugged and powerful.
example: A hefty athlete.
etymology: 19th century. From heft (“weight”) + -y. The similarity with German heftig (“vigorous, violent, intense”) is apparently coincidental. From the German are Dutch, Danish, Norwegian heftig, Swedish häftig.

definition: Extremely wicked, deeply criminal.
example: Heinous accusations.

definition: The act of stealing.
etymology: Probably pronunciation variation of hoist.

definition: A very light colorless element that is one of the six inert gasses; the most difficult gas to liquefy; occurs in economically extractable amounts in certain natural gases (as those found in Texas and Kansas).
etymology: From New Latin helium, from Ancient Greek ἥλιος (hḗlios, “sun”) (because its presence was first theorised in the Sun's atmosphere) with the suffix + -ium. Probably coined by Norman Lockyer.

definition: The series of inert gases.
A curve that lies on the surface of a cylinder or cone and cuts the element at a constant angle.
example: Helix piercing.
etymology: From Latin helix, from Ancient Greek ἕλιξ (hélix, “something twisted or spiral”).

definition: Someone who is a very fierce fighter.
100 halers equal 1 koruna Slovakia.
etymology: Borrowed from German Heller. Doublet of halier.

definition: A person who contributes to the fulfillment of a need or furtherance of an effort or purpose.
etymology: From Middle English helpere, from Old English *helpere, from Proto-West Germanic *helpārī (“helper”), equivalent to help + -er.

definition: A plant fiber.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English hemp, from Old English henep, from Proto-West Germanic *hanapi, from Proto-Germanic *hanapiz. Doublet of cannabis and canvas.

definition: Seed of cannabis plant; can be eaten raw, ground into a meal, sprouted, or made into dried sprout powder.
Nontechnical term for any hawks said to prey on poultry.
A severe form of hepatitis.
Of or relating to herbs.
example: Herbal tea, herbal medicine.
etymology: borrowed from Old French herbal. By surface analysis, herb + -al

definition: A medicine made from plants and used to prevent or treat disease or promote health.
Tea-like drink made of leaves of various herbs.
The use of plants or plant extracts for medicinal purposes (especially plants that are not part of the normal diet).
Occurring among members of a family usually by heredity.
example: Duke is a hereditary title which was created in Norman times.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English hereditarie, from Latin hērēditārius, from hērēditās (“inheritance”), from hērēs (“heir”).

definition: A disease or disorder that is inherited genetically.
A disease or disorder that is inherited genetically.
(genetics) attributes acquired via biological heredity from the parents.
Any opinions or doctrines at variance with the official or orthodox position.
The qualities of a hero or heroine; exceptional or heroic courage when facing danger (especially in battle).
example: He showed great heroism in battle.
etymology: From French héroïsme, equivalent to hero + -ism.

definition: Viral diseases causing eruptions of the skin or mucous membrane.
etymology: From Latin herpēs, from Ancient Greek ἕρπης (hérpēs, “herpes”, literally “a creeping”), from ἕρπειν (hérpein, “to creep”).

definition: Any of the animal viruses that cause painful blisters on the skin.
Valuable flesh of fatty fish from shallow waters of northern Atlantic or Pacific; usually salted or pickled.
etymology: From Middle English hering, from Old English hǣring, from Proto-West Germanic *hāring (“herring”), further etymology unknown.

definition: Based on pickled herring.
Lacking decisiveness of character; unable to act or decide quickly or firmly.
example: I am hesitant to recommend him as a manager because he has a short temper.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin haesitans, present participle of haesitare (“to stick fast, to hesitate”).

definition: Of or pertaining to a number system having 16 as its base.
etymology: First attested about 1830, from Pennsylvania German hexe (“to practice witchcraft”), from German hexen (compare Hexe (“witch”)). The noun appeared later, in the 1850s.

definition: A wrench for Allen screws.
An interruption in the intensity or amount of something.
example: The band decided to go on hiatus, citing creative differences.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin hiātus (“opening”) (mid-16th century), from hiō (“stand open, yawn”).

definition: Classified according to various criteria into successive levels or layers.
example: It has been said that only a hierarchical society with a leisure class at the top can produce works of art.
etymology: From hierarchy + -ical; compare French hiérarchique.

definition: A structure of data having several levels arranged in a treelike structure.
A vowel sound made with your tongue near the top of your mouth.
Being in a tense state.
example: A high-strung guitar.

definition: Pretentiously elegant.
example: A high-toned restaurant.

definition: Being in a tense state.
The quality of being high or lofty.
etymology: From Middle English hyghnesse; equivalent to high + -ness.

definition: A public secondary school usually including grades 9 through 12.
example: He goes to the neighborhood highschool.

definition: The side or slope of a hill.
etymology: From hill + side.

definition: The back limb of a quadruped.
A posterior appendage such as a leg or the homologous structure in other animals.
Be a hindrance or obstacle to.
example: A drought hinders the growth of plants.
etymology: From Middle English hindren, from Old English hindrian, from Proto-Germanic *hindrōną, *hinderōną (“to hinder”), from Proto-Germanic *hinder (“back”) (adverb).

definition: Understanding the nature of an event after it has happened.
example: Hindsight is always better than foresight.
etymology: From hind + sight, 19th c. Compare Latinate retrospect.

definition: A joint that holds two parts together so that one can swing relative to the other.
etymology: From Middle English henge (“hinge”), from Old English *henġ or *henġe (“hinge”), from Proto-West Germanic *hangiju or *hangī; compare Old English *henġe- in henġeclif (“overhanging cliff”), Old English henġen (“hanging;

definition: A freely moving joint in which the bones are so articulated as to allow extensive movement in one plane.
Be contingent on.
etymology: 1700, hinge (verb) + on.

definition: Be contingent on.
The socket part of the ball-and-socket joint between the head of the femur and the innominate bone.
Someone who rejects the established culture; advocates extreme liberalism in politics and lifestyle.
etymology: From hip + -ster. First attested for someone carrying something on their hip in the U.S. in the 1920s. Attested as a variant of hepster in the 1940s, for a follower of the latest fashions/trends/styles.

definition: The study of linguistic change.
A period of time spent in military service.
example: His truck sported a heavy-duty hitch for his boat.
etymology: Probably from Middle English hicchen, hytchen, icchen (“to move; to move as with a jerk”), of obscure origin. Lacks cognates in other languages. Compare itch, hike.

definition: Pull up.
example: He hitched up his socks and pants.

definition: An imaginary being similar to a person but smaller and with hairy feet; invented by J.R.R. Tolkien.
etymology: Coined in its current sense by J. R. R. Tolkien in the 1930s, featured in the novels The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings.

definition: Widely distributed in warm clear shallow streams.
Vine widely distributed in eastern North America producing racemes of purple to maroon flowers and abundant (usually subterranean) edible one-seeded pods resembling peanuts.
Tropical American tree having edible yellow fruit.
Widely distributed in warm clear shallow streams.
The quality of being holy.
etymology: From Middle English holynesse, holinesse, halinesse, from Old English hāliġnes (“holiness, a holy thing, rites”), from Proto-West Germanic *hailagnassī, equivalent to holy + -ness.

definition: Emphasizing the organic or functional relation between parts and the whole.
etymology: From hol- + -istic. See holism.

definition: Medical care of the whole person considered as subject to personal and social as well as organic factors.
example: Holistic medicine treats the mind as well as the body.

definition: The theory that the parts of any whole cannot exist and cannot be understood except in their relation to the whole.
example: Holism holds that the whole is greater than the sum of its parts.

definition: Eurasian perennial herb having pale pink flowers and curved pods; naturalized in Britain and North America grasslands on calcareous soils; important forage crop and source of honey in Britain.
An appliance that does a particular job in the home.
The state or condition of having no home (especially the state of living in the streets).
etymology: From homeless + -ness.

definition: The opening page of a web site; also, the first page opened when a web browser is launched (default or start-up page).
The home and adjacent grounds occupied by a family.
etymology: From Middle English hamstede, hemstede (attested in placenames), from Old English hāmstede (“homestead”), from Proto-West Germanic *haimastadi (“homestead”). By surface analysis, home + stead.

definition: A law conferring privileges on owners of homesteads.
Nocturnal badger-like carnivore of wooded regions of Africa and southern Asia.
etymology: From their badger-like appearance and their liking for honey.

definition: Australasian bird with tongue and bill adapted for extracting nectar.
A honey-colored edible mushroom commonly associated with the roots of trees in late summer and fall; do not eat raw.
A gland (often a protuberance or depression) that secretes nectar.
Smelling of honey.
A disorderly outburst or tumult.
example: There was a big hoo-ha about it in the papers, and then the world completely forgot the matter.
etymology: Perhaps from Yiddish הו־האַ (hu-ha, “a hullabaloo”). The second sense is likely expressive; compare such similar terms in other languages as Spanish juju.

definition: A catch that holds the hood of a car shut.
An ornament on the front of the hood of a car emblematic of the manufacturer.
A long overcoat with a hood that can be pulled over the head.
A wrench with a hook that fits over a nut or bolt head.
A golf shot that curves to the left for a right-handed golfer.
example: He took lessons to cure his hooking.

definition: A light curved skeleton to spread out a skirt.
example: The cheese hoop, or cylinder in which the curd is pressed in making cheese.
etymology: From Middle English hoop, hoope, from Old English hōp (“mound, raised land;

definition: Vigorous spreading North American tree having dark brown heavy wood; leaves turn gold in autumn.
Pine of Australia and New Guinea; yields a valuable light even-textured wood.
etymology: The tree's bark has horizontal bands resembling hoops (compare image).

definition: Any of various harmless North American snakes that were formerly believed to take tail in mouth and roll along like a hoop.
A game played on a court by two opposing teams of 5 players; points are scored by throwing the ball through an elevated horizontal hoop.
example: Let's shoot some hoops!

definition: Prostrate European herb with small yellow flowers and curved black pods; naturalized in North America.
(of an automobile) having the engine modified to give extra power.
example: A hopped-up jalopy.

definition: Funnel-shaped receptacle; contents pass by gravity into a receptacle below.
example: To catch a big fish, use a hopper that jumps across the pond surface.
etymology: From Middle English hoppere, alteration of *hoppe (found in grashoppe (“grasshopper”)), from Old English *hoppa (“one who hops, hopper”), equivalent to hop + -er.

definition: Twining perennials having cordate leaves and flowers arranged in conelike spikes; the dried flowers of this plant are used in brewing to add the characteristic bitter taste to beer.
In a horizontal direction.
example: A gallery quite often is added to make use of space vertically as well as horizontally.
etymology: From horizontal + -ly.

definition: Of or relating to or caused by hormones.
example: Hormonal changes.
etymology: From hormone + -al.

definition: Yellow-flowered Eurasian glaucous herb naturalized in along sandy shores in eastern North America.
Causing fear or dread or terror.
example: Horrendous explosions shook the city.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin horrendus, future passive participle (gerundive) of horreō (“to dread”) + -ous.

definition: Of a dreadful kind.
example: The beginning art students displayed their horribly executed paintings with hopeful faces.
etymology: From Middle English horribly, horribely, horribliche, horriblelyche, equivalent to horrible + -ly.

definition: Exceedingly bad.
example: When she was bad she was horrid.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin horridus (“rough, bristly, savage, shaggy, rude”), from horrere (“to bristle”). See horrent, horror, ordure.

definition: Stricken with horror.
Provoking horror.
example: An alarming, even horrifying, picture.

definition: Stricken with horror.
Tree having palmate leaves and large clusters of white to red flowers followed by brown shiny inedible seeds.
etymology: Calque of translingual Castanea equina (literally “equine chestnut”).

definition: European herb somewhat resembling celery widely naturalized in Britain coastal regions and often cultivated as a potherb.
The back of a horse.
example: They came on horseback across the plains.
etymology: From Middle English horsebacke, horsebak, horsbak, equivalent to horse + back.

definition: A person skilled in equitation.
The sport of sitting on the back of a horse while controlling its movements.
A lodging for travelers (especially one kept by a monastic order).
etymology: Borrowed from French hospice, from Old French hospise, from Latin hospitium (“hospitality, an inn”). Doublet of hospitium.

definition: A chaplain in a hospital.
Occupancy rate for hospitals.
A hotel providing overnight lodging for travelers.
etymology: From Middle English hostel, from Old French hostel, ostel, from Late Latin hospitale (“hospice”), from Classical Latin hospitalis (“hospitable”) itself from hospes (“host”) + -alis (“-al”). Doublet of hotel and hospital.

definition: A woman host.
example: The host and hostess greeted their guests at the door.
etymology: From Middle English hostesse, from Middle French hostesse, from Old French ostesce, made up of oste (“host”) + -esce (“feminine marker”).

definition: Fighting; acts of overt warfare.
example: The outbreak of hostilities.

definition: Prone to emotion.
example: Hot-blooded Latin-Americans.

definition: Occupancy rate for hotels.
A telephone line that provides direct and prompt information or advice to the caller in relation to a specific subject.
example: If you've got any problems with the product, ring our hotline.
etymology: From hot + line.

definition: Any of several breeds of dog used for hunting typically having large drooping ears.
example: The hounds were baying a fox.
etymology: From Middle English hounden, from the noun (see above).

definition: Any of several breeds of dog used for hunting typically having large drooping ears.
Small hardy brown-and-grey bird native to Europe.
An appliance that does a particular job in the home.
etymology: From household + appliance.

definition: A servant who is employed to perform domestic task in a household.
example: She was their third housekeeper, but after a month or so she also gave up.
etymology: From house + keeper.

definition: A wife who manages a household while her husband earns the family income.
etymology: From Middle English houswyf, housewif, huswijf, equivalent to house + wife;

definition: Be undecided about something; waver between conflicting positions or courses of action.
etymology: The verb is derived from Middle English hoveren (“to float in the air, hover; to stay”), probably from hoven (“hover; of a bird: to fly high in the air, soar”) (which it displaced) + -er- (frequentative suffix).

definition: Extraordinarily good or great; used especially as intensifiers.
example: A howling success.
etymology: From Middle English howlynge, howelynge, equivalent to howl + -ing (gerund suffix).

definition: A married man; a woman's partner in marriage.
example: Laura thought Jack was the most wonderful hubby in the world.
etymology: Diminutive of husband + -y.

definition: Take on color or become colored.
example: In highlights it hued to a dull silver-grey.
etymology: From Middle English hewe, from Old English hīew (“appearance, form, species, kind; apparition; hue, color; beauty;

definition: Marked by humanistic values and devotion to human welfare.
example: Released the prisoner for humanitarian reasons.

definition: Subdued or brought low in condition or status.
example: 1656 The Humbled Sinner Resolved what He Should Do to be Saved, title of book by Obadiah Sedgwick.

definition: Subdued or brought low in condition or status.
Causing awareness of your shortcomings.
A light movable barrier that competitors must leap over in certain races.
A footrace in which contestants must negotiate a series of hurdles.
An oil lamp with a glass chimney and perforated metal lid to protect the flame from high winds; candlestick with a glass chimney.
Causing hurt.
example: Her hurtful unconsidered words.
etymology: From hurt + -ful.

definition: Become quiet or still; fall silent.
example: Hush my baby!
etymology: From Middle English huschen (“to hush”) (as past participle husht (“silent; hushed”) and interjection husht (“quiet!”)). Cognate with Low German huschen, hüssen (“to hush; lull”), German huschen (“to shoo;

definition: A bribe paid to someone to insure that something is kept secret.
example: The scandal was even greater when it was announced that hush money had been paid to keep the faulty products unannounced.

definition: Deep-fried cornbread ball (southern).
Cover up a misdemeanor, fault, or error.
example: Hush up now; you have talked too much.

definition: Muscular and heavily built.
example: Clothing sizes for husky boys.
etymology: From husk + -y; in relation to voice, from the sense "dry as a husk" or "tough as a husk".

definition: Trouble that cannot be overcome by a single effort because of its many aspects or its persistent and pervasive quality.
example: We may be facing a hydra that defies any easy solution.
etymology: After the Hydra, from Greek mythology, which grew two new heads every time one of its heads was cut off.

definition: Containing combined water (especially water of crystallization as in a hydrate).
example: Stay hydrated.

definition: A colorless corrosive gas (HCl).
(chemistry, physics) an electrode in which hydrogen gas is adsorbed on platinum.
A common disorder in which blood pressure remains abnormally high (a reading of 140/90 mm Hg or greater).
etymology: From hyper- + tension.

definition: A state that resembles sleep but that is induced by suggestion.
example: Clinical hypnosis.
etymology: From modern scholarly Ancient Greek ὕπνωσις (húpnōsis), which formation closes the derivational gap between the ancient words ὑπνόω (hupnóō, “I put to sleep”) and ὑπνωτικός (hupnōtikós, “sleep-inducing, soporific”).

definition: A person who professes beliefs and opinions that he or she does not hold in order to conceal his or her real feelings or motives.
etymology: From Old French ypocrite (Modern French hypocrite), from Latin hypocrita, from Ancient Greek ὑποκριτής (hupokritḗs, “actor, hypocrite”), from ὑποκρίνομαι (hupokrínomai, “to answer, act, feign”).

definition: Professing feelings or virtues one does not have.
example: Hypocritical praise.

definition: Characterized by or arising from psychoneurotic hysteria.
example: During hysterical conditions various functions of the human body are disordered.
etymology: From hysteric + -al, from Latin hystericus, from Ancient Greek ὑστερικός (husterikós, “suffering in the womb, hysterical”), from ῠ̔στέρᾱ (hŭstérā, “womb”).

definition: An ax used by mountain climbers for cutting footholds in ice.
A rink with a floor of ice for ice hockey or ice skating.
example: The crowd applauded when she skated out onto the ice.

definition: Obstructed by ice.
example: Ice-clogged rivers.

definition: Someone who engages in ice skating.
A large mass of ice floating at sea; usually broken off of a polar glacier.
A strong sweetened coffee served over ice with cream.
Strong tea served over ice.
The formation of frost or ice on a surface.
example: The Cessna pilots reported that moderate icing was present between 13,000 and 4,000 feet in the cloud layers.
etymology: Gerund of the verb to ice.

definition: Finely powdered sugar used to make icing.
Capable of being identified.
example: I don't know where he was from because he had no identifiable accent.
etymology: From identify + -able.

definition: Insanely irresponsible.
example: An idiotic idea.
etymology: From idiot + -ic.

definition: Cause to start burning; subject to fire or great heat.
example: Great heat can ignite almost any dry matter.

definition: An induction coil that converts current from a battery into the high-voltage current required by spark plugs.
Contrary to or forbidden by law.
example: An illegitimate seizure of power.
etymology: First attested in 1536, from Latin illēgitimus, most likely an adapted borrowing of Middle French illegitime, equivalent to il- + legitimate, see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3).

definition: The illegitimate offspring of unmarried parents.
Not able to read or write.
example: About half of the population in Ethiopia is illiterate.
etymology: First attested in 1425–1475, in Middle English;

definition: A person unable to read.
Introduce light into.
example: Say my name / and every color illuminates. / We are shining / […].
etymology: From Latin illūminātus, see Etymology 1 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more. For sense 3, see also Lumières.

definition: A condition of spiritual awareness; divine illumination.
example: The room was filled with soft illumination from the candles.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French illumination, from Late Latin illūminātiō, from Latin illumino. Equivalent to illuminate + -ion.

definition: A measure of illumination.
An artist who makes illustrations (for books or magazines or advertisements etc.).
Widely known and esteemed.
example: An illustrious judge.
etymology: From Latin illūstris (“bright, shining; distinguished, prominent, illustrious”) + -ous (suffix forming adjectives from nouns, to denote possession or presence of a quality in any degree).

definition: Capable of being imagined.
etymology: From Middle English ymaginable, from Latin imāginābilis; equivalent to imagine + -able.

definition: (used of persons or artifacts) marked by independence and creativity in thought or action.
example: An imaginative use of material.
etymology: From Middle English ymagynatif, from Middle French imaginatif, from Medieval Latin imāginātīvus. By surface analysis, imagine + -ative.

definition: The kind of mental comparison that is expressed in similes or metaphors or allegories.
A lack of balance or state of disequilibrium.
example: A hormonal imbalance.

definition: Reproduce someone's behavior or looks.
example: The mime imitated the passers-by.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin imitātus, perfect active participle of imitor (“to copy, portray, imitate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Cognate with French imiter.

definition: The doctrine that representations of nature or human behavior should be accurate imitations.
example: A pale imitation.
etymology: From Middle English imitacioun, from Middle French imitacion, from Old French imitacion, from Latin imitatio.

definition: Fabric made to look like leather.
Completely neat and clean.
example: The apartment was immaculate.
etymology: From Late Middle English immaculat, immaculate (“blameless; flawless, spotless;

definition: Sinking until covered completely with water.
etymology: From late Middle English, borrowed from Late Latin immersiō, immersiōnem (“dipping”).

definition: Resembling frostbite but without freezing; resulting from exposure to cold and wet.
Deliberately violating accepted principles of right and wrong.
etymology: From im- + moral.

definition: The quality or state of being immortal.
example: In Greek mythology, Tithonus was granted immortality but not eternal youth.
etymology: From Middle English immortalitee, immortalite, from Old French immortalité, from Latin immortālitās. Morphologically immortal + -ity.

definition: Fracture in which one broken end is wedged into the other broken end.
Showing lack of favoritism.
example: The cold neutrality of an impartial judge.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French impartial. See im- + partial.

definition: Without fault or error.
example: Speaks impeccable French.
etymology: From Middle French impeccable, from Latin impeccabilis (“not liable to sin”), from im- (“not”) + peccare (“to err, to sin”).

definition: A verb in the imperative mood.
Not perfect; defective or inadequate.
example: Had only an imperfect understanding of his responsibilities.
etymology: From Middle English imperfit, from Old French imparfit (modern French imparfait), from Latin imperfectus. Spelling modified 15c. to conform Latin etymology. See im- + perfect.

definition: A tense of verbs used in describing action that is on-going.
Largest known mammoth; of America.
Large American moth having yellow wings with purplish or brownish markings; larvae feed on e.g. maple and pine trees.
A force that moves something along.
example: The outbreak of World War II in 1939 gave a new impetus to receiver development.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin impetus (“a rushing upon, an attack, assault, onset”), from impetō (“to rush upon, attack”), from in- (“upon”) + petō (“to seek, fall upon”).

definition: Fix or set securely or deeply.
example: The dentist implanted a tooth in the gum.
etymology: From Middle French implanter, from Latin implantō. By surface analysis, im- + plant.

definition: (used especially of ideas or principles) deeply rooted; firmly fixed or held.
example: Implanted convictions.

definition: Culpably involved.
example: Named three officials implicated in the plot.

definition: Implied though not directly expressed; inherent in the nature of something.
example: An implicit agreement not to raise the subject.
etymology: From Middle French implicite, from Latin implicitus, past participle of implico (“to infold, involve, entangle”); see implicate.

definition: In the nature of something though not readily apparent.
The commercial activity of buying and bringing in goods from a foreign country.
Poor enough to need help from others.
example: The impoverished soil here can not support any crop.

definition: Not practical; not workable or not given to practical matters.
example: Refloating the ship proved impractical because of the expense.
etymology: From im- + practical.

definition: A distinctive influence.
example: English stills bears the imprint of the Norman invasion.
etymology: From Old French empreinte, from the past participle of empreindre, from Latin imprimere.

definition: Not likely to be true or to occur or to have occurred.
example: An improbable event.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin improbābilis. By surface analysis, im- + probable.

definition: A fraction whose numerator is larger than the denominator.
In an improper way.
example: He checked whether the wound had healed improperly.
etymology: From Middle English improprelich, impropreliche, impropurly, inproperlye; equivalent to improper + -ly or im- + properly.

definition: Done or made using whatever is available.
example: Crossed the river on improvised bridges.

definition: A relay that maintains either contact position indefinitely without power applied to the coil.
A turbine that is driven by jets direct against the blades.
Proceeding from natural feeling or impulse without external stimulus.
example: An impulsive gesture of affection.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French impulsif, from Latin impulsivus.

definition: In a hurried or hasty manner.
example: Hastily, he scanned the headlines.

definition: In position.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin in + sitū, ablative singular of situs.

definition: Without losing equilibrium.
example: She took all his criticism in stride.

definition: Of a biological process occurring in an artificial environment outside the living organism.
example: In vitro fertilization.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin in vitro, from vitrum (“glass”).

definition: Of a biological process occurring within a living organism.
example: In vivo techniques.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin in vīvō.

definition: Being in the original position; not having been moved.
example: An in-situ investigator.

definition: Capable of being reached only with great difficulty or not at all.
example: Physically inaccessible.
etymology: From Middle French inaccessible, from Late Latin inaccessibilis, equivalent to in- + accessible. Piecewise doublet of unaccessible.

definition: Without knowledge or intention.
etymology: From inadvertent + -ly.

definition: Directed or moving inward or toward a center.
example: The inbound train.
etymology: From in- + bound.

definition: A new personification of a familiar idea.
example: The incarnation of evil.
etymology: From Middle English incarnacion, borrowed from Old French incarnacion, from Medieval Latin, Ecclesiastical Latin incarnatio, from Late Latin incarnari (“to be made flesh”).

definition: A substance that produces a fragrant odor when burned.
etymology: From Middle English encens, from Old French encens (“sweet-smelling substance”) from Late Latin incensum (“burnt incense”, literally “something burnt”), neuter past participle of incendō (“to set on fire”).

definition: Any of various tropical trees of the family Burseraceae yielding fragrant gums or resins that are burned as incense.
Fragrant wood of two incense trees of the genus Protium.
(sometimes followed by ‘to’) minor or casual or subordinate in significance or nature or occurring as a chance concomitant or consequence.
example: Incidental expenses.
etymology: From incident + -al.

definition: (frequently plural) an expense not budgeted or not specified.
example: He requested reimbursement of $7 for incidental expenses.

definition: Music composed to accompany the action of a drama or to fill intervals between scenes.
example: The incidental music helped give the programme its evocative atmosphere.

definition: An attitude of mind especially one that favors one alternative over others.
example: He had an inclination to give up too easily.
etymology: From Middle English inclinacioun, inclinacyon, from Old French inclination and Latin inclīnātiō. Morphologically incline + -ation.

definition: Not compatible.
example: Incompatible personalities.
etymology: Borrowed from French incompatible.

definition: Lack of physical or intellectual ability or qualifications.
etymology: From French incompétence, equivalent to in- + competence.

definition: Fracture that does not go across the entire width of the bone.
Take the trouble to do something; concern oneself.
Not suited to your comfort, purpose or needs.
example: It is inconvenient not to have a telephone in the kitchen.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French inconvenient, from Latin inconvenientem.

definition: Consolidating two or more things; union in (or into) one body.
example: After the city's incorporation into the capital district, the population rose.
etymology: From Middle English incorporacioun, from Old French incorporacion, from Late Latin incorporatio. By surface analysis, incorporate + -ion.

definition: Increasing gradually by regular degrees or additions.
example: Lecturers enjoy … steady incremental growth in salary.
etymology: From increment + -al.

definition: The increase or decrease in costs as a result of one more or one less unit of output.
Make oneself subject to; bring upon oneself; become liable to.
example: People who smoke incur a great danger to their health.
etymology: From Middle English incurren, from Anglo-Norman encurir, Middle French encourir, from Old French encorre, from Latin incurrere.

definition: Vague or not clearly defined or stated.
example: Must you be so indefinite?
etymology: From Late Latin indēfīnītus. Morphologically in- + definite.

definition: A determiner (as ‘a’ or ‘some’ in English) that indicates nonspecific reference.
The set of functions F(x) + C, where C is any real number, such that F(x) is the integral of f(x).
An estimated quantity.
An electrode that responds to the excitation signal without affecting the composition of the solution being measured.
example: The indicator electrode forms an electrochemical half cell with the interested ions in the test solution.

definition: Unbiased impartial unconcern.
example: His daughter's indifference towards the sexist group made him wonder if she felt no empathy for the bullied.
etymology: From Middle French indifférence, from Late Latin indifferentia. By surface analysis, in- + difference.

definition: In microeconomic theory, a graph showing different bundles of goods between which a consumer is indifferent.
Marked by a lack of interest.
example: The universe is neither hostile nor friendly; it is simply indifferent.
etymology: From Old French indifferent, from Latin indifferens. By surface analysis, in- + different.

definition: A blue dye obtained from plants or made synthetically.
Small deep blue North American bunting.
Deciduous subshrub of southeastern Asia having pinnate leaves and clusters of red or purple flowers; a source of indigo dye.
Large dark-blue nonvenomous snake that invades burrows; found in southern North America and Mexico.
Not to be dispensed with; essential.
example: Foods indispensable to good nutrition.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French indispensable, from Medieval Latin indispensābilis, corresponding to in- + dispensable.

definition: Act of bringing about a desired result.
example: Inducement of sleep.

definition: A coil for producing a high voltage from a low-voltage source.
Not producing desired results; wasteful.
example: An inefficient campaign against drugs.
etymology: From in- + efficient.

definition: Not eligible.
example: Ineligible to vote.
etymology: From French inéligible.

definition: The early stage of growth or development.
example: Space tourism is still in its infancy.
etymology: From Middle English infancie, from Latin īnfantia (“infancy, early childhood; childishness”), equivalent to infant + -cy.

definition: Communicate a disease to.
example: Your children have infected you with this head cold.
etymology: From Middle French infect, from Latin infectus, perfect passive participle of inficiō (“dye, taint”).

definition: The reasoning involved in drawing a conclusion or making a logical judgment on the basis of circumstantial evidence and prior conclusions rather than on the basis of direct observation.
etymology: From Latin inferentia. Morphologically infer + -ence.

definition: Any place of pain and turmoil.
example: The inferno of the engine room.
etymology: From Italian inferno (“hell”), from Latin infernus (“of the lower regions”), inferna (“the lower regions”); see infernal. The meaning "big fire" came as a figurative use from the traditional idea of hellfire.

definition: The quality of being unfaithful.
etymology: From Middle English infidelite, from Middle French infidelité (modern French infidélité) and its etymon Latin īnfidēlitās. Equivalent to infidel + -ity.

definition: Cause (a liquid) to enter by penetrating the interstices.
example: The spy infiltrated the high-tech company and stole many secrets.
etymology: From Middle English infiltrate (adjective), from Medieval Latin infiltrātus, from infiltrō.

definition: A health facility where patients receive treatment.
etymology: From Medieval Latin infirmaria, from Latin infirmus.

definition: Designed to be filled with air or gas.
example: An inflatable mattress.
etymology: From inflate + -able.

definition: Impose something unpleasant.
example: They inflicted terrible pains on her to obtain a confession.
etymology: From Latin īnflīctus, from in- + flīctus, past participle of īnflīgō (“to knock or strike against”), from in- + flīgō (“strike”).

definition: A person who supplies information.
etymology: From inform + -ant.

definition: Electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths longer than visible light but shorter than radio waves.
A solution obtained by steeping or soaking a substance (usually in water).
example: An extract of rooibos and chamomile makes a refreshing infusion.
etymology: From Middle English infusioun, from Old French infusion, from Latin infusio, infusionem (“a pouring into, a wetting, a dyeing, a flow”), from infundo.

definition: Showing inventiveness and skill.
example: An ingenious solution to the problem.

definition: Be an inhabitant of or reside in.
example: The people inhabited the islands that are now deserted.
etymology: From Old French enhabiter, from Latin inhabitāre (in + habitāre).

definition: Draw deep into the lungs in by breathing.
example: Clinton smoked marijuana but never inhaled.
etymology: From Latin inhalare (“to breathe on (breathe in)”), from in (“in, into, on”) + halare (“to breathe”).

definition: Prohibit, forbid, or prevent from doing something.
example: Contact between the young was inhibited by strict social customs.
etymology: From Latin inhibitus, perfect passive participle of inhibeō (“to hold in, check, restrain”), from in (“in, at, on”), + habeō (“to have, hold, keep”).

definition: (psychology) the conscious exclusion of unacceptable thoughts or desires.
etymology: From Middle English inhibicioun, inhibicione from Old French inibicion, from Latin inhibitio. Morphologically inhibit + -ion.

definition: A substance that retards or stops an activity.
example: I found daily meditation to be a useful inhibitor of negative thoughts.
etymology: From inhibit + -or.

definition: Without compunction or human feeling.
etymology: From Middle English inhumayne, from Middle French inhumain and its etymon Latin inhūmānus.

definition: A cruel act; a deliberate infliction of pain and suffering.
Give an injection to.
example: We injected the glucose into the patient's vein.
etymology: From Latin iniectus, injectus, participle of iniciō, injiciō (“to throw in”), from in- + iaciō (“I throw”).

definition: A formal command or admonition.
etymology: From Middle English iniunccyon, iniunccion, from Old French injonctïon, from Latin iniūnctiō (“command, injunction”).

definition: Cause injuries or bodily harm to.
example: The rugby team's star player got injured in a violent collision.
etymology: A back-formation from injury, from Middle English injurie, from Anglo-Norman injurie, from Latin iniūria (“injustice; wrong; offense”), from in- (“not”) + iūs, iūris (“right, law”).

definition: A cartridge that contains ink and can be replaced.
An arm off of a larger body of water (often between rocky headlands).
example: We hit a bad chop at the inlet.
etymology: From Middle English inlāte (“inlet, entrance”), from inleten (“to let in”), equivalent to in- + let. Compare Low German inlat (“inlet”), German Einlass (“inlet, entrance”).

definition: Not established by conditioning or learning.
example: Innate ideas.
etymology: The adjective is first attested in the 1420s, the verb in 1602;

definition: Immunity to disease that occurs as part of an individual's natural biologic makeup.
Address a question to and expect an answer from.
example: I inquired about their special today.
etymology: From Latin inquīrō (“to seek for”), composed of in- (“in, at, on; into”) + quaerō (“to seek, look for”), of uncertain origin, but possibly from Proto-Italic *kʷaizeō, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeh₂- (“to acquire”).

definition: A severe interrogation (often violating the rights or privacy of individuals).
etymology: From Old French inquisicion, from Latin inquisitio, from inquirere.

definition: In an insane manner.
example: She behaved insanely.
etymology: From insane + -ly.

definition: Written (by handwriting, printing, engraving, or carving) on or in a surface.
Not responsive to physical stimuli.
example: Insensitive to radiation.
etymology: From in- + sensitive.

definition: A message (spoken or written) that is introduced or inserted.
example: With many insertions in the margins.
etymology: From insert + -ion.

definition: A clinch with the end of the line inside the loop.
Exhibiting insight or clear and deep perception.
example: An insightful parent.
etymology: A recent formation from insight + -ful.

definition: Continual and persistent demands.
etymology: From Middle English insistence, derived from Old French insister (“to insist”). Compare Middle French insistance. Morphologically insist + -ence.

definition: An inability to sleep; chronic sleeplessness.
example: My mother suffers from insomnia.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin īnsomnia, from Latin in- (“without”) + somnus (“sleep”, noun) + -ia, equivalent to in- + somn- + -ia.

definition: As a matter of instinct.
example: He instinctively grabbed the knife.
etymology: From instinctive + -ly.

definition: Impart skills or knowledge to.
example: He instructed me in building a boat.
etymology: From Latin īnstrūctus, perfect passive participle of īnstruō (“I instruct; I arrange, furnish, or provide”).

definition: An artifact (that is instrumental in accomplishing some end) for accomplishing some end.
example: He had a wonderful instrumentation.
etymology: From instrument + -ation.

definition: Be careful or certain to do something; make certain of something.
example: I'm not insured against burglary.
etymology: First attested in c. 1440, as a variant of Middle English ensuren (from Anglo-Norman enseurer, itself from Old French en- + seür (“sure”), probably influenced by Old French asseürer (“to assure”));

definition: An organized rebellion aimed at overthrowing a constituted government through the use of subversion and armed conflict.
example: Suppress the insurgency by isolating the rebels from the rest of the population.
etymology: From insurgent + -cy.

definition: Any of the natural numbers (positive or negative) or zero.
example: An integer is a number that is not a fraction.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin integer (“whole”), from Proto-Italic *n̥tagros (“untouched”). Doublet of entier and entire. Related to English tact, thack, and thwack.

definition: The part of calculus that deals with integration and its application in the solution of differential equations and in determining areas or volumes etc.
Knowledge and intellectual ability.
example: He has a keen intellect.
etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin intellēctus (“understanding, intellect”), from Latin intellegō (“understand; reason”), from inter (“between, among”) + legō (“read”), with connotation of bind.

definition: Of or relating to the intellect.
example: Intellectually gifted children.
etymology: From intellectual + -ly.

definition: Made more intense.
example: The intensified scrutiny of the candidate's background.

definition: A multimedia system in which related items of information are connected and can be presented together.
The act of intercepting; preventing something from proceeding or arriving.
example: He resorted to the interception of his daughter's letters.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin interceptiō; compare French interception.

definition: A junction of highways on different levels that permits traffic to move from one to another without crossing traffic streams.
etymology: From Old French entrechange, by surface analysis, inter- + change.

definition: (mathematics, logic) such that the arguments or roles can be interchanged.
example: The arguments of the symmetric relation, ‘is a sister of,’ are interchangeable.
etymology: From interchange + -able.

definition: Reciprocally connected.
etymology: From inter- + connected.

definition: Drawing from or characterized by participation of two or more fields of study.
example: Interdisciplinary studies.
etymology: From inter- + disciplinary.

definition: An overhaul between the regular times for overhauling.
The trade or act of decorating the interior of a building or room, especially with regard to color combination, paint, fabrics, carpeting, etc.
A literary genre that presents a fictional character's sequence of thoughts in the form of a monologue.
Stopping and starting at irregular intervals.
example: Intermittent rain showers.
etymology: From Middle French intermittent, from Latin intermittens (“sending between”), from prefix inter- (“among, on”) + mittens (“sending”), from mittere (“to send”).

definition: An auditor who is an employee of the company whose records are audited and who provides information to the management and board of directors.
Occurring among or involving several people.
example: Interpersonal situations in which speech occurs.
etymology: From inter- + personal.

definition: An explanation of something that is not immediately obvious.
example: The edict was subject to many interpretations.

definition: Between races.
example: Interracial conflict.

definition: An act of delaying or interrupting the continuity.
etymology: From Middle English interrupcioun, from Old French interrupcion, from Latin interruptio.

definition: Interstellar space including streams of protons moving from the stars.
The space between stars.
Occurring or falling between events or points in time.
example: So much had happened during the intervening years.

definition: Of or relating to or inside the intestines.
example: Intestinal disease.
etymology: From Latin intestīnālis. By surface analysis, intestine + -al.

definition: Secretions by glands lining the walls of the intestines.
Make timid or fearful.
example: Her boss intimidates her.
etymology: From Medieval Latin intimidātus, perfect passive participle of Latin intimidō (“to intimidate, terrify”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from in- (“in”) + timidus (“afraid, timid”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix); see timid.

definition: Made timid or fearful as by threats.
The act of intimidating a weaker person to make them do something.
etymology: From intimidate + -ion. Compare French intimidation; perhaps modeled on it.

definition: Impatience with annoyances.
example: His intolerance of interruptions.
etymology: Borrowed from French intolérance, itself from in- (“not”) + tolérance or borrowed from Latin intolerantia (“insolence, insufferableness; (very rare) intolerance”). By surface analysis, in- + tolerance.

definition: Unwilling to tolerate difference of opinion.
example: I am intolerant of lactose, so I can't drink milk.
etymology: First attested in the first half of the 18th century; either borrowed from French intolérant (early 17th century) or from its source, Latin intolerāns.

definition: Stupefied or excited by a chemical substance (especially alcohol).
example: A noisy crowd of intoxicated sailors.

definition: A crafty and involved plot to achieve your (usually sinister) ends.
example: His betrayal was the beginning of a complex intrigue intended to give him control of the company.
etymology: Borrowed from French intrigue, from Italian intricare, from Latin intrīcō (“to entangle, perplex, embarrass”). Doublet of intricate.

definition: Belonging to a thing by its very nature.
example: Form was treated as something intrinsic, as the very essence of the thing.
etymology: From Middle French intrinsèque, from Latin intrīnsecus (“on the inside, inwardly”), from *intrim, an assumed adverbial form of inter (“within”) + secus (“by, on the side”).

definition: A substance produced by the mucosa of the stomach and intestines that is essential for the absorption of vitamin B12.
example: Lack of intrinsic factor can result in pernicious anemia.

definition: Fraud (as by use of forged documents or false claims or perjury) that misleads a court or jury and induces a finding for the one perpetrating the fraud.
Someone who intrudes on the privacy or property of another without permission.
example: All intruders will be shot!
etymology: From intrude + -er.

definition: Any entry into an area not previously occupied.
example: She viewed sales calls as an unwelcome intrusion.
etymology: From Middle English intrusioun, from Old French intrusion, from Medieval Latin intrūsiō, from intrūdō, from Latin in- + trūdō.

definition: Tending to intrude (especially upon privacy).
example: She felt her presence there was intrusive.
etymology: Back-formation from intrusion, + -ive.

definition: Without variation or change, in every case.
example: He is invariably late for meetings.
etymology: From invariable + -ly.

definition: (used of persons or artifacts) marked by independence and creativity in thought or action.
example: The invention of the knitting frame by another ingenious English clergyman.
etymology: From Middle English inventif, inventyfe, borrowed from Old French inventif, borrowed from Medieval Latin inventivus. By surface analysis, invent + -ive.

definition: Reversed (turned backward) in order or nature or effect.
example: Multiplication is the inverse operation to division.
etymology: Recorded since 1440, from Latin inversus, the past participle of invertere (“to invert”), itself from in- (“against, in”) + vertere (“to turn”).

definition: A function obtained by expressing the dependent variable of one function as the independent variable of another; f and g are inverse functions if f(x)=y and g(y)=x.
example: Halving is the inverse function of doubling.

definition: Being in such a position that top and bottom are reversed.
example: A quotation mark is sometimes called an inverted comma.

definition: A hang performed on the rings with the body upside down.
Incapable of being overcome or subdued.
example: An invincible army.
etymology: From Middle French invincible, from Latin invincibilis (“unconquerable”), from in- (“not”) + vincibilis (“conquerable”), from vincere (“to conquer”).

definition: An itemized statement of money owed for goods shipped or services rendered.
example: I've already rendered the invoices for payment.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French envois pl, plural of envoi, from the verb envoyer (“to send”). See also envoy.

definition: Summon into action or bring into existence, often as if by magic.
example: The envoy invoked the King of Kings's magnanimity to reduce his province's tribute after another drought.
etymology: From Middle English *invoken, envoken, borrowed from Old French envoquer, from Latin invocāre (“to call upon”), itself from in- + vocare (“to call”). Doublet of invocate.

definition: Not subject to the control of the will.
example: Involuntary manslaughter.
etymology: From in- + voluntary, from Late Latin involontarius, from in + volontarius.

definition: A muscle that contracts without conscious control and found in walls of internal organs such as stomach and intestine and bladder and blood vessels (excluding the heart).
A trust created by a court (regardless of the intent of the parties) to benefit a party that has been wrongfully deprived of its rights.
Relating to or existing in the mind or thoughts.
example: A concern with inward reflections.
etymology: From Middle English inward, from Old English inweard, corresponding to in + -ward.

definition: Toward an axis, as in a sunflower; the oldest flowers are near the edge, the youngest in the center.
Moving or directed toward the center or axis, especially when spinning or traveling in a curve.
Biometric identification by scanning the iris of the eye.
example: Biometric technologies such as iris scanning.

definition: A foundry where cast iron is produced.
A spot caused the staining with rust or ink.
Pathology in which iron accumulates in the tissues; characterized by bronzed skin and enlarged liver and diabetes mellitus and abnormalities of the pancreas and the joints.
Metal shackles; for hands or legs.
example: He’s been clapped in irons!

definition: Extreme prejudice.
A strong spontaneous and irrational motivation.
example: The mass media and advertisers channel our irrational impulses.

definition: A motivation that is inconsistent with reason or logic.
Impossible to resist; overpowering.
example: Irresistible (or resistless) impulses.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin irresistibilis, equivalent to ir- + resistible.

definition: An urge to do or say something that might be better left undone or unsaid.
In spite of everything; without regard to drawbacks.
etymology: From ir- + respective.

definition: Incapable of being reversed.
example: Irreversible momentum toward revolution.
etymology: From ir- + reversible.

definition: Any process that is not reversible.
A ditch to supply dry land with water artificially.
The act of providing an item for general use or for official purposes (usually in quantity).
example: The issuance of an order.
etymology: From issue + -ance.

definition: Scrape or rub as if to relieve itching.
example: He started learning to drive and he has been itching for opportunities to practice ever since.
etymology: From Middle English icche, ȝicche, from Old English ġiċċe (“itch”), from Proto-Germanic *jukjǭ (“itch”), of unknown origin. Cognate with Scots yeuk (“itch, itchiness”), Dutch jeuk (“itch”), German jucken.

definition: An irritating cutaneous sensation that produces a desire to scratch.
etymology: From Middle English icchynge, ichynge, ycchenge, yecchyng, ʒicchunge (also unassibilated as ʒykynge), equivalent to itch + -ing.

definition: Very strong or irresistible impulse to travel.
A sharp hand gesture (resembling a blow).
example: He warned me with a jab with his finger.
etymology: Originally a Scottish (unclear if Scots or Scottish English) form of English job (“peck, poke, thrust”), from Middle English jobben.

definition: A man who is a stupid incompetent fool.
etymology: From jack + ass.

definition: A large bat of the southwestern United States having spots and enormous ears.
A game in which jackstones are thrown and picked up in various groups between bounces of a small rubber ball.
Vigorous Philippine evergreen twining liana; grown for spectacular festoons of green flowers that resemble lobster claws.
etymology: The bluish-green colour of the flowers is thought to resemble the precious stone jade.

definition: Extremely crowed or filled to capacity.
example: A suitcase jammed with dirty clothes.

definition: Deliberate radiation or reflection of electromagnetic energy for the purpose of disrupting enemy use of electronic devices or systems.
example: The broadcasts' effectiveness was limited by constant jamming.

definition: An annual of tropical Asia naturalized in United States.
An annual of tropical Asia naturalized in United States.
Any fungus of the order Tremellales or Auriculariales whose fruiting body is jellylike in consistency when fresh.
Propulsion by means of the discharge of a jet of fluid toward the rear.
Propelled by (or as if propelled by) a jet engine.
A holy struggle or striving by a Muslim for a moral or spiritual or political goal.
etymology: Borrowed from Arabic جِهَاد (jihād, “struggle; effort”).

definition: Continue talking or writing in a desultory manner.
example: This novel rambles on and jogs.
etymology: Of uncertain origin. Originally with the meaning of "to shake up and down." Possibly from Middle English joggen, a variant of jaggen (“to pierce, prod, stir up, arouse”); see jag (“sharp projection”).

definition: Running at a jog trot as a form of cardiopulmonary exercise.
example: His jogging of my memory helped me recall what happened that day.
etymology: From jog + -ing.

definition: Jointed and nearly leafless desert shrub having reduced scalelike leaves and reddish fleshy seeds.
A hinge with two long straps; one strap is fastened to the surface of a moving part (e.g., a door or lid) and the other is fastened to the adjacent stationary frame.
Variety of large almond from Malaga, Spain; used in confectionery.
Of or relating to or having the characteristics of journalism.
example: Journalistic writing.
etymology: From journal + -istic (“adjective”). Also parsed directly as journalist + -ic (“adjective”), also used in sense of related journalism (having to do with journalism).

definition: Full of or producing joy.
example: Make a joyful noise.
etymology: From joy + -ful.

definition: Full of or characterized by joy.
example: Felt a joyous abandon.
etymology: From Middle English joyous, joious, from Old French joieus, from joie + -eus.

definition: A special anniversary (or the celebration of it).
A one-way peephole in a door.
A sport adapted from jujitsu (using principles of not resisting) and similar to wrestling; developed in Japan.
example: He started doing judo at the age of eight.
etymology: Borrowed from Japanese 柔(じゅう)道(どう) (jūdō, literally “the soft way”).

definition: A large bottle with a narrow mouth.
example: 2014, Alan Kenworthy, Jugs: Buying, Caring For, Grooming, Health, Training and Understanding Your Jug Dog or Puppy, Feel Happy Limited.
etymology: From Middle English jugge, of uncertain origin. Possibly a variant of Middle English jubbe, jobbe, iubbe, geobbe, itself of unknown origin; or perhaps continuing (in altered form) Old English ċēac (“pitcher; jug”).

definition: A musical group that uses jugs and washboards and kazoos and other improvised instruments.
Inexpensive wine sold in large bottles or jugs.
Of great mass; huge and bulky.
example: A jumbo jet.
etymology: From Jumbo (1860–1885), the name given to a large African elephant from East Africa that was purchased in 1882 by American showman P. T. Barnum (1810–1891) for the Ringling Bros. and Barnum & Bailey Circus.

definition: A very large jet plane.
Orchid having both male and female flowers in the same raceme; when a sensitive projection at the base of the column of the male flower is touched the pollen is suddenly ejected.
Female jungle fowl.
An accumulation of refuse and discarded matter.
A group of military officers who rule a country after seizing power.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish junta (literally "a thing gathered or joined"), feminine form of junto, from Latin iunctus, perfect passive participle of iungō (“join”). Attested from 1623.

definition: A temporary mast to replace one that has broken off.
An outcome (good or bad) that is well deserved and fitting.
example: It may appear that they're getting ahead by cheating, but they'll get their just deserts in the end.

definition: Informal terms for money.
Australian annual sometimes cultivated for its racemes of purple flowers and edible yellow egg-shaped fruit.
Sluggish tailless Australian arboreal marsupial with grey furry ears and coat; feeds on eucalyptus leaves and bark.
An irregular unauthorized court.
etymology: From kangaroo + court. The etymology is uncertain;

definition: Small Australian wallaby that resembles a hare and has persistent teeth.
Small silky-haired pouched rodent; similar to but smaller than kangaroo rats.
Any of various leaping rodents of desert regions of North America and Mexico; largest members of the family Heteromyidae.
The 10th letter of the Greek alphabet.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek κάππα (káppa), ultimately from Proto-Semitic *kapp- (“palm, hand”). Doublet of kaph.

definition: Singing popular songs accompanied by a recording of an orchestra (usually in bars or nightclubs).
etymology: Borrowed from Japanese カラオケ (karaoke), from 空(から) (kara, “empty”) + オケ (oke, “orchestra”), a clipping of オーケストラ (ōkesutora), from English orchestra.

The basic unit of thermodynamic temperature adopted under the Systeme International d'Unites.

A player who kicks the football.

definition: Relating to the motion of material bodies and the forces associated therewith.

definition: Closed with a lace.

An athlete who plays lacrosse.

Flee; take to one's heels; cut and run.

Heat absorbed or radiated during a change of phase at a constant temperature and pressure.
The time that elapses between a stimulus and the response to it.
A milky exudate from certain plants that coagulates on exposure to air.

definition: A water-base paint that has a latex binder.
Strong espresso coffee with a topping of frothed steamed milk.

definition: An arrangement of points or particles or objects in a regular periodic pattern in 2 or 3 dimensions.
etymology: From Middle English latis, from Middle French lattis (“lathing”), from Old French lattis, from latte (“a lath”), from Frankish *lattu (“a lath”), from Proto-Germanic *laþô (“board; plank;

Armament in the form of a device capable of launching a rocket.

European willow tree with shining leathery leaves; widely naturalized in the eastern United States.

Branching aromatic Mediterranean shrub with woolly stems and leaves and yellow flowers.
Of pink tinged with lavender.
Very generous.

definition: (of individuals) adhering strictly to laws and rules and customs.

Soil composed mainly of decaying leaves.
Any of various small moths or dipterous flies whose larvae burrow into and feed on leaf tissue especially of the family Gracilariidae.
Having or covered with leaves.

Make legal.

Be applicable to; as to an analysis.

Common North American green or brownish frog having white-edged dark oval spots.

Any of several large lizards with many dark spots; of western United States and northern Mexico.
Decrease in size, extent, or range.

Malignant neoplasm of blood-forming tissues; characterized by abnormal proliferation of leukocytes; one of the four major types of cancer.

definition: An expected time to live as calculated on the basis of statistical probabilities.
A raft to use if a ship must be abandoned in an emergency.

A defensive football player who takes a position close behind the linemen.

Street names for gamma hydroxybutyrate.
Termination of a business operation by using its assets to discharge its liabilities.

Being four more than fifty.
The axle of a self-propelled vehicle that provides the driving power.
Small usually brightly-colored viviparous surface-feeding fishes of fresh or brackish warm waters; often used in mosquito control.
The financial means whereby one lives.

Loss of sensation in a small area of the body (as when a local anesthetic is injected for a tooth extraction).
A determination of the place where something is.

definition: Of or relating to lines of longitude.

definition: Plundering during riots or in wartime.

definition: A neoplasm of lymph tissue that is usually malignant; one of the four major types of cancer.

definition: Suitable for or suggestive of singing.

definition: A serviceman in the artillery.
