etymology: Borrowed from Spanish macho (“male”), from Latin masculus. Doublet of male.

definition: A light patterned cotton cloth.
etymology: From Madras, former name of the Indian city Chennai, where it was first produced.

definition: An artist of consummate skill.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian maestro, from Latin magistrum (“master”). Doublet of magister, master, and meister.

definition: In a magical manner.
example: It disappeared magically.
etymology: From magic + -ally or magical + -ly.

definition: A light silver-white ductile bivalent metallic element; in pure form it burns with brilliant white flame; occurs naturally only in combination (as in magnesite and dolomite and carnallite and spinel and olivine).
A white solid mineral that occurs naturally as periclase; a source of magnesium.
A measure of the strength of a magnetic field over a given area.
(physics) the angle that a magnetic needle makes with the plane of the horizon.
An imaginary line passing through both magnetic poles of the Earth.
A short strip of magnetic tape attached to a credit card or debit card; it contains data that will tell a reading device who you are and what your account number is, etc.
A large wine bottle for liquor or wine.
etymology: From Latin magnum, neuter of magnus (“great”). * (bottle): Ellipsis of magnum bonum. * (handgun): Name registered 1935 by Smith & Wesson Inc., of Springfield, Massachusetts.

definition: Wood of any of various mahogany trees; much used for cabinetwork and furniture.
etymology: A word of unknown origin, concocted in either English or Middle Dutch from one or more exotic phytonyms and common European words.

definition: Tropical trees and shrubs including many important timber and ornamental trees.
Any of various tropical timber trees of the family Meliaceae especially the genus Swietinia valued for their hard yellowish- to reddish-brown wood that is readily worked and takes a high polish.
Of brown tinged with red.
Pouch used in the shipment of mail.
A private box for delivery of mail.
etymology: From mail + box.

definition: The diagonal of a square matrix running from the upper left entry to the lower right entry.
example: In a diagonal matrix, non-zero elements appear only in the main diagonal.

definition: Rotor consisting of large rotating airfoils on a single-rotor helicopter that produce the lift to support the helicopter in the air.
Tall annual cereal grass bearing kernels on large ears: widely cultivated in America in many varieties; the principal cereal in Mexico and Central and South America since pre-Columbian times.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish maíz, from Taíno *mahis, *mahisi, from Proto-Arawak *marikɨ. Cognate with Lokono marisi, Wayuu maiki.

definition: The maximum lobe in the radiation pattern which is intended to be along the forward axis and which gives the effect of a beam.
An overall beauty treatment (involving a person's hair style and cosmetics and clothing) intended to change or improve a person's appearance.
Transmits the malaria parasite.
Parasitic protozoan of the genus Plasmodium that causes malaria in humans.
Fern of North America and Europe whose rhizomes and stalks yield an oleoresin used to expel tapeworms.
A failure to function normally.
etymology: From mal- (“bad, incorrect”) + function.

definition: Feeling a need to see others suffer.
example: Your voice positively drips malice.
etymology: From Middle English malice, borrowed from Old French malice, from Latin malitia (“badness, bad quality, ill-will, spite”), from malus (“bad”).

definition: Disgraceful gossip about the private lives of other people.
Professional wrongdoing that results in injury or damage.
example: The widow sued her surgeon for malpractice.
etymology: From mal- + practice.

definition: Treat with malt or malt extract.
etymology: From Middle English malt, from Old English mealt, from Proto-West Germanic *malt, from Proto-Germanic *maltą (“malt”), from *maltaz (“soft; nesh; weak; squashy;

definition: A lager of high alcohol content; by law it is considered too alcoholic to be sold as lager or beer.
A white crystalline sugar formed during the digestion of starches.
Whiskey distilled in Scotland; especially whiskey made from malted barley in a pot still.
Informal terms for a mother.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin mamma.

definition: So exceedingly large or extensive as to suggest a giant or mammoth.
example: A mammoth ship.
etymology: From obsolete Russian ма́мант (mámant), modern ма́монт (mámont), probably from a Uralic word, such as Proto-Mansi *mān-oŋt (“earth horn”). Possibly influenced by behemoth.

definition: A person who eats human flesh.
Capable of being managed or controlled.
etymology: From manage + -able.

definition: Showy crested Asiatic duck; often domesticated.
etymology: Native to Northeast China and Amur.

definition: Shrub or small tree having flattened globose fruit with very sweet aromatic pulp and thin yellow-orange to flame-orange rind that is loose and easily removed; native to southeastern Asia.
Injunction requiring the performance of some specific act.
Long coarse hair growing from the crest of the animal's neck.
etymology: From Middle English mane, mayne, from Old English manu (“mane”), from Proto-West Germanic *manu, from Proto-Germanic *manō (“mane”), from Proto-Indo-European *mony-, *mon- (“neck”).

definition: An irrational but irresistible motive for a belief or action.
Affected with or marked by frenzy or mania uncontrolled by reason.
example: Outbursts of drunken violence and manic activity and creativity.
etymology: From mania + -ic; Ancient Greek μανικός (manikós). Compare maniac.

definition: A mental disorder characterized by episodes of mania and depression.
A mood disorder; an affective disorder in which the victim tends to respond excessively and sometimes violently.
A clear appearance.
example: A manifestation of great emotion.
etymology: From Middle English manifestacion, manyfestacion, manyfestacioun; from Late Latin manifestātiō. In the political sense, a semantic loan from French manifestation. By surface analysis, manifest + -ation.

definition: A pipe that has several lateral outlets to or from other pipes.
etymology: From Middle English manifold, from Old English maniġfeald (“manifold, various, varied, complicated, numerous, abundant, plural”), from Proto-Germanic *managafalþaz, equivalent to many + -fold.

definition: A lightweight paper used with carbon paper to make multiple copies.
example: An original and two manifolds.

definition: Having a crew.
example: A manned earth satellite was considered a necessary research step.

definition: The force of workers available.
example: Phased increases in manpower.
etymology: From man + power.

definition: Homicide without malice aforethought.
etymology: From Middle English manslaȝter, manslauter, equivalent to man + slaughter, or taken as an adaptation of Old English mansliht (“murder; killing of a person”), from mann (“person”) + sliht (“killing”), see manslaught.

definition: Hare-like rodent of the Pampas of Argentina.
etymology: Borrowed from Old Norse mara, from Proto-Germanic *marǭ, cognate with Old English mare or mære. Doublet of mare. See nightmare.

definition: A cocktail made of tequila and triple sec with lime and lemon juice.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish margarita. Doublet of Margaret (and various forms, q.v.), margarite, Margherita, and marguerite.

definition: In a marginal manner.
example: Marginally interesting.
etymology: From marginal + -ly.

definition: In a clearly noticeable manner.
example: Sales of luxury cars dropped markedly.
etymology: From marked + -ly.

definition: Someone skilled in planning marketing campaigns.
Of purple tinged with maroon.
Having maroon spots.
Nobleman (in various countries) ranking above a count.
etymology: From Middle English markis, from Old French markis, marchis, from Late Latin marchensis, from Old High German marcha and Frankish *marku, from Proto-Germanic *markō, from Proto-Indo-European *mórǵs (“edge, boundary”).

definition: A business that arranges marriage contracts.
Any of various squash plants grown for their elongated fruit with smooth dark green skin and whitish flesh.
A wood rabbit of marshy coastal areas from North Carolina to Florida.
A coot found in North America.
Scrambling perennial of damp or marshy areas of Eurasia and North America with purplish flowers.
Any of various plants of the genus Limonium of temperate salt marshes having spikes of white or mauve flowers.
A cocktail made of gin (or vodka) with dry vermouth.
Extraordinarily good or great; used especially as intensifiers.
example: A marvelous collection of rare books.
etymology: First attested from 1300 as Middle English merveilous, from Old French merveillus, from merveille (“a wonder”) + -us. Doublet of merveilleux. See also marvel.

definition: Makeup that is used to darken and thicken the eye lashes.
example: Apply mascara.
etymology: From Italian maschera (“mask”).

definition: A rhyme of but a single stressed syllable, as in disdain, complain.
example: In English-language poetry, especially serious verse, masculine rhymes comprise a majority of all rhymes.

definition: Seed of the mung bean plant; used for food.
Potato that has been peeled and boiled and then mashed.
Solitary wasp that constructs nests of hardened mud or clay for the young.
Structure built of stone or brick by a mason.
example: He studied masonry for five years.
etymology: From Middle English masonry, masonrie, partly from Old French maçonerie and partly from mason + -ry.

definition: A condition in which a large group of people exhibit the same state of violent mental agitation.
The use of spectroscopy to determine the masses of small electrically charged particles.
Becoming proficient in the use of something; having mastery of.
example: His mastering the art of cooking took a long time.

definition: Someone who creates new things.
etymology: From master + mind.

definition: Mediation in order to bring about a marriage between others.
example: Patty, your timing is excellent. There's Claude over there. Want me to do some matchmaking?
etymology: From match + making.

definition: The pairing of people or things as for comparison or competition.
example: It was a good match-up but the home team won.
etymology: Deverbal from match up.

definition: An informal use of the Latin word for mother; sometimes used by British schoolboys or used facetiously.
etymology: From Latin māter (“mother”), partly via Late Middle English matere. Doublet of mata and mother. Ancestor of matrix.

definition: With respect to material aspects.
example: Psychologically similar but materially different.
etymology: From Middle English materialy; equivalent to material + -ly.

definition: A notation used by mathematicians.
Fully ripe; at the height of bloom.
Someone who exhibits great independence in thought and action.
example: Among historians he was a maverick because of his belief that history is meaningless.
etymology: Named after Texan lawyer and politician Samuel Maverick (1803–1870), who refused to brand his cattle. For probable origin and meaning, see Maverick.

definition: Used of women's clothing having a hemline at the ankle.
example: Wanted a maxi-length coat.
etymology: Back-formation from maximum on the analogy of minimum and mini.

definition: A saying that is widely accepted on its own merits.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman maxime and Middle French maxime, from Late Latin maxima (“axiom”), noun use of the feminine singular form of Latin maximus (apparently as used in the phrase prōpositiō maxima (“greatest premise”)).

definition: The willful and unlawful crippling or mutilation of another person.
example: To commit mayhem.
etymology: The noun is derived from Late Middle English mayehem, maihem, a late form of maym, maim (“disfigurement, injury, mutilation;

definition: Of or relating to a mayor or the office of mayor.
example: Mayoral elections.
etymology: From mayor + -al.

definition: Made of fermented honey and water.
etymology: From Middle English mede, from Old English medu, from Proto-West Germanic *medu, from Proto-Germanic *meduz, from Proto-Indo-European *médʰu (“honey; honey wine”).

definition: Common lily of the eastern United States having nodding yellow or reddish flowers spotted with brown.
Common edible mushroom found naturally in moist open soil; the cultivated mushroom of commerce.
Scrambling perennial Eurasian wild pea having yellowish flowers and compressed seed pods; cultivated for forage.

Any of various herbs of the genus Thalictrum; sometimes rhizomatous or tuberous perennials found in damp shady places and meadows or stream banks; have lacy foliage and clouds of small purple or yellow flowers.
The arithmetic mean of the absolute values of deviations from the mean of a distribution.
An acute and highly contagious viral disease marked by distinct red spots followed by a rash; occurs primarily in children.
etymology: Either from Middle Dutch masels (“blood blisters, measels”) or Middle Low German maselen (“red blemishes, measels”), both from Old High German masala (“blood blister, phlegmon”). Doublet of measlings.

definition: Capable of being measured.
example: Measurable depths.
etymology: From Old French mesurable, equivalent to measure + -able. Doublet of mensurable.

definition: A mill for grinding meat.
A baked loaf of ground meat.
A utensil consisting of a steel tank and mixing paddles, used for preparing meat for sausages.
In a mechanical manner; by a mechanism.
example: This door opens mechanically.
etymology: From mechanical + -ly.

definition: A negotiator who acts as a link between parties.
Any of several Old World herbs of the genus Medicago having small flowers and trifoliate compound leaves.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin medicus m (“of or belonging to healing, curative, medical; as a noun, medicus, masculine, a physician, doctor, surgeon”), Late Latin medica f (“a female physician, midwife”), from mederi (“to heal”).

definition: A prediction of the course of a disease.
Involving medical practice.
example: Medically trained nurses.
etymology: From medical + -ly.

definition: The ancient quarter of many cities in northern Africa.
example: Although Hicham usually worked in the new town, he still lived in the medina.
etymology: Borrowed from Arabic مَدِينَة (madīna, “town, city”).

definition: Reflect deeply on a subject.
etymology: First attested in 1560;

definition: A musical composition consisting of a series of songs or other musical pieces from various sources.
example: A fruit medley.
etymology: From Middle English medle, from Anglo-Norman medlee, Old French medlee, from the feminine past participle of early Medieval Latin misculō (“to mix”). Compare meddle. Doublet of melee.

definition: Humble in spirit or manner; suggesting retiring mildness or even cowed submissiveness.
example: Meek and self-effacing.
etymology: From Middle English meek, meke, meoc, probably a borrowing from Old Norse mjúkr (“soft; meek”), from Proto-Germanic *meukaz, *mūkaz (“soft; supple”), from Proto-Indo-European *mewg-, *mewk- (“slick, slippery; to slip”);

definition: Japanese ornamental tree with fragrant white or pink blossoms and small yellow fruits.
Unhurried and relaxed.
example: A mellow conversation.
etymology: The adjective is derived from Late Middle English melowe, melwe (“ripe, mellow; juicy; sweet”) [and other forms];

definition: Become more relaxed, easygoing, or genial.
example: With age, he mellowed.

definition: A bite of melon cut as a sphere.
Tropical American shrub or small tree having huge deeply palmately cleft leaves and large oblong yellow fruit.
A record of things worth remembering.
example: George has a collection of World War II memorabilia.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin memorābilia (“things to be remembered”); its use as noun is after Ancient Greek ἀπομνημονεύματα (apomnēmoneúmata) of the neuter plural of memorābilis (“memorable”).

definition: A written proposal or reminder.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin memorandum, neuter of memorandus (“to be remembered”).

definition: Sewing that repairs a worn or torn hole (especially in a garment).
example: Her stockings had several mends.
etymology: From Middle English menden (“to cure; to do good to, benefit; to do or make better, improve; to get better, recover; to keep in a good state; to put right, amend;

definition: A store where men's clothes are sold.
Sustained dull painful emotion.
Exhaustion that affects mental keenness.
The sound made by a cat (or any sound resembling this).
etymology: Alteration of earlier mew, from Middle English mewen, mouwen (“to mew, meow”), of onomatopoeic origin.

definition: Marked by materialism.
etymology: From Middle English mercenarye (“someone paid to work, hireling”), from Latin mercēnārius (“hired for money”), from mercēs (“reward, wages, price”).

definition: A dealer in textiles (especially silks).
etymology: From Anglo-Norman marcer, mercer (“merchant, textile merchant”), from merz (“commodity”) (from Latin merx).

definition: Showing or giving mercy.
example: Sought merciful treatment for the captives.
etymology: From Middle English merciful, mercyful, equivalent to mercy + -ful. Displaced native Old English mildheort.

definition: A white poisonous soluble crystalline sublimate of mercury; used as a pesticide or antiseptic or wood preservative.
The act of joining together as one.
example: The merging of the two groups occurred quickly.

definition: Of or happening at noon.
example: Meridian hour.
etymology: Sense 1.1 (“celestial meridian”) is ultimately modelled after Latin merīdiāna līnea (“meridian line”). Sense 5.2 (“midday rest; siesta”) is modelled after Late Latin meridiana (“midday;

definition: Small falcon of Europe and America having dark plumage with black-barred tail; used in falconry.
etymology: From Middle English merlioun, merlion, marlyon, merlyon, merlinge, from Old French emerillon, esmerillon, from Old Frankish *smiril (“falcon, hawk”), from Proto-Germanic *smirilaz (“falcon, merlin”).

definition: Half woman and half fish; lives in the sea.
example: A mermaid smoothie.
etymology: From Middle English mermayde (“maid of the sea”), from mere (“sea, lake”) + maid, equivalent to mer- + maid.

definition: Data about data.
example: A library catalog is metadata because it describes publications.
etymology: From meta- + data.

definition: Of or pertaining to atmospheric phenomena, especially weather and weather conditions.
example: Meteorological factors.
etymology: From meteorology + -ical.

definition: A small unmanned balloon set aloft to observe atmospheric conditions.
Any organism of microscopic size.
Of or involving or caused by or being microbes.
example: Microbial warfare.
etymology: From microbe + -ial.

definition: The branch of biology that studies microorganisms and their effects on humans.
etymology: From micro- + biology.

definition: A small flat rectangular piece of glass on which specimens can be mounted for microscopic study.
A small platform on a microscope where the specimen is mounted for examination.
Of or relating to or used in microscopy.
example: Microscopic analysis.
etymology: From microscope + -ic.

definition: The study of microscopic structures of tissues and organs.
The areas that is visible through a microscope.
Research with the use of microscopes.
etymology: From micro- + -scopy.

definition: (linguistics) Any vowel sound made with a somewhat elevated position of some certain part of the tongue, in relation to the palate; midway between the high and the low.
example: A consonant and a following mid vowel must agree in backness.

definition: The time of life between 70 and 80.
The time of life between 60 and 70.
The time of life between 20 and 30.
The middle of the day.
example: One indicates the time as one hour after twelve midday or midnight.
etymology: From Middle English midday, from Old English middæġ (“midday, noon”), equivalent to mid- + day.

definition: Moldboard plow with a double moldboard designed to move dirt to either side of a central furrow.
Used of women's clothing having a hemline at mid-calf.
example: Midiskirts.

definition: Of or coming from the middle of a region or country.
etymology: From Middle English mydlonde, equivalent to mid- + land.

definition: The middle of the gestation period.
example: I only got a C on the midterm, so I really have to study for the final.
etymology: From mid- + term.

definition: An examination administered in the middle of an academic term.
An examination administered in the middle of an academic term.
A woman skilled in aiding the delivery of babies.
example: Modernly, a hospital midwife is usually a registered nurse.
etymology: From Middle English midwif, corresponding to mid (“with”) + wif (“woman, wife, female”).

definition: A severe recurring vascular headache; occurs more frequently in women than men.
etymology: First appears c. 1425.

definition: Move from one country or region to another and settle there.
example: Many Germans migrated to South America in the mid-19th century.
etymology: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin migrātus, perfect passive participle of migrō (“to migrate, change, transport”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

definition: To a moderate degree.
example: He was mildly interested.
etymology: From mild + -ly.

definition: A chaplain in one of the military services.
A group of military officers who rule a country after seizing power.
Congenital disorder consisting of an inability to digest milk and milk products; absence or deficiency of lactase results in an inability to hydrolyze lactose.
Relating to a millennium or span of a thousand years.
example: A millennial fair.
etymology: The adjective is a learned borrowing from Late Latin mīllennium (“millennium”) + English -al (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives; and forming nouns).

definition: Corrugated edge of a coin.
Machine tool in which metal that is secured to a carriage is fed against rotating cutters that shape it.
example: The casting was mounted on a milling machine so that its sides could be squared.

definition: Machinery that processes materials by grinding or crushing.
Constituting an imitation.
example: The mimic warfare of the opera stage.
etymology: From Latin mīmicus, from Ancient Greek μῑμικός (mīmikós, “belonging to mimes”), from μῖμος (mîmos, “imitator, actor”); see mime.

definition: Tropical Asian starlings.
etymology: Borrowed from Hindi मैना (mainā)/Urdu مینا (mainā), from Sanskrit मदन (madana).

definition: Bearing in mind; attentive to.
example: Ever mindful of her health.
etymology: From Middle English myndeful, myndefull, from Old English ġemyndful (“of good memory”), equivalent to mind + -ful.

definition: Extracted from a source of supply as of minerals from the earth.
Lack of a mineral micronutrient that is essential for normal nutrition or metabolism.
An inorganic fertilizer which contains trace minerals.
A thick black tar intermediate between petroleum and asphalt.
Of or relating to artistic minimalism.
etymology: From minimal + -ist.

definition: Low shrub of the eastern United States with downy twigs.
Being or having the character of a miracle.
etymology: From Middle French miraculeux. Displaced native Old English wundorlīċ.

definition: (Old Testament) food that God gave the Israelites during the Exodus.
An optical illusion in which atmospheric refraction by a layer of hot air distorts or inverts reflections of distant objects.
etymology: An unadapted borrowing from French mirage c. 1812.

definition: (physics) parity is conserved in a universe in which the laws of physics are the same in a right-handed system of coordinates as in a left-handed system.
Like or characteristic of a mirror image.
etymology: From mirror (verb) + -ed (suffix forming past tenses).

definition: Failure of a plan.
etymology: From mis- + carriage.

definition: Consisting of a haphazard assortment of different kinds.
example: Miscellaneous accessories.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin miscellāneus, from miscellus (“mixed”), from misceō (“mix”).

definition: Reckless or malicious behavior that causes discomfort or annoyance in others.
example: Drink led to mischief.
etymology: From Middle English myschef, meschef, meschief, mischef, from Old French meschief, from meschever (“to bring to grief”), from mes- (“badly”) + chever (“happen;

definition: Someone who deliberately stirs up trouble.
Reckless or malicious behavior that causes discomfort or annoyance in others.
A crime less serious than a felony.
example: He was charged with a misdemeanor rather than a felony.
etymology: From mis- + demeanor.

definition: Unnecessary and unforeseen trouble resulting from an unfortunate event.
example: The worst tour I have ever had the misfortune to experience.
etymology: From mis- + fortune.

definition: Poorly conceived or thought out.
etymology: From misguide + -ed (suffix forming adjectives; and past tense and past participle forms of regular verbs).

definition: Information that is incorrect.
example: Spread misinformation on the internet.
etymology: From mis- + information.

definition: Put in the wrong place or position.
example: She was penalized for a spelling mistake or a misplaced accent.

definition: A young female.
etymology: From miss + -y.

definition: In a mistaken or erroneous manner.
example: He mistakenly believed it.
etymology: From mistaken + -ly.

definition: Filled or abounding with fog or mist.
example: It's very misty this morning; I can't see a thing!
etymology: From Middle English misty, mysty, misti, from Old English mistiġ (“misty, dark”), from Proto-West Germanic *mistig (“misty”), equivalent to mist + -y.

definition: Having eyes blurred as with tears.
example: Sad and misty-eyed.

definition: To act in such a way as to cause an offense to seem less serious.
etymology: From Middle French mitigation, from Latin mītigātiō.

definition: The (prehensile) extremity of the superior limb.
example: He extended his mitt.
etymology: Clipping of mitten.

definition: A nuisance that is both a public nuisance and a private nuisance at the same time.
An utterance expressing pain or disapproval.
example: Let out a deep moan.
etymology: From Middle English mone, mane, mān, (also as mene), from Old English *mān, *mǣn (“complaint; lamentation”), from Proto-West Germanic *mainu, from Proto-Germanic *mainō (“opinion; mind”).

definition: Act of assembling and putting into readiness for war or other emergency:.
example: A national mobilization to fight climate change.
etymology: From French mobilisation or mobilize + -ation.

definition: Resembling sculpture.
example: Her finely modeled features.

definition: (from a combination of MOdulate and DEModulate) electronic equipment consisting of a device used to connect computers by a telephone line.
etymology: Clipping of modulator-demodulator.

definition: Quality of being moderate and avoiding extremes.
example: Mr. Chairman, at this moment I stand astonished at my own moderation!
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French [Term?], from Old French moderacion, from Latin moderātiō. By surface analysis, moderate + ion.

definition: Any substance used to slow down neutrons in nuclear reactors.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin moderātor. First attested as Middle English moderatour. By surface analysis, moderate + -or.

definition: The quality of being current or of the present.
example: A shopping mall would instill a spirit of modernity into this village.
etymology: From modern + -ity, a calque of Latin modernitās.

definition: Making modern in appearance or behavior.
example: The modernization of Nigeria will be a long process.
etymology: From modernize + -ation or French modernisation.

definition: A youth subculture that began in London in the early 1960s; a working-class movement with highly stylized dress and short hair; listened to rhythm and blues music and travelled on motor scooters.
A musical passage moving from one key to another.
example: Garamond has much modulation, while Helvetica has very little.
etymology: From Late Middle English modulacion, modulacioun (“act of making music or singing; harmony;

definition: A magic power or magic spell.
example: Look at the way the chicks are checking out Daniel on the dancefloor. He's still got plenty of mojo.
etymology: Probably of Creole origin, cognate with Gullah moco (“witchcraft”), Fula moco'o (“medicine man”). The origin of the drug sense is uncertain, possibly related to Spanish mojar (“to toast (celebrate with a drink)”).

definition: A biologist who studies the structure and activity of macromolecules essential to life.
Reduced to liquid form by heating.
example: A mass of molten rock.
etymology: From Middle English molten, from Old English molten, ġemolten (“melted, molten”), from Proto-Germanic *multanaz, past participle of Proto-Germanic *meltaną (“to melt”). Cognate with Scots moltin, Swedish multen.

definition: Informal terms for a mother.
etymology: A variant of mama.

definition: Large migratory American butterfly having deep orange wings with black and white markings; the larvae feed on milkweed.
etymology: Believed to have been named in honor of King William III of England, as the butterfly’s main color is that of the king’s secondary title, Prince of Orange.

definition: One whose business is to exchange the money of one country for that of another country.
example: The money changers in the temple.

definition: Concealing the source of illegally gotten money.
A project that generates a continuous flow of money.
Adjustable wrench that has one fixed and one adjustable jaw.
etymology: Already in use, and not unfamiliar among mechanics, by 1832; see discussion and references at Monkey wrench § Etymology and history.

definition: Adjustable wrench that has one fixed and one adjustable jaw.
Speech you make to yourself.
etymology: First attested in c. 1550. Borrowed from Middle French monologue, modeled on dialogue, ultimately from Medieval Greek μονόλογος (monólogos). By surface analysis, mono- + -logue.

definition: An oxide containing just one atom of oxygen in the molecule.
etymology: Formed as mon- + oxide; compare the earlier dioxide, pentoxide, and tetroxide.

definition: An open woodland in a tropical area with monsoon climate.
A paste-up made by sticking together pieces of paper or photographs to form an artistic image.
etymology: , La matière denaturalisée. Destruction 2. (Denatured Matter. Destruction 2.; c. 1923), from the collection of the Fries Museum in Leeuwarden, Friesland, Netherlands.

definition: Inability to see clearly in dim light; due to a deficiency of vitamin A or to a retinal disorder.
example: The cavalry messenger dismounted after his moon blindness made it unsafe to ride on through the wilderness.
etymology: Once believed to be caused by exposure of the eyes to moonlight during sleep.

definition: Secure in or as if in a berth or dock.
example: The vessel moored in the stream.
etymology: From Middle English mor, from Old English mōr, from Proto-West Germanic *mōr, from Proto-Germanic *mōraz, from Proto-Indo-European *móri. Cognates include Welsh môr, Old Irish muir (from Proto-Celtic *mori);

definition: An evergreen shrub with leathery leaves.
Reddish-brown grouse of upland moors of Great Britain.
To wash or wipe with or as if with a mop.
example: Mop the hallway now.
etymology: From Middle English mappe (also as mappel), perhaps borrowed from Walloon mappe (“napkin”), from Latin mappa (“napkin, cloth”).

definition: The handle of a mop.
To wash or wipe with or as if with a mop.
example: Mop the hallway now.

definition: (of trees) having a bushy top without a leader.
example: Mop-headed cabbage palms.

definition: Anything that serves to increase morale.
example: The sight of flowers every morning was my morale builder.

definition: Something or someone who influences by building or strengthening morale.
Suggesting an unhealthy mental state.
example: Morbid interest in death.
etymology: From Latin morbidus (“diseased”), from morbus (“sickness”), itself from the root of morī (“to die”) or directly from Proto-Indo-European *mer- (“to rub, pound, wear away”).

definition: The branch of biology that deals with the structure of animals and plants.
etymology: Borrowed from German Morphologie. By surface analysis, morpho- + -logy.

definition: The next day.
example: Whenever he arrives she leaves on the morrow.
etymology: From Middle English morwe, apocopic form of morwen, from Old English morgen, from Proto-West Germanic *morgan, *morgin, from Proto-Germanic *murganaz, *murginaz; compare Dutch morgen and German Morgen.

definition: Slender-bodied non-stinging insect having iridescent wings that are outspread at rest; adults and nymphs feed on mosquitoes etc.
A marauder and plunderer (originally operating in the bogs between England and Scotland).

East Indian legume having hairy foliage and small yellow flowers followed by cylindrical pods; used especially in India for food and forage and as a soil conditioner; sometimes placed in genus Phaseolus.
etymology: Borrowed from Hindi मोठ (moṭh), from Proto-New Indo-Aryan *𑀫𑁄𑀝𑁆𑀞 (*moṭṭha). See there for more.

definition: Any of various moths that have powdery wings.
Any of various orchids of the genus Phalaenopsis having often drooping glossy broad obovate or oval leaves usually dark green flushed purple or mottled grey and silver.
Showing signs of wear and tear.
Resistant to damage by moths.
The kinship relation between an offspring and the mother.
example: The nation's motherhood.
etymology: From Middle English moderhode, moderhede, equivalent to mother + -hood.

definition: A design or figure that consists of recurring shapes or colors, as in architecture or decoration.
example: See how the artist repeats the scroll motif throughout the work?
etymology: From French motif (1848), with the meaning of "main idea or theme". Doublet of motive.

definition: Impelling to action.
example: It may well be that ethical language has primarily a motivative function.

definition: Of or relating to motivation.
etymology: From motivation + -al.

definition: A broad highway designed for high-speed traffic.
etymology: From motor + way.

definition: Loose soil rich in organic matter.
etymology: Via Middle English molde, moulde (“mould, cast”) and Old French modle, from Latin modulus.

definition: Large-footed short-winged birds of Australasia; build mounds of decaying vegetation to incubate eggs.
Birch of western United States resembling the paper birch but having brownish bark.
Small East Indian tree having orchid-like flowers and hard dark wood.
A variety of cat's foot.
Common European mountain fern having fragrant lemon or balsam scented fronds.
Asiatic plant resembling spinach often used as a potherb; naturalized in Europe and North America.
Narrow-striped nearly extinct zebra of southern Africa.
Having hills and crags.
etymology: From mountain + -ous after Middle French montagneux, from Late Latin montāniōsus, from montānia, from Latin montem (“mountain”).

definition: Feel sadness.
example: She is mourning her dead child.
etymology: From Middle English mornen, mournen, from Old English murnan, from Proto-Germanic *murnaną. Cognate with French morne (“gloomy”).

definition: Of temperate regions; having dark purple wings with yellow borders.
Wild dove of the United States having a mournful call.
etymology: mourning + dove, referring to the bird's call, which is regarded as mournful or plangent.

definition: A small rectangular free-reed instrument having a row of free reeds set back in air holes and played by blowing into the desired hole.
Projects successive frames from a reel of film to create moving pictures.
A coot found in North America.
Wrestle in mud.
A round sheet of paper, foil, or silicone with scallop-pressed edges, giving the muffin a round cup shape.
example: A variety of sizes for muffin cases are available.

definition: A round sheet of paper, foil, or silicone with scallop-pressed edges, giving the muffin a round cup shape.
example: A variety of sizes for muffin cases are available.

definition: Formerly an itinerant male peddler of muffins.
Hybrid offspring of a male donkey and a female horse; usually sterile.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English mule, from Anglo-Norman mule (“she-mule”) and Old English mūl, both ultimately from Latin mūlus, from Proto-Indo-European *mukslós.

definition: Long-eared deer of western North America with two-pronged antlers.
A worker who drives mules.
California shrub with slender leafy shoots that are important browse for mule deer.
A reflective thinker characterized by quiet contemplation.
etymology: From mull (“to heat and spice, etc.”, verb) + -er (suffix forming agent nouns).

definition: Of or relating to or including several cultures.
example: A multicultural event.
etymology: From multiculture + -al or multi- + cultural.

definition: A statistical technique that predicts values of one variable on the basis of two or more other variables.
A chronic progressive nervous disorder involving loss of myelin sheath around certain nerve fibers.
etymology: Ellipsis of multiple cerebral sclerosis, i.e. appearance of hardenings or nodules dispersed throughout parts of the central nervous system, in the brain or spinal cord.

definition: The act of producing offspring or multiplying by such production.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French, from Old French multiplicacion, from Latin multiplicatio, multiplicationem; ~equivalent to multiplicate + -ion.

definition: A sign indicating the operation of multiplication.
Greatly increased as by multiplication.
Of or relating to walls.
example: Mural painting.
etymology: Borrowed from French mural, from Latin muralis, from murus (“wall”).

definition: A decorative printed wallpaper usually placed on only one wall; the print can either be custom or chosen from a predefined set.
(physiology) a shortening or tensing of a part or organ (especially of a muscle or muscle fiber).
(physiology) a shortening or tensing of a part or organ (especially of a muscle or muscle fiber).
An anchor used for semipermanent moorings; has a bowl-shaped head that will dig in however it falls.
Flattened disk-shaped stony coral (usually solitary and unattached).
Toxic condition caused by eating certain species of mushrooms (especially Amanita species).
(music) notation used by musicians.
In a musical manner.
example: She sang very musically.
etymology: From Middle English musicallye, musikili; equivalent to musical + -ly.

definition: An odorous glandular secretion from the male musk deer; used as a perfume fixative.
etymology: From Middle English muske, borrowed from Old French musc, from Late Latin muscus, from Ancient Greek μόσχος (móskhos), from Middle Persian [script needed] (mwšk' /⁠muʃk⁠/) whence Persian مشک (mošk).

definition: Small heavy-limbed upland deer of central Asia; male secretes valued musk.
Large crested wild duck of Central America and South America; widely domesticated.
etymology: From musk + duck, from its musky odour.

definition: Rose native to Mediterranean region having curved or climbing branches and loose clusters of musky-scented flowers.
Large shaggy-coated bovid mammal of Canada and Greenland; intermediate in size and anatomy between an ox and a sheep.
Small freshwater turtle having a strong musky odor.
An unshaved growth of hair on the upper lip.
example: He looked younger after he shaved off his mustache.

definition: A drinking cup with a bar inside the rim to keep a man's mustache out of the drink.
Fragrant California annual herb having lanceolate leaves and clusters of rose-purple flowers.
Leaves eaten as cooked greens.
A plaster containing powdered black mustard; applied to the skin as a counterirritant or rubefacient.
A gathering of military personnel for duty.
example: He was thrown in the brig for missing muster.
etymology: From Middle English musteren, borrowed from Anglo-Norman mostrer, Middle French monstrer, moustrer (whence the noun monstre, which gave the English noun), from Latin mōnstrō (“to show”), from moneō (“to admonish”).

definition: A call of the names of personnel at a military assembly.
Engage somebody to enter the army.
Release from military service.
A list of names of officers and men in a military unit or ship's company.
Gather or bring together.
example: Muster the courage to do something.

definition: Soundless Eurasian swan; commonly domesticated.
etymology: So called because it is not very vocal (though not entirely mute).

definition: In a softened tone.
example: Muted trumpets.

definition: Open rebellion against constituted authority (especially by seamen or soldiers against their officers).
etymology: From Middle French mutiner.

definition: A large indefinite number.
example: He faced a myriad of details.
etymology: From French myriade, from Late Latin mȳriadem (accusative of mȳrias), from Ancient Greek μυριάς (muriás, “number of 10,000”), from μυρίος (muríos, “numberless, countless, infinite”). By surface analysis, myria- + -ad.

definition: Widely cultivated as a groundcover for its dark green shiny leaves and usually blue-violet flowers.
etymology: From Middle English mirtille, from Old French mirtille, mirtile, from myrte, from Latin myrtillus, from myrtus + -illus, from Ancient Greek μύρτος (múrtos, “myrtle”).

definition: Similar to Audubon's warbler.
Trees and shrubs yielding a fragrant oil.
Perennial marsh plant having swordlike leaves and aromatic roots.
Small evergreen shrub or tree of southeastern United States; often forms almost impenetrable thickets in sandy coastal areas.
In a cryptic manner.
etymology: From Middle English misteriusly, equivalent to mysterious + -ly.

definition: Based on or told of in traditional stories; lacking factual basis or historical validity.
example: Mythical centaurs.
etymology: From Latin mȳthicus + -al; by surface analysis, myth + -ical.

definition: An imaginary being of myth or fable.
A monster renowned in folklore and myth.
A monster renowned in folklore and myth.
A place that exists only in imagination; a place said to exist in fictional or religious writings.
Continually complaining or faultfinding.
example: Nagging parents.

definition: A cosmetic lacquer that dries quickly and that is applied to the nails to color them or make them shiny.
(philosophy) the philosophical doctrine that physical objects continue to exist when not perceived.
Having a tail that is hairless.
Your grandmother.
example: We had my nan over for Christmas dinner.
etymology: From Nan, pet form of the formerly very common female given names Anne and Agnes. As a nursemaid and grandmother, a clipping of earlier nana, from nanny under the probable influence of mama, also from Nan. Compare Mary.

definition: A type of short chunky heel.
example: Shoes with nan heels look terrible to me, but they are actually more comfortable than ballet flats.

definition: Female goat.
Plant with an elongated head of broad stalked leaves resembling celery; used as a vegetable in east Asia.
etymology: From the regional and colloquial Japanese term 菜っ葉 (nappa, “leaves of any vegetable”).

definition: A message that tells the particulars of an act or occurrence or course of events; presented in writing or drama or cinema or as a radio or television program.
example: His narrative was interesting.

definition: Having a relatively narrow body.
Reduced in size as by squeezing together.
example: His narrowed eyes.

definition: An instance of becoming narrow.
example: Narrowings of the road.

definition: Of or in or relating to the nose.
example: Nasal passages.
etymology: From Middle English, from Medieval Latin nāsālis, from nāsus (“the nose”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix). Doublet of nasalis.

definition: An elongated rectangular bone that forms the bridge of the nose.
Either of the two cavities lying between the floor of the cranium and the roof of the mouth and extending from the face to the pharynx.
Relating to or accompanying birth.
example: Natal injuries.
etymology: From Middle English natal, natale (“native, one’s own; inherited;

definition: The date on which a person was born.
Tall Australian timber tree yielding tough hard wood used for staves etc.
Tree bearing pear-shaped fruit with a thick woody epicarp.
An old name for sulfur.
Labor and childbirth without medical intervention; no drugs are given to relieve pain or aid the birth process.
example: Natural childbirth is considered the safest for the baby.

definition: Relating to or involving ships or shipping or navigation or seamen.
example: Nautical charts.
etymology: From Middle French nautique (“of or relating to sailors or navigation”) or its etymon, Classical Latin nauticus (“of or relating to ships, seafaring”), + -al (adjectival suffix).

definition: A nautical unit of length (15 ft).
A former British unit of length equivalent to 6,080 feet (1,853.184 meters); 800 feet longer than a statute mile.
The interdiction of a nation's lines of communication at sea by the use of naval power.
The ship's officer in charge of navigation.
etymology: From Latin nāvigātor. By surface analysis, navigate + -or.

definition: Used to express negation.
example: The nays have it.
etymology: From Middle English nai, nei, from Old Norse nei (“no”), contraction of ne (“not”) + ei (“ever”), itself from Proto-Germanic *nai (“never”), *nē (“not”). More at no.

definition: (comparative of ‘near’ or ‘close’) within a shorter distance.
example: They drew nearer.

definition: With neatness.
example: She put the slippers under the bed neatly.
etymology: From neat + -ly.

definition: A sweet liquid secretion that is attractive to pollinators.
etymology: From Latin nectar, from Ancient Greek νέκταρ (néktar, “nourishment of the gods”), from Proto-Indo-European *neḱ- (“perish, disappear”) + *-tr̥h₂ (“overcoming”), from *terh₂- (“to overcome, pass through, cross over”).

definition: The character of the negative electric pole.
etymology: From negative + -ity.

definition: Characterized by neglect and undue lack of concern.
example: Negligent parents.
etymology: From Middle English necligent, negligent, from Old French negligent, from Latin negligēns.

definition: So small as to be meaningless; insignificant.
example: The effect was negligible.
etymology: From negligence/negligent + -ible, as if from New Latin *negligibilis, from Latin neglegō (“to neglect”) + -ibilis (“-ible”).

definition: A stout spreading or semi-climbing tropical shrub with round brownish-red warty fruit; Africa.
Twining vine with hairy foliage and dark purplish-brown flowers.
An emotional disorder that leaves you exhausted and unable to work.
In an anxiously nervous manner.
example: We watched the stock market nervously.
etymology: From nervous + -ly.

definition: A place suitable for nesting.
A muskmelon vine with fruit that has a thin reticulated rind and sweet green flesh.
The electrical discharge that travels along a nerve fiber.
A disorder of the nervous system.
Atom bomb that produces lethal neutrons with less blast.
Radiation of neutrons (as by a neutron bomb).
A star that has collapsed under its own gravity; it is composed of neutrons.
Having just or recently arisen or come into existence.
example: New-sprung nations.

definition: Any new participant in some activity.
etymology: From Middle English newe-comere, equivalent to new- + comer. Compare Old English nīwcumen (“new comer, neophyte, novice”).

definition: An alloy whose main constituent is nickel.
An addiction to nicotine.
Toxic condition caused by the ingestion or inhalation of large amounts of nicotine.
Inability to see clearly in dim light; due to a deficiency of vitamin A or to a retinal disorder.
Doorlock operated by a knob on the inside and a key on the outside.
European songbird noted for its melodious nocturnal song.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English nyghtyngale, nightingale, niȝtingale, alteration (with intrusive n) of nyghtgale, nightegale, from Old English nihtegala, nihtegale (“nightingale;

definition: Happening every night.
example: Nightly television now goes on until 3:00 or 4:00 a.m.
etymology: From Middle English nyȝtly, nihtlich, nihtlic, from Old English nihtlīċ, nihtelīċ (“nocturnal, nightly, of the night, at night”), equivalent to night + -ly.

definition: The time after sunset and before sunrise while it is dark outside.
etymology: From Middle English nyght tyme, nyȝttyme, equivalent to night + time. Compare Dutch nachttijd, German Nachtzeit, Danish nattetid, Swedish nattetid.

definition: A quantity of no importance; thing (object:), singular, negative pronoun; pronoun, thing, singular; quantifier: negative existential.
example: Reduced to nil all the work we had done.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin nīl, a contraction of nihil, nihilum (“nothing”). See nihilism, nihility.

definition: Sever or remove by pinching or snipping.
example: Nip off the flowers.

definition: The small projection of a mammary gland.
etymology: From earlier neple, nypil, neble, believed to be a diminutive of nib, neb (“tip, point”), equivalent to nib + -le. Compare Old English nypel (“elephant trunk”), formed analogously as "a protuberance from one's neb" .

definition: A rubber or plastic shield to protect the nipples of nursing women.
etymology: From nipple + shield. First use appears c. 1799 in the writings of Michael Underwood.

definition: (Hinduism and Buddhism) the beatitude that transcends the cycle of reincarnation; characterized by the extinction of desire and suffering and individual consciousness.
etymology: Borrowed from Sanskrit निर्वाण (nirvāṇa, “blown or put out, extinguished”), from निस् (nis, “out”) + वा (vā, “to blow”), the second part cognate with Russian ве́тер (véter, “wind”), weather, vent and wind.

definition: Any compound containing the nitrate group (such as a salt or ester of nitric acid).
etymology: Borrowed from French nitrate.

definition: A highly poisonous brown gas (NO2).
A toxic compound resembling mustard gas in structure; important in cancer treatment.
Any of several oxides of nitrogen formed by the action of nitric acid on oxidizable materials; present in car exhausts.
A privileged class holding hereditary titles.
example: The castle was once home to the Scottish nobility.
etymology: From Old French nobilité, from Latin nobilitas. Equivalent to noble + -ity.

definition: (law) a trivial sum (usually $1.00) awarded as recognition that a legal injury was sustained (as for technical violations of a contract).
Not aromatic.
etymology: From non- + aromatic.

definition: Filled by appointment rather than by election.
Without words.
Prose writing that is not fictional.
example: Encyclopedias, how-to manuals and biographies are all considered nonfiction and so are kept in the nonfiction section.
etymology: From non- + fiction.

definition: Designating or involving an equation whose terms are not of the first degree.
example: A film with a nonlinear plot.
etymology: From non- + linear.

definition: A system whose performance cannot be described by equations of the first degree.
(of a journey especially a flight) occurring without stops.
example: A nonstop flight to Atlanta.
etymology: From non- + stop.

definition: A flight made without intermediate stops between source and destination.
example: How many nonstops are there to Dallas?

definition: A ribbonlike strip of pasta.
example: She slurped a long noodle up out of her soup.
etymology: Borrowed from Dutch noedel (“noodle”), or from its etymon German Nudel (“piece of pasta, noodle”); further etymology uncertain, probably a variant of Knödel (“dumpling”), from Middle High German knödel (“dumpling;

definition: Very hairy mammoth common in colder portions of the Northern Hemisphere.
A flute that is played by blowing through the nostrils.
Unhappy about being away and longing for familiar things or persons.
etymology: From nostalgia + -ic.

definition: Not interfering or meddling.
A technical system of symbols used to represent special things.
example: This section lists all algebraic notation used in this book.
etymology: From Latin notātiō, equivalent to notate + -ion or note + -ation.

definition: A note promising to pay a certain amount of money at a certain time.
Worthy of attention.
example: A noteworthy fact is that her students rarely complain.
etymology: From note + -worthy.

definition: In a noticeable manner.
example: He changed noticeably over the years.
etymology: From noticeable + -ly.

definition: Counter where notions are sold.
To a notorious degree.
example: European emigres, who notoriously used to repair to the British Museum to write seditious pamphlets.
etymology: From Middle English notoryously, equivalent to notorious + -ly.

definition: Despite anything to the contrary (usually preceding a concession).
example: He, notwithstanding, persisted in his inquiries.
etymology: From Middle English notwithstandinge, notwithstondyng, natwithstandyng, equivalent to not + withstanding. Compare Middle English notgainstonding, not aȝenstondynge, of similar meaning and formation.

definition: Someone who has entered a religious order but has not taken final vows.
example: I'm only a novice at coding, so my programs frequently have bugs that more experienced programmers would avoid.

definition: A chemist who specializes in nuclear chemistry.
A physicist who specializes in nuclear physics.
etymology: From nuclear physics + -ist.

definition: The use of a nuclear reactor either to produce electricity to power an engine (as in a nuclear submarine) or to directly heat a propellant (as in nuclear rockets).
The quality of an embarrassing situation.
Strike at with firepower or bombs.
example: If a nuclear war ever breaks out, military facilities are likely to be nuked first.
etymology: Clipping of nuclear weapon. The verb is derived from the noun.

definition: A numbered list.
etymology: From Middle English nombrynge; equivalent to number + -ing.

definition: An illegal daily lottery.
A tale in rhymed verse for children.
etymology: From how Victorian and Edwardian parents used to tell such rhymes to their children in the nursery, i.e. the children's bedroom.

definition: Help develop, help grow.
example: Nurture his talents.
etymology: From Middle English norture, noriture, from Old French norriture, norreture, from Late Latin nutritura (“nourishment”), from Latin nutrire (“to nourish”).

definition: An artery that supplies the medullary cavity of the long bone.
The shell around the kernel of a nut.
etymology: From Middle English notschelle, from Old English hnutsċiell, from Proto-West Germanic *hnutskallju, equivalent to nut + shell.

definition: A tree of the genus Castanopsis.
Porridge made of rolled oats.
etymology: From Middle English otemele, from ote (“oat”) + mele (“meal, coarse-ground grains”). Equivalent to oat + meal.

definition: Cookies containing rolled oats.
White-flowered West Indian plant whose root yields arrowroot starch.
(West Indies) followers of a religious system involving witchcraft and sorcery.
etymology: Borrowed from Japanese 帯 (obi, “belt”).

definition: With objectivity.
example: We must look at the facts objectively.
etymology: From objective + -ly.

definition: Morally or legally constraining or binding.
example: Attendance is obligatory.
etymology: From Middle English obligatorie, from Latin obligatōrius.

definition: (followed by ‘to’ or ‘of’) lacking conscious awareness of.
example: Oblivious of the mounting pressures for political reform.
etymology: From Middle English oblivious, from Latin oblīviōsus (“forgetful, oblivious”), formed from oblīvium (“forgetfulness, oblivion”) + -ōsus (“full of, overly, prone to”), from oblīvīscor (“to forget”).

definition: Causing disapproval or protest.
example: Throwing stones at the bus is another example of your obnoxious behaviour.

definition: Characterized by or constituting an obsession.
example: The obsessional character of his response.
etymology: From obsess + -ive.

definition: Cause an eclipse of (a celestial body) by intervention.
example: Planets and stars often are occulted by other celestial bodies.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin occultus (“hidden, secret”).

definition: Supernatural practices and techniques.
example: He is a student of the occult.

definition: An act of being a tenant or occupant.
The percentage of all rental units (as in hotels) are occupied or rented at a given time.
North Atlantic rockfish.
Relating to or occurring or living in or frequenting the open ocean.
example: Oceanic islands like Bermuda.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin ōceanicus. By surface analysis, ocean + -ic. Doublet of oceany.

definition: Bird of the open seas.
A lyric poem with complex stanza forms.
example: Write an ode to someone.
etymology: From Middle French ode, from Late Latin ōda, from Ancient Greek ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”). Doublet of Aoede.

definition: Any property detected by the olfactory system.
etymology: From Middle English odour, borrowed from Anglo-Norman odour, from Old French odor, from Latin odor. Cognates * Swedish odör (“bad smell”)

definition: Offending against or breaking a law or rule.
example: Contracts offending against the statute were canceled.

definition: The person who holds an office.
Many times at short intervals.
example: We often met over a cup of coffee.
etymology: From Middle English oft (also ofte, often > Modern English often), from Old English oft (“often”), from Proto-West Germanic *oftu, *oftō, from Proto-Germanic *uftō (“often”).

definition: A gland that secretes oil.
A refinery for petroleum.
A cargo ship designed to carry crude oil in bulk.
Soluble in oil.
example: Oil-soluble pigments.

definition: Containing an unusual amount of grease or oil.
example: Oily fried potatoes.
etymology: From Middle English oylei, equivalent to oil + -y. Compare German ölig (“oily”), Swedish oljig (“oily”).

definition: Olive-colored sea turtle of tropical Pacific and Indian and the southern Atlantic oceans.
Majestic in manner or bearing; superior to mundane matters.
example: Olympian detachment.

definition: Threatening or foreshadowing evil or tragic developments.
example: Ominous rumblings of discontent.
etymology: From Latin ōminōsus (“full of foreboding”), from ōmen (“forbidden fruit, omen”), from Old Latin osmen, of uncertain origin, with many origins proposed (see ōmen).

definition: A mistake resulting from neglect.
example: E&O insurance (for errors and omissions) covers both errors of commission and errors of omission.
etymology: From Middle English omissioun, from Old French omission, from Late Latin omissio, omissionem, from Latin omitto.

definition: The branch of medicine concerned with the study and treatment of tumors.
etymology: First attested 1857. By surface analysis, onco- + -logy.

definition: One part in sixteen equal parts.
Having a single wing.
Situated or taking place on the area of a stage visible to the audience.
etymology: From on + stage.

definition: Forward in time or order or degree.
example: From the sixth century onward.
etymology: From on + -ward.

definition: The act of moving forward (as toward a goal).
Not transmitting or reflecting light or radiant energy; impenetrable to sight.
example: Opaque windows of the jail.
etymology: From Middle English opake, from Latin opacus (“shaded, shady, dark”) (of unknown origin), later reinforced from Middle French opaque. Doublet of ubac.

definition: A gemstone that is opaque.
Any very successful means of achieving a result.
etymology: From its use in Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves, translating French Sésame, ouvre-toi in Antoine Galland's version of the Ali Baba story in the One Thousand and One Nights, possibly based on an oral Arabic source.

definition: A syllable ended by a vowel or diphthong.
A vowel that you pronounce with your tongue on the bottom of your mouth.
Without obstructions to passage or view.
example: The openness of the prairies.
etymology: From Middle English *opennesse, from Old English openness (“openness, publicity”), equivalent to open + -ness. Cognate with Old High German offannussi (“disclosure, revelation, openness”).

definition: A large cloak worn over evening clothes.
Binocular microscope used in surgery to provide a clear view of small and inaccessible parts of the body (as in microsurgery).
Someone addicted to opium.
A building where opium is sold and used.
Weighing heavily on the senses or spirit.
example: The atmosphere was oppressive.
etymology: From oppress + -ive.

definition: The point where the optic nerve enters the retina; not sensitive to light.
The cranial nerve that serves the retina.
Optical device having a triangular shape and made of glass or quartz; used to deviate a beam or invert an image.
A computer peripheral device enabling printed material, including characters and diagrams, to be scanned and converted into a form that can be stored in a computer.
Make optimal; get the most out of; use best.
example: Optimize your resources.
etymology: Back-formation from optimist. First attested in 1844.

definition: Caused by herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1).
Alimentary tract smear of material obtained from the mouth.
(linguistics) an ordinary vowel that is produced without nasalization.

Long bench with backs; used in church by the congregation.
example: In many churches some pews are reserved for either clerical or liturgical officials such as canons, or for prominent families.
etymology: From Middle English pewe, from Old French puiee, puïe (“balustrade, balcony”), from Latin podia, plural of podium (“parapet, podium”), from Ancient Greek πόδιον (pódion, “little foot”), from πούς (poús, “foot”).

definition: The illusion that a limb still exists after it has been amputated.
A company that makes and sells pharmaceuticals.
example: We're investing in pharma and biotech.
etymology: Clipping of pharmaceutical.

definition: Someone trained in the science of drugs (their composition and uses and effects).
A health professional trained in the art of preparing and dispensing drugs.
etymology: From pharmacy (“the art of preparing drugs, a drug, especially laxatives”) + -ist.

definition: Modulation of the phase of the carrier wave.
An index of the relation between any two sets of scores that can both be represented on ordered binary dimensions (e.g., male-female).
Voluntary promotion of human welfare.
example: As public funding is reduced, we depend increasingly on private philanthropy.
etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin philanthrōpia, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek φιλανθρωπία (philanthrōpía). By surface analysis, phil- + -anthropy.

definition: Small dun-colored North American flycatcher.
etymology: From early 18th c. Imitative, influenced by the name Phoebe.

definition: Small dun-colored North American flycatcher.
Fraudulent; having a misleading appearance.
example: A good jeweler should be able to tell a real stone from a phony one.
etymology: Of unknown origin. Perhaps an alteration of fawny (“gilt brass ring used by swindlers”) (1781), from Irish fáinne (“ring”).

definition: A salt of phosphoric acid.
etymology: From French phosphate. By surface analysis, phosphoric acid + -ate (“salt or ester”).

definition: A multivalent nonmetallic element of the nitrogen family that occurs commonly in inorganic phosphate rocks and as organic phosphates in all living cells; is highly reactive and occurs in several allotropic forms.
example: For quotations using this term, see Citations:phosphorus.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin phōsphorus, from Ancient Greek φωσφόρος (phōsphóros, “the bearer of light”), from φῶς (phôs, “light”) + φέρω (phérō, “to bear, carry”).

definition: A decorative printed wallpaper usually placed on only one wall; the print can either be custom or chosen from a predefined set.
A quantum of electromagnetic radiation; an elementary particle that is its own antiparticle.
Pendulum consisting of an actual object allowed to rotate freely around a horizontal axis.
A scientist trained in physics.
etymology: From physics + -ist. Coined by the English polymath William Whewell (1794–1866) in his book The Philosophy of the Inductive Sciences (1840): see the quotation.

definition: The study of anatomy in its relation to function.
Constitution of the human body.
example: Her large frame and muscular physique stands out among most other students.
etymology: From French physique.

definition: A person who plays the piano.
example: By the time she became the world's greatest pianist, she had already practised for thousands of hours on her prized piano.
etymology: From French pianiste, from Italian pianista. Analyzable as piano + -ist.

definition: A group of four players, including a piano player, a violin player, a viola player and a cello player.
A stool for piano players; usually adjustable in height.
Sheet music for the piano (a piano score) that was once music for other instruments that was reduced as kind of projection to its most basic components within a two line staff for piano.
example: Piano reduction lessens the complexity of an existing score or composition to make analysis, performance, or practice easier or more clear.

definition: A person employed to keep watch for some anticipated event.
example: A picket fence.
etymology: From French piquet, from piquer (“to pierce”).

definition: A boat serving as a picket.
A line of people acting as pickets.
etymology: From picket (“stake driven into the ground; soldier or small unit of soldiers assigned to perform a duty; protester positioned outside a workplace, etc., during a strike; the protest itself”) + line.

definition: A ship serving as a picket.
A barrel holding vinegar in which cucumbers are pickled.
Exacting especially about details.
example: I am very picky about the way my kitchen is laid out.
etymology: From pick + -y.

definition: A postcard with a picture on one side.
Having a hole cut through.
example: Pierced ears.

definition: Tall coarse perennial American herb having small white flowers followed by blackish-red berries on long drooping racemes; young fleshy stems are edible; berries and root are poisonous.
Small falcon of Europe and America having dark plumage with black-barred tail; used in falconry.
A raised shelter in which pigeons are kept.
Tropical woody herb with showy yellow flowers and flat pods; much cultivated in the tropics.
etymology: So called as they are used as feed for domesticated pigeons.

definition: Disability in which the toes are turned inward; often associated with knock-knee.
A child's coin bank (often shaped like a pig).
Dry coloring material (especially a powder to be mixed with a liquid to produce paint, etc.).
example: Chlorophyll is the pigment responsible for most plants' green colouring.
etymology: From Middle English pigment, from Latin pigmentum (“pigment”), itself from pingō (“to paint”) + -mentum; variants of this word may have been known in Old English (e.g. 12th century pyhmentum).

definition: Someone who journeys in foreign lands.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English pilegrim, from Old English pilegrī̆m, from Old French pelegrin, from Latin peregrīnus (“foreigner”). Doublet of peregrine.

definition: A column of wood or steel or concrete that is driven into the ground to provide support for a structure.
Bed linen consisting of a decorative cover for a pillow.
Very hard unsalted biscuit or bread; a former ship's staple.
Someone who procures customers for whores (in England they call a pimp a ponce).
etymology: Origin unknown. Perhaps from French pimpant (“smart, sparkish”) or German Pimpf (“a boy, a youth, a young squirt”). The Old English near-synonym was rendered by Old English forspennend (literally “a solicitor”).

definition: European weed naturalized in southwestern United States and Mexico having reddish decumbent stems with small fernlike leaves and small deep reddish-lavender flowers followed by slender fruits that stick straight up; often grown for forage.
A curl of hair made by dampening a strand of hair and curling it and holding the curl with a clip or bobby pin.
etymology: From pin + curl.

definition: A wrench that has a projecting pin that fits into a socket on the object to be turned.
(baseball) a substitute for the regular batter.
example: I’ll be sending a pinch hitter to do the presentation because I have the flu.
etymology: From pinch hit + -er.

definition: Small finch of North American coniferous forests.
Large beetle whose larvae bore holes in pine trees.
A game (trademark Ping-Pong) resembling tennis but played on a table with paddles and a light hollow ball.
etymology: Onomatopoeic. The name “ping-pong” was in wide use before British manufacturer J. Jaques & Son Ltd trademarked it in 1901. Jaques sold the rights to the “ping-pong” name in the United States to Parker Brothers.

definition: Of lavender tinged with pink.
(architecture) a slender upright spire at the top of a buttress or tower.
etymology: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French pinacle, pinnacle, from Late Latin pinnāculum (“a peak, pinnacle”), from Latin pinna (“a pinnacle”); see pin. Doublet of panache.

definition: A very brief moment.
example: They were strangers sharing a pinpoint of time together.
etymology: From pin + point.

definition: Having or showing or expressing reverence for a deity.
example: Pious readings.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin pīus (“pious, dutiful, blessed, kind, devout”), from Proto-Indo-European *pewH- (“pure”). Cognate with Old English fǣle (“faithful, trusty, good; dear, beloved”). More at feal.

definition: A disease of poultry.
example: 1912, D. H. Lawrence, letter to Edward Garnett I've got the pip horribly at present.
etymology: From Middle English pippe, from Middle Dutch pip, from post-classical Latin pipita, from Latin pītuīta (“mucus, phlegm, head cold”). Doublet of pituita.

definition: A clamp for holding pipe that is to be cut or threaded.
A smoker who uses a pipe.
Adjustable wrench for gripping and turning a pipe; has two serrated jaws that are adjusted to grip the pipe.
A thin strip of covered cord used to edge hems.
example: The piping of a house.

definition: Crow-sized black-and-white bird; a good mimic often caged.
Mechanical device that has a plunging or thrusting motion.
etymology: Borrowed from French piston.

definition: A chamber within which piston moves.
Seal consisting of a split metal ring that seals the gap between a piston and the cylinder wall.
Connecting rod that moves or is moved by a piston.
New World vipers with hollow fangs and a heat-sensitive pit on each side of the head.
Rise and fall of the voice pitch.
A wedge used to loft the golf ball over obstacles.
A freely moving joint in which movement is limited to rotation.
example: The articulation of the radius and ulna in the arm is a pivot joint.

definition: A one-handed basketball shot made while whirling on the pivot foot.
A shop where pizzas are made and sold.
example: The gang and I went to the pizza parlor to order some pizza and kill a little time.

definition: (football) a kicker who makes a place kick for a goal.
A cloth having a crisscross design.
etymology: From Scots plaid, of uncertain origin; perhaps from a past participle form of ply. Scottish Gaelic plaide (“blanket”) is probably a borrowing from Scots.

definition: A basic style of weave in which the weft and warp threads intertwine alternately to produce a checkerboard effect.
Unmistakably (‘plain’ is often used informally for ‘plainly’).
example: You are plainly wrong.
etymology: From Middle English playnly, pleinly, pleyneliche, equivalent to plain + -ly.

definition: (of a moving wave) vibrating in a single plane.
example: Plane-polarized light.

definition: Cover with planks.
example: The streets were planked.
etymology: From Middle English plank, planke, borrowed from Old French planke, Old Northern French planque (compare French planche, from Old French planche), from Vulgar Latin planca, from palanca, from Latin phalanga.

definition: Drop heavily.
Cover with planks.
example: The streets were planked.

definition: A bed of boards (without a mattress).
Related to the leafhoppers and spittlebugs but rarely damages cultivated plants.
Any substance produced by plants that is similar in its properties to extracellular bacterial toxin.
Printing from an intaglio plate that has been converted to a relief print by making a plaster cast of it, thereby causing lines that were originally incised to stand out above the surface.
A person (considered to be) without human failings.
example: He's no plaster saint.

definition: Rocking chair on a stationary base.
A blond whose hair is a pale silvery (often artificially colored) blond.
A large shallow dish used for serving food.
etymology: From Middle English plater, from Anglo-Norman plater, dissimilatory variant of platel, from Old French plate (“metal plate”) (see plate). Doublet of plateau.

definition: Capable of or suitable for being played or played on.
example: A playable lie in golf.
etymology: From play + -able.

definition: The act of reproducing recorded sound.
example: He was allowed to hear the playback of his testimony.
etymology: From play + back. Sense 2 is from French playback, a pseudo-anglicism of this term.

definition: Someone who writes plays.
etymology: From play + wright (“builder, craftsman”).

definition: (criminal law) a negotiation in which the defendant agrees to enter a plea of guilty to a lesser charge and the prosecutor agrees to drop a more serious charge.
example: His admission was part of a plea bargain with the prosecutor.

definition: Having an odor that is pleasing.
In a good-humoured manner.
example: ‘I'll do the dishes,’ he said pleasantly.
etymology: From Middle English pleasauntly; equivalent to pleasant + -ly.

definition: Someone motivated by desires for sensual pleasures.
Existing in great number or quantity.
example: Rhinoceroses were once plentiful here.
etymology: From Middle English plentiful, plentyfull, plentefull, equivalent to plenty + -ful.

definition: A situation from which extrication is difficult especially an unpleasant or trying one.
example: The woeful plight of homeless people.
etymology: From Middle English plit (“fold, wrinkle, bad situation”), conflation of Middle English pliht, plight (“risky promise, peril”) (from Old English pliht "danger, risk";

definition: With planning and intention.
(of a coin) altered by the insertion of a plug of base metal.
A rich steamed or boiled pudding that resembles cake.
For Chinese dishes: plum preserves and chutney.
etymology: Calque of Chinese 梅子醬 /梅子酱 (méizǐjiàng, “plum sauce”)

definition: An Italian variety of cherry tomato that is shaped like a plum.
etymology: From its resemblance to a plum.

definition: A craftsman who installs and repairs pipes and fixtures and appliances.
etymology: From Middle English plumber, from Old French plummier (French plombier); from Latin plumbārius, from plumbum (“lead or lead shot”). The verb sense “to botch” is perhaps from the negative stereotype of the occupation.

definition: A fixture for the distribution and use of water in a building.
Thrust or throw into.
example: To plunge the body into water.
etymology: From Middle English plungen, ploungen, Anglo-Norman plungier, from Old French plongier, (Modern French plonger), from unattested Late Latin frequentative *plumbicō (“to throw a leaded line”), from plumbum (“lead”).

definition: Characterized by extravagance and profusion.
example: They lived in a plush apartment complex.
etymology: From French peluche (“fluff, plush”). The fact that historically (in past centuries) plush upholstery was so expensive as to be socially exclusive undoubtedly connects the senses of "luxurious" and "soft".

definition: (of textures) resembling plush.
A laminate made of thin layers of wood.
example: After the hurricane there was a severe regional shortage of plywood, especially exterior plywood.
etymology: From ply (“sheet”) + wood.

definition: A small comb suitable for carrying in a pocket.
A flap that covers the access to a pocket.
A small calendar designed to fit in a pocket or a wallet; it comes in various versions, from a simple plastic card, to a booklet or a notebook.
example: My grandfather still uses pocket calendars.

definition: Arousing affect.
example: Poignant grief cannot endure forever.
etymology: From Middle English poynaunt, poynant, borrowed from Anglo-Norman puignant, poynaunt etc., present participle of poindre (“to prick”), from Latin pungō (“prick”). Doublet of pungent.

definition: Marked by balance or equilibrium and readiness for action.
example: A gull in poised flight.

definition: Any of various Australian evergreen shrubs of the genus Gastrolobium having whorled compound leaves poisonous to livestock and showy yellow to deep reddish-orange flowers followed by two-seeded pods.
A sharp hand gesture (resembling a blow).
A person active in party politics.
etymology: Clipping of politician.

definition: A glacier near the Arctic or Antarctic poles.
A large hare of northern North America; it is almost completely white in winter.
The phenomenon in which waves of light or other radiation are restricted in direction of vibration.
etymology: Borrowed from French polarisation. By surface analysis, polarize + -ation or polar + -ization.

definition: An acute viral disease marked by inflammation of nerve cells of the brain stem and spinal cord.
etymology: First element of polio(myelitis).

definition: The work of making something smooth and shiny by rubbing or waxing it.
example: Every Sunday he gave his car a good polishing.

definition: A machine that uses an abrasive and a work wheel for polishing the surfaces of various materials and articles.
In a polite manner.
example: The policeman answered politely, ‘Now look here, lady … ’.
etymology: From polite + -ly.

definition: Avoidance of expressions or actions that can be perceived to exclude or marginalize or insult people who are socially disadvantaged or discriminated against.
etymology: From politically correct + -ness.

definition: A tame parrot.
The fine spores that contain male gametes and that are borne by an anther in a flowering plant.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin pollen (“fine flour”), used by Carl Linnaeus in the 18th century to describe the spores produced in the anthers of flowers.

definition: The number of pollen grains (usually ragweed) in a standard volume of air over a twenty-four hour period and a specified time and place.
(botany) a slender tubular outgrowth from a pollen grain when deposited on the stigma for a flower; it penetrates the style and conveys the male gametes to the ovule.
Rendered unwholesome by contaminants and pollution.
example: Polluted lakes and streams.

definition: Gaudy tropical fishes with parrotlike beaks formed by fusion of teeth.
A small agile horse specially bred and trained for playing polo.
Reflect deeply on a subject.
example: I have spent days pondering the meaning of life.
etymology: From Middle English ponderen, from Old French ponderer (“to weigh, balance, ponder”) from Latin ponderāre (“to weigh, ponder”), from pondus (“weight”), from pendere (“to weigh”); see pendent and pound.

definition: People in general considered as a whole.
example: The populace despised their ignorant leader.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French populace, from Italian popolaccio, from popolo + -accio (“pejorative suffix”), from Latin populus.

definition: Someone who advocates the rights of the common people over those of the elite.
etymology: From Latin populus + English -ist.

definition: Densely populated.
example: China is the most populous country in the world.
etymology: First used in English in the mid 15th century; from Latin populosus (“full of people, populous”).
