definition: A fine usually white clay formed by the weathering of aluminous minerals (as feldspar); used in ceramics and as an absorbent and as a filler (e.g., in paper).
Any tiny hole admitting passage of a liquid (fluid or gas).
example: I could sense the sweat dripping out of all my pores.
etymology: From Middle English pore, from Old French pore, from Latin porus, from Ancient Greek πόρος (póros, “passage”).

definition: Able to absorb fluids.
example: The partly porous walls of our digestive system.
etymology: From Old French poros, from Latin porus (“an opening”). By surface analysis, pore + -ous.

definition: A lightweight, precast, concrete building material invented in the mid-1920s that simultaneously provides structure, insulation, and fire- and mold-resistance.
Increase in blood pressure in the veins of the portal system caused by obstruction in the liver (often associated with alcoholic cirrhosis), causing enlargement of the spleen and collateral veins.
A representation by picture or portraiture.
The character of the positive electric pole.
etymology: From positive + -ity.

definition: The logical fallacy of believing that temporal succession implies a causal relation.
etymology: From Latin post hoc.

definition: As fast as possible; with all possible haste.
example: Send it to me post-haste.
etymology: From the former instruction on letters "haste, post, haste," later reinterpreted as a compound of post + haste.

definition: Meter for bulk mailings that imprints correct prepaid postage on pieces of mail and records the total charge.
A small adhesive token stuck on a letter or package to indicate that postal fees have been paid.
example: The postage stamps on the letters from overseas were almost as interesting as the letters themselves.

definition: A card for sending messages by post without an envelope.
etymology: From post + card.

definition: Located at or near or behind a part or near the end of a structure.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin posterior (“that comes or follows after; later, latter”).

definition: One of two roots of a spinal nerve that passes dorsally from the spinal cord and that consists of sensory fibers.
One of two roots of a spinal nerve that passes dorsally from the spinal cord and that consists of sensory fibers.
Of or relating to studies beyond a bachelor's degree.
etymology: From post- + graduate.

definition: Hold back to a later time.
example: Let's postpone the exam.
etymology: From Latin postpōnō (“to put after; to postpone”) from post (“after”) + pōnō (“to put; to place”), compare forestall.

definition: Belonging to the period after a war.
example: Postwar resettlement.
etymology: From post- + war.

definition: Black-and-yellow beetle that feeds in adult and larval stages on potato leaves; originally of eastern Rocky Mountains; now worldwide.
Fungus causing a disease in potatoes characterized by black scurfy spots on the tubers.
A disease of the leaves of potato plants.
Greyish-brown moth whose larva is the potato tuberworm.
Made of grated potato and egg with a little flour.
The power or right to give orders or make decisions.
example: A place of potency in the state.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin potentia. Doublet of Potenza.

definition: A medicinal or magical or poisonous beverage.
example: He hoped to win the princess's heart by mixing the love potion the witch gave him into her drink.
etymology: From Middle English pocioun, borrowed from Old French pocion, from Latin pōtiō (“a drinking”), pōtiōnis, from pōtāre (“to drink”). Displaced native Old English drenċ whence Modern English drench. Doublet of poison.

definition: Any of various solitary wasps that construct vase-shaped cells of mud for their eggs.
Marked by foolish or unreasoning fondness.
example: The noise that the neighbour's kids were making was driving Fred potty.
etymology: From pot (“chamberpot”) + -y (diminutive suffix).

definition: Toilet consisting of a small seat used by young children.
Shaped like a pouch.
Poor enough to need help from others.
example: The small village was poverty-stricken, with many families struggling to afford even basic necessities like food and water.

definition: Used of competitive activities in which only women take part.
example: Powder-puff baseball.

definition: Consisting of fine particles.
example: Powdered cellulose.

definition: Dehydrated milk.
Sugar granulated into a fine powder.
A loom operated mechanically.
Equipment failure resulting when the supply of power fails.
example: The ice storm caused a power outage.

definition: A device that transfers power from an engine (as in a tractor or other motor vehicle) to another piece of equipment (as to a pump or jackhammer).
A highly energetic and indefatigable person.
example: The company has been a powerhouse in its industry for many years.
etymology: From power + house.

definition: Lacking power.
example: The traffic warden was powerless to stop me driving away.
etymology: From Middle English pouerles, powerles, equivalent to power + -less.

definition: Skillful after much practice.
Concerned with practical matters.
example: A matter-of-fact (or pragmatic) approach to the problem.
etymology: From Middle French pragmatique, from Late Latin pragmaticus (“relating to civil affair;

definition: Wild crab apple of western United States with fragrant pink flowers.
North American annual with red or rose-colored flowers.
Perennial cottony-white herb of southwestern United States.
A large wagon with broad wheels and an arched canvas top; used by the United States pioneers to cross the prairies in the 19th century.
Slender shrubby willow of dry areas of North America.
Existing previously or before something.
example: Variations on pre-existent musical themes.

definition: Affording no ease or reassurance.
example: A precarious truce.
etymology: From Latin precārius (“begged for, obtained by entreaty”), from prex, precis (“prayer”). Compare French précaire, Portuguese precário, and Spanish and Italian precario.

definition: A precautionary measure warding off impending danger or damage or injury etc.
example: He put an ice pack on the injury as a precaution.
etymology: From French précaution, Latin praecautio, from praecavere, praecautum (“to guard against beforehand”); prae (“before”) + cavere (“be on one's guard”). See pre-, and caution.

definition: Status established in order of importance or urgency.
example: … its precedence as the world's leading manufacturer of pharmaceuticals.
etymology: From Middle French précédence (“the state of preceding, anteriority”). Morphologically precede + -ence.

definition: A substance from which another substance is formed (especially by a metabolic reaction).
etymology: Inherited from Middle English precursour, from Middle French precurseur or its etymon Latin praecursor (“forerunner”). By surface analysis, precurse + -or.

definition: Characterized by plundering or pillaging or marauding.
example: Predatory warfare.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin praedātōrius, equivalent to predator + -y.

definition: Any animal that lives by preying on other animals.
Set in advance.
example: At a predetermined time.
etymology: From pre- + determined.

definition: A situation from which extrication is difficult especially an unpleasant or trying one.
example: Finds himself in a most awkward predicament.
etymology: From Middle English predicament, from Old French predicament, from Late Latin praedicāmentum (“that which is predicated, a predicament, category”).

definition: Of or relating to prediction; having value for making predictions.
example: The amount of rain in April is predictive of the number of mosquitoes in May.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin praedictivus, from praedico. Equivalent to predict + -ive.

definition: Most frequent or common.
etymology: From Middle French prédominant, ultimately from Medieval Latin praedominans. By surface analysis, pre- + dominant.

definition: A short introductory essay preceding the text of a book.
example: The book included a brief preface explaining the author's motivations for writing.

definition: More desirable than another.
example: Coffee is preferable to tea.
etymology: From prefer + -able, probably after Middle French preferable. Compare preference, preferential, etc.

definition: Belonging to or existing in times before recorded history.
example: Prehistoric settlements.

definition: The time during the development of human culture before the appearance of the written word.
Something that serves as a preceding event or introduces what follows.
etymology: From Middle French prélude (“singing to test a musical instrument”), from Medieval Latin preludium, from Latin praelūdere.

definition: (of childbirth) before the end of the normal period of gestation.
example: The child was born prematurely.
etymology: From premature + -ly.

definition: Deeply absorbed in thought.
example: A preoccupied frown.

definition: Used especially of mail; paid in advance.
Preceding and preparing for something.
example: Preparatory steps.
etymology: From Middle English preparatori, from Late Latin praeparatorius. By surface analysis, prepare + -atory.

definition: A private secondary school.
Issue commands or orders for.
example: The doctor prescribed aspirin.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin praescrībere, from prae- (“before, in front”) and scrībere (“to write”).

definition: Fruit preserved by cooking with sugar.
The leader of a group meeting.
Autoclave for cooking at temperatures above the boiling point of water.
Something serving to conceal plans; a fictitious reason that is concocted in order to conceal the real reason.
example: The reporter called the company on the pretext of trying to resolve a consumer complaint.
etymology: From Latin praetextum (“an ornament, etc., wrought in front, a pretense”), neuter of praetextus, past participle of praetexere (“to weave before, fringe or border, allege”).

definition: A strike that is carried out in order to deter expected aggression by hostile forces.
The branch of medicine concerned with preventing disease.
example: The medical establishment doesn't profit from preventive medicine.

definition: A strike that is carried out in order to deter expected aggression by hostile forces.
Having a high price.
example: High-priced merchandise.
etymology: From price + -y.

definition: The body of ordained religious practitioners.
example: Tibet is a society ruled the priesthood.
etymology: From Middle English presthed, presthede, presthod, presthode, from Old English prēosthād (“priesthood”), equivalent to priest + -hood. Compare Dutch priesterheid (“priesthood”).

definition: Indicating the most important performer or role.
example: Prima ballerina.
etymology: Derived from Italian prima, derived from Latin prīma.

definition: Serving as an essential component.
etymology: Probably partly from Medieval Latin prīmālis, from Latin prīmus (“first”) + -ālis, and partly from prime + -al.

definition: Meridian at zero degree longitude from which east and west are reckoned (usually the Greenwich longitude in England).
The first or preliminary coat of paint or size applied to a surface.
The diagonal of a square matrix running from the upper left entry to the lower right entry.
For the most part.
etymology: From Middle English principaly. By surface analysis, principal + -ly.

definition: Assign a priority to.
example: We have too many things to do and must prioritize.
etymology: From priority + -ize. First attested in 1967 as U.S. government jargon, becoming more widespread through the 1970s and ’80s, but still denounced as officialese by purists into the 1990s.

definition: A polyhedron with two congruent and parallel faces (the bases) and whose lateral faces are parallelograms.
A chaplain in a prison.
Completely free from dirt or contamination.
example: Pristine mountain snow.
etymology: From Middle French pristin, borrowed from Latin prīstinus.

definition: A nuisance that interferes with your interest in and private use and enjoyment of your land.
Changing something from state to private ownership or control.
etymology: Calque of German Privatisierung (with English -ation), derived from Latin prīvātus (“apart from the state; private”), with reference to post-First World War German economic principles.

definition: Hidden from general view or use.
example: A privy place to rest and think.
etymology: From Middle English pryvy, prive, from Old French privé (“private”), from Latin prīvātus (“deprived”), perfect passive participle of prīvō (“to bereave, deprive; to free, release”). Doublet of private.

definition: An advisory council to a ruler (especially to the British Crown).
etymology: From Middle English prive (“secret, private, confidential”) + counseil.

definition: Allowance for a monarch's personal expenses.
Done for the public good without compensation.
etymology: Abbreviated from Latin prō bonō publicō (“for the public good”).

definition: Descriptive of any event or stimulus or process that has an effect on events or stimuli or processes that occur subsequently.
example: Proactive inhibition.
etymology: From pro- + active; originally coined 1933 by Paul Whiteley and Gerald Blankfort in a psychology paper, used in technical sense.

definition: Declare formally; declare someone to be something; of titles.
example: He was proclaimed King.
etymology: From Middle English proclamen, proclaime, from Old French proclamer, from Latin prōclāmō, prōclāmāre, from prō- (“forth”) + clāmō (“to shout, cry out”).

definition: A formal public statement.
example: The Tuesday meetings are only thirty minutes now. That proclamation was made in the previous meeting.
etymology: From Middle English proclamacion, from Anglo-Norman and Old French proclamacion, from Late Latin proclāmātiō, from the verb Latin prōclāmō.

definition: An unusually gifted or intelligent (young) person; someone whose talents excite wonder and admiration.
example: She is a chess prodigy.
etymology: From Middle English prodige (“portent”), from Latin prōdigium (“omen, portent, prophetic sign”).

definition: Someone who earns a living by playing or teaching golf.
The expertness characteristic of a professional person.
etymology: From professional + -ism.

definition: The quality of having great facility and competence.
example: To attain (or to reach) proficiency.
etymology: From proficient or its etymon, Latin prōficiēns (present participle of prōficiō), + -ency.

definition: Having or showing knowledge and skill and aptitude.
example: A proficient engineer.
etymology: From Latin proficiens, present participle of proficere (“to go forward, advance, make progress, succeed, be profitable or useful”), from pro (“forth, forward”) + facere (“to make, do”); see fact.

definition: Recording a person's behavior and analyzing psychological characteristics in order to predict or assess their ability in a certain sphere or to identify a particular group of people.
Totally deaf; unable to hear anything.
Advancing in amount or intensity.
example: Increase something progressively.
etymology: From progressive + -ly.

definition: An optical device for projecting a beam of light.
example: A depth charge projector.
etymology: Partly from Latin projector (“person who throws away”); partly directly from project + -or.

definition: In a prominent way.
example: The new car was prominently displayed in the driveway.
etymology: From prominent + -ly.

definition: Persuasion formulated as a suggestion.
The spreading of something (a belief or practice) into new regions.
example: Plant propagation.
etymology: From Middle French propagation, from Old French propagacion, from Latin propagatio. Morphologically propagate + -ion.

definition: A mechanical device that rotates to push against air or water.
example: The plane’s propeller spun rapidly before takeoff.
etymology: From propel + -er.

definition: An airplane that is driven by a propeller.
Any font whose different characters have different widths.
The population is divided into subpopulations (strata) and random samples are taken of each stratum.
(law) someone who owns (is legal possessor of) a business.
etymology: Probably from proprietary + -or.

definition: A propelling force.
etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin propulsio, propulsionis, from the past participle of Latin propello (“to drive forward, drive forth, drive away, drive out”).

definition: A system that provides a propelling or driving force.
A government official who conducts criminal prosecutions on behalf of the state.
A government official who conducts criminal prosecutions on behalf of the state.
Make steady progress; be at the high point in one's career or reach a high point in historical significance or importance.
Clothing that is intended to protect the wearer from injury.
A tariff imposed to protect domestic firms from import competition.
Relatively long in duration; tediously protracted.
example: Protracted negotiations.

definition: Serving or tending to provoke, excite, or stimulate; stimulating discussion or exciting controversy.
example: A provocative remark.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French provocatif, and its source, Late Latin provocativus, from Latin provocare.

definition: Causing or tending to cause anger or resentment.
example: A provoking delay at the airport.

definition: A superior skill that you can learn by study and practice and observation.
etymology: From Middle English prowesse, prouwesse, proues, prouesce, prouesse (“bravery in battle; act of bravery; excellence; nobility of character; intelligence”), from Old French proeche, proesce, proeësche (“goodness;

definition: Careful and sensible; marked by sound judgment.
example: A prudent manager.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English prudent, from Old French prudent, from Latin prūdēns, contracted from prōvidēns (“foresight”) (English providence), the present participle of prōvideō (“to forsee; to provide for”).

definition: A neutral meson with a large mass.
Get excited or stimulated.
example: The children were all psyched up after the movie.

definition: That which is responsible for one's thoughts, feelings, and conscious brain functions; the seat of the faculty of reason.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin psychē, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ψυχή (psukhḗ, “soul”).

definition: Producing distorted sensory perceptions and feelings or altered states of awareness or sometimes states resembling psychosis.
example: Psychedelic drugs like psilocybin and mescaline.

definition: A psychoactive drug that induces hallucinations or altered sensory experiences.
A musical style that emerged in the 1960s; rock music inspired by or related to drug-induced experience.
etymology: The album The Psychedelic Sounds of the 13th Floor Elevators (1966) first used psychedelic to describe music; the band The 13th Floor Elevators is sometimes credited with coining the term.

definition: Phenomena that appear to contradict physical laws and suggest the possibility of causation by mental processes.
With regard to psychology.
example: War that caught them in its toils either psychologically or physically.
etymology: From psychological + -ly.

definition: Someone with a sociopathic personality; a person with an antisocial personality disorder (‘psychopath’ was once widely used but has now been superseded by ‘sociopath’).
etymology: From German psychopathisch, from Ancient Greek ψυχή (psukhḗ, “soul”) + πάθος (páthos, “suffering”).

definition: The branch of psychiatry concerned with psychological methods.
etymology: From psycho- + therapy.

definition: A meeting of people for psychotherapeutic purposes.
Characteristic of or suffering from psychosis.
etymology: Derived in English from psychosis + -tic; compare French psychotique, German psychotisch. Attested from the late 19th century. Compare earlier neurotic.

definition: (psychology) an erroneous belief that is held in the face of evidence to the contrary.
A person afflicted with psychosis.
Creeping perennial herb distinguished by red berries and clustered leaf whorls at the tips of shoots; Greenland to Alaska.
Wade or dabble in a puddle.
example: The ducks and geese puddled in the backyard.

definition: Batter for making light hollow cases to hold various fillings.
Dough used for very light flaky rich pastries.
One of two arteries (branches of the pulmonary trunk) that carry venous blood from the heart to the lungs.
Circulation of blood between the heart and the lungs.
Congestion in the lungs.
The additional volume of air that the lungs can inhale and exhale when breathing to the limit of capacity in times of stress.
The artery that carries venous blood from the right ventricle of the heart and divides into the right and left pulmonary arteries.
A semilunar valve between the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery; prevents blood from flowing from the artery back into the heart.
Any of four veins that carry arterial blood from the lungs to the left atrium of the heart.
The central cavity of a tooth containing the pulp (including the root canal).
A coarse vine widely cultivated for its large pulpy round orange fruit with firm orange skin and numerous seeds; subspecies of Cucurbita pepo include the summer squashes and a few autumn squashes.
Something that makes repeated and regular interruptions or divisions.
example: Different languages have different rules for punctuation.
etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin punctuātiō (“a marking with points, a writing, agreement”), from punctuō (“to mark with points, settle”). Morphologically, punctuate + -ion.

definition: The marks used to clarify meaning by indicating separation of words into sentences and clauses and phrases.
Liable to or deserving punishment.
example: Punishable offenses.
etymology: From punish + -able.

definition: Inflicting punishment.
example: Punitive justice.
etymology: From Middle French punitif, from Medieval Latin pūnitīvus, from pūniō (“to punish”).

definition: (law) compensation in excess of actual damages (a form of punishment awarded in cases of malicious or willful misconduct).
A teenager or young adult who is a performer (or enthusiast) of punk rock and a member of the punk youth subculture.
Kick the ball.
etymology: From Old English punt, from Latin pontō (“Gaulish flat-bottomed boat, pontoon”), from pons (“bridge”); readopted from Middle Low German punte (“ferry boat”) or Middle Dutch ponte (“ferry boat”) of the same origin.

definition: A person who buys.
etymology: From purchase + -er.

definition: The act of cleaning by getting rid of impurities.
example: Air purification.
etymology: From Old French purificacion, from Latin pūrificātiō.

definition: Erect to decumbent short-lived perennial having red-purple to pink flowers; the most commonly grown forage clover.
Any of several attractive evergreen shrubs of Australia grown for their glossy deep green foliage and flowers in rich blues and intense violets.
With intention; in an intentional manner.
example: I purposely left the door unlocked.
etymology: From Middle English purposly; equivalent to purpose + -ly.

definition: A wide broom that is pushed ahead of the sweeper.
Pink clusters of densely packed flowers on prostrate stems resemble upturned pads of cats' feet; grow in coniferous forests of western North America.
Pink clusters of densely packed flowers on prostrate stems resemble upturned pads of cats' feet; grow in coniferous forests of western North America.
Filled with bewilderment.
example: Puzzled that she left without saying goodbye.

definition: A quarter of the circumference of a circle.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English quadrant, from Old French cadran, quadrant and its etymon Latin quadrāns, -antis (“fourth part of something, quarter”). Doublet of quadrans.

definition: Strange in an interesting or pleasing way.
example: Quaint dialect words.
etymology: From Middle English queynte, quoynte, from Anglo-Norman cointe, queinte and Old French cointe (“pretty, clever, knowing”), from Latin cognitus, past participle of cognōscō (“to know”).

definition: Shake with fast, tremulous movements.
etymology: From Middle English quaken, from Old English cwacian (“to quake, tremble, chatter”), from Proto-Germanic *kwakōną (“to shake, quiver, tremble”), itself likely of imitative origin.

definition: A contestant who meets certain requirements and so qualifies to take part in the next stage of competition.
example: The tournament was won by a late qualifier.
etymology: From qualify + -er.

definition: An adjective that ascribes to its noun the value of an attribute of that noun (e.g., ‘a nervous person’ or ‘a musical speaking voice’).
Involving distinctions based on qualities.
example: Qualitative change.
etymology: From Late Latin (or Medieval Latin) quālitātīvus. Equivalent to quality + -ative.

definition: The act of decomposing a substance into its constituent elements.
An angry dispute.
example: They had a quarrel.
etymology: From Middle English querele (“altercation, dispute; argument, debate; armed combat; trial by combat; basis for dispute, complaint; claim, legal suit; a lament;

definition: Having some resemblance.
example: A quasi success.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin quasi (“as if”).

definition: A contract created by law for reasons of justice without any expression of assent.
Resembling something that is religious.
Having the power but not the rank or title of a king.
example: One of the quasi-royal rulers of Africa.

definition: Wharf usually built parallel to the shoreline.
etymology: The current spelling replaced the spelling key in the 1690s to emulate the spelling but (at least originally) not the pronunciation of the equivalent modern French quai.

definition: A queen who serves as ruler when the king cannot.
A form containing a set of questions; submitted to people to gain statistical information.
example: Carry out a questionnaire.
etymology: Borrowed from French questionnaire, from Late Latin quaestionarius, from quaestio (English question) + -arius, from quaerō (“to question”) (English query).

definition: Most quickly.
The basic unit of money in Great Britain and Northern Ireland; equal to 100 pence.
example: Seven quid for a toastie? Are you taking the mick?!
etymology: Borrowed from Latin quid (“what, something”), neuter singular of quis (“who”).

definition: Stitch or sew together.
example: Quilt the skirt.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English quilte, quylte, from Anglo-Norman quilte and Old French coilte, cuilte (compare French couette), from Latin culcita. Doublet of quoit.

definition: On equal terms by payment or requital.
example: We're now quits.
etymology: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

definition: Small wild dog of eastern Asia having facial markings like those of a raccoon.
Raccoon-like omnivorous mammal of Mexico and the southwestern United States having a long bushy tail with black and white rings.
Someone who drives racing cars at high speeds.
With respect to race.
example: Racially integrated.
etymology: From racial + -ly.

definition: A loud and disturbing noise.
example: He bought a new tennis racket two days ago.
etymology: From Middle English raket, of uncertain origin. Possibly cognate with Middle French rachette, requette (“palm of the hand”). From Arabic رَاحَةْ اَلْيَد (rāḥat al-yad, “palm of the hand”).

definition: Club for players of racket sports.
Relating to or near the radius.
example: The radial aspect of the forearm.
etymology: From Medieval Latin radiālis (“radial”), from Latin radius. By surface analysis, radius + -al.

definition: An internal-combustion engine having cylinders arranged radially around a central crankcase.

Largest branch of the brachial plexus; extends down the humerus to the lateral epicondyle where it divides into one branch that goes to the skin on the back of the hand and another that goes to the underlying extensor muscles.
Pulse of the radial artery (felt in the wrist).
Pneumatic tire that has radial-ply casing.
Superficial veins ascending the radial side of the forearm; combines with the ulnar veins to form the brachial vein.
Velocity along the line of sight toward or away from the observer.
Radiating or as if radiating light.
example: A radiant sunrise.
etymology: From Middle English radyant, from Latin radiāns, radiantis, present participle of radiāre (“to emit rays or beams”).

definition: Energy that is transmitted in the form of (electromagnetic) radiation; energy that exists in the absence of matter.
Heating a building by radiation from panels containing hot water or electrical heaters.
Any object that radiates energy.
Cap on the opening in the top of a radiator through which a coolant liquid can be added.
Not transparent to X-rays or other forms of radiation.
example: Barium sulfate is radiopaque.

definition: The spontaneous disintegration of a radioactive substance along with the emission of ionizing radiation.
A flat float (usually made of logs or planks) that can be used for transport or as a platform for swimmers.
example: They floated down the river on an inflatable raft.
etymology: Late Middle English, of North Germanic origin, from West Old Norse raptr, from Proto-Germanic *raf-tra-, from Proto-Indo-European *rap-tro-, from *rep- (“stake, beam”).

definition: A foundation (usually on soft ground) consisting of an extended layer of reinforced concrete.
A cloth doll that is stuffed and (usually) painted.
example: The tornado flung the man around like a rag doll.

definition: Someone who takes spoils or plunder (as in war).
etymology: From raid + -er.

definition: Characterized by plundering or pillaging or marauding.
example: A raiding party.

definition: A barrier consisting of a horizontal bar and supports.
example: During the war, everyone's railings were taken away to make bombers.
etymology: By surface analysis, rail + -ing.

definition: A short stretch of railroad track used to store rolling stock or enable trains on the same line to pass.
A wheeled vehicle consisting of a self-propelled engine that is used to draw trains along railway tracks.
Rain heavily.
example: Put on your rain coat — it's pouring outside!
etymology: From figurative sense of pouring from buckets.

definition: A stout cylindrical cactus of the southwest United States and adjacent Mexico.
A forest with heavy annual rainfall.
etymology: From rain + forest, a calque of German Regenwald.

definition: A prince or king in India.
Move through with or as if with a rake.
example: She raked her fingers through her hair.
etymology: The verb is partly derived from rake (“tool with a row of pointed teeth”) (see etymology 1) and from Middle English raken (“to rake; to gather by raking; to rake away (debris); to cover with something;

definition: The handle of a rake.
Earn large sums of money.
Take money from an illegal transaction.
Bring to light.
example: He raked up the misdeeds of his predecessor.

definition: A percentage (of winnings or loot or profit) taken by an operator or gangster.
Violently angry and destructive behavior.
etymology: From Scots rampage, equivalent to ramp + -age. Perhaps influenced by Middle English rampnen (“to force, ram”), from Old English *hrampian, from Proto-West Germanic *hrampōn (“to obstruct, hinder”), see ramp.

definition: An arch whose support is higher on one side than on the other.
Set up or distributed in a deliberately random way.
A measuring instrument (acoustic or optical or electronic) for finding the distance of an object.
Noteworthy scarcity.
etymology: From rare + -ity, borrowed from Middle French rarité, from Latin rāritās; compare French rareté. See also rare.

definition: Woody brambles bearing usually red but sometimes black or yellow fruits that separate from the receptacle when ripe and are rounder and smaller than blackberries.
Of the red of fresh raspberries.
Any of several rabbit-sized ratlike Australian kangaroos.
A workman employed to destroy or drive away vermin.
A series of short sharp taps (as made by strokes on a drum or knocks on a door).
Formally approved and invested with legal authority.
A rapid series of short loud sounds (as might be heard with a stethoscope in some types of respiratory disorders).
example: The death rattle.
etymology: From Middle English ratelen, of uncertain origin;

definition: Recite volubly or extravagantly.
example: He could rattle off the names of all the chemical elements.

definition: Recite volubly or extravagantly.
example: He could rattle off the names of all the chemical elements.

definition: Talk incessantly and tiresomely.
Much-branched erect herb with bright yellow flowers; distributed from Massachusetts to Florida.
North American bugbane found from Maine and Ontario to Wisconsin and south to Georgia.
A run that is the result of the batter's performance.
example: He had more than 100 rbi last season.

definition: Re-equip a factory or plant.
etymology: From re- + equip.

definition: A process of using up or consuming again.
Propulsion that results from the ejection at high velocity of a mass of gas to which the vehicle reacts with an equal and opposite momentum.
Schizophrenia of abrupt onset and relatively short duration (a few weeks or months).
Easily deciphered.
example: If that sign were still readable we'd know where we are!
etymology: Inherited from Middle English redable. By surface analysis, read + -able.

definition: A philosopher who believes that universals are real and exist independently of anyone thinking of them.
etymology: From real + -ist.

definition: In a realistic manner.
example: Let's look at the situation realistically.
etymology: From realistic + -ally.

definition: Property consisting of houses and land.
etymology: From Middle French realité (“property, possession”). Doublet of reality.

definition: An edge tool for cutting grass or crops; has a curved blade and a short handle.
Someone who helps to gather the harvest.
etymology: From Middle English reper, repare, repere, *riper (the last, attested only in surnames Ryper, Riper, etc.), from Old English rīpere (“reaper”), equivalent to reap + -er.

definition: Logically valid.
The act of reassuring; restoring someone's confidence.
etymology: From re- + assurance.

definition: Give reassurance to; give or restore confidence in; cause to feel sure or certain.
example: I reassured him that we were safe.
etymology: From Old French rasseürer (French rassurer), from re- + asseürer; as if re- + assure.

definition: Restoring confidence and relieving anxiety.
example: A very reassuring remark.

definition: Give a reduction in the price during a sale.
example: The store is rebating refrigerators this week.
etymology: From Old French rabatre < batre. See also abate.

definition: Resisting control or authority.
example: Temperamentally rebellious.
etymology: From Middle English rebellious; equivalent to rebel + -ious.

definition: Spiritually reborn or converted.
etymology: From re- + born.

definition: A summary at the end that repeats the substance of a longer discussion.
example: He refused to buy recaps because he didn't trust them not to come apart on the highway.
etymology: From re- + cap.

definition: A secretary whose main duty is to answer the telephone and receive visitors.
etymology: Recorded since 1901, derived from reception + -ist.

definition: Open to arguments, ideas, or change.
example: Receptive to reason and the logic of facts.
etymology: From Late Middle English receptive, receptyue (“capable of receiving something;

definition: Load anew.
etymology: From Old French rechargier, from Old French re- + Old French chargier.

definition: Recite in elocution.
example: Janice is able to recite pi to 100 decimals.
etymology: From Middle English reciten, from Old French reciter, from Latin recitō.

definition: Problem solving that involves numbers or quantities.
example: By that reckoning, it would take six weeks to go five miles.
etymology: Gerund of the verb reckon, from reckon + -ing. Compare Dutch rekening, German Rechnung.

definition: Claim back.
etymology: From Middle English reclaymen, recleymen, reclamen, from Anglo-Norman reclamer (noun reclaim and Middle French reclamer (noun reclaim), from Latin reclāmō, reclāmāre. Equivalent to re- + claim.

definition: Delivered from danger.
example: Reclaimed words like "queer" or "gay" are usually offensive to the in-group when used by outsiders.

definition: Easily perceived; easy to become aware of.
example: This situation produces recognizable stress symptoms.
etymology: From recognize + -able.

definition: The ability to recall past occurrences.
example: Alas that distant event isn't within my recollection anymore.
etymology: Via French récollection or the verb recollect, both from Latin recollectus, the past participle of recolligere (“to collect again”), itself from re- + colligere (“to gather”).

definition: The act of reconnoitring (especially to gain information about an enemy or potential enemy).
example: An exchange of fire occurred on a reconnaissance mission.
etymology: Borrowed from French reconnaissance (“recognition”). Doublet of recognizance.

definition: The act of reconnoitring (especially to gain information about an enemy or potential enemy).
example: An exchange of fire occurred on a reconnaissance mission.

definition: A military airplane used to gain information about an enemy.
Fast armored military vehicle with four-wheel drive and open top.
Adapted to social or economic change.
example: A reconstructed feminist.

definition: An automatic mechanical device on a record player that causes new records to be played without manual intervention.
Act of turning to for assistance.
example: Have recourse to the courts.
etymology: From Middle English recours (noun) and recoursen (verb), from Old French recours, from Latin recursus, past participle of recurrō.

definition: Someone who supplies members or employees.
example: The army recruiter promised that I'd see the world and learn useful skills if I enlisted.
etymology: From recruit + -er.

definition: A person authorized to conduct religious worship.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English rectour, rector, from Old French rector, rectour and Latin rēctor.

definition: Cause to repeat a cycle.
etymology: From re- + cycle.

definition: North American forest tree with light green leaves and edible nuts.
Birch of swamps and river bottoms throughout the eastern United States having reddish-brown bark.
Erect to decumbent short-lived perennial having red-purple to pink flowers; the most commonly grown forage clover.
Autumn-flowering elm of southeastern United States.
etymology: Calque of translingual Ulmus rubra.

definition: Any diversion intended to distract attention from the main issue.
etymology: (figurative): One possible origin of the idiom was that red herring were used to train dogs to track scents.

definition: Succulent carpet-forming plant having small brilliant reddish-pink flowers; southwestern United States.
Any of several raspberries bearing red fruit.
Medium-sized spruce of eastern North America; chief lumber spruce of the area; source of pulpwood.
Dichromacy characterized by lowered sensitivity to long wavelengths of light resulting in an inability to distinguish red and purplish blue.
Endowed with or exhibiting great bodily or mental health.
Of something having a lavender color tinged with red.
Of a color at the end of the color spectrum (next to orange); resembling the color of blood or cherries or tomatoes or rubies.
etymology: From Middle English redisch; equivalent to red + -ish.

definition: A variable color that lies beyond blue in the spectrum.
A shade of brown with a tinge of red.
An orange color closer to red than to yellow.
A shade of purple tinged with red.
Of brown tinged with red.
Of grey tinged with red.
Of grey tinged with red.
Of orange tinged with red.
Of a pink color that is close to red.
Of purple tinged with red.
Of violet tinged with red.
Saved from the bondage of sin.
Design anew, make a new design for.
etymology: From re- + design.

definition: The act of improving by renewing and restoring.
example: The redevelopment of the hero's character in a comic book.
etymology: From re- + development.

definition: Distributing again.
example: The revolution resulted in a redistribution of wealth.
etymology: From re- + distribution.

definition: An unstressed, central variant of a fuller vowel.
example: The most common reduced vowel is schwa.

definition: Repetition of messages to reduce the probability of errors in transmission.
A system of checking for errors in computer functioning.

Tall marsh plant with cylindrical seed heads that explode when mature shedding large quantities of down; its long flat leaves are used for making mats and chair seats; of North America, Europe, Asia and North Africa.
A square knot used in a reef line.
Election again.
example: He did not run for reelection.
etymology: From re- + election.

definition: Improve or perfect by pruning or polishing.
example: Refine one's style of writing.
etymology: From re- + fine.

definition: An industrial plant for purifying a crude substance.
etymology: From refine + -ry.

definition: The process of removing impurities (as from oil or metals or sugar etc.).
An industry that produces and delivers oil and oil products.
Without volition or conscious control.
example: A reflex knee jerk.
etymology: From Late Latin reflexus, past participle of reflectere (“to bend back”), equivalent to re- + flex. Photography sense is from noun sense meaning “reflection”. Compare English reflect.

definition: An automatic instinctive unlearned reaction to a stimulus.
An angle greater than 180 degrees (but less than 360).
The neural path of a reflex.
Camera that allows the photographer to view and focus the exact scene being photographed.
An automatic instinctive unlearned reaction to a stimulus.
With restored energy.
Dough formed into a roll and chilled in the refrigerator then sliced and baked.
Belonging to or befitting a supreme ruler.
example: Regal attire.
etymology: From Middle English regal, from Old French regal (“regal, royal”), from Latin rēgālis (“royal, kingly”), from rex (“king”); also regere (“to rule”).

definition: The period of time during which a regent governs.
example: The country was governed by a regency while the king was still a minor.
etymology: From Middle English regencie (cf. regente), from Medieval Latin regentia, from Latin regēns, present participle of regō. By surface analysis, regent + -cy; compare also + -ency (“abstract-noun suffix”).

definition: Members of a governing board.
etymology: From Middle English regent, from Anglo-Norman regent, Middle French regent, and their source, Latin regēns (“ruling; ruler, governor, prince”), present participle of regō (“to govern, to steer”).

definition: Popular music originating in the West Indies; repetitive bass riffs and regular chords played on the off beat by a guitar.
etymology: From Jamaican Creole rege (“rags; a quarrel”), see rag; originally used in the 1960s to describe a Jamaican dance. Compare ragtime. Broader musical sense popularized by the 1968 Maytals song “Do the Reggay”.

definition: (medicine) a systematic plan for therapy (often including diet).
etymology: From Middle English regimen, from Middle French regimen and its etymon, Latin regimen (“guidance, direction, government, rule”). Doublet of regime.

definition: Loss of sensation in a region of the body produced by application of an anesthetic agent to all the nerves supplying that region (as when an epidural anesthetic is administered to the pelvic region during childbirth).
A person employed to keep a record of the owners of stocks and bonds issued by the company.
etymology: From Medieval Latin registrārius, from registrum (“register”) + -ārius (“agent of use”). See more at register. By surface analysis, register /registry (“a record”) + -ar.

definition: The use of regression to make quantitative predictions of one variable from the values of another.
A smooth curve fitted to the set of paired data in regression analysis; for linear regression the curve is a straight line.
The equation representing the relation between selected values of one variable (x) and observed values of the other (y); it permits the prediction of the most probable values of y.
A right prism whose bases are regular polygons.
example: The height of a regular prism is the distance between the bases.

definition: Exercising power or authority.
example: The reigning world heavyweight champion said he'd defend his title once more and then retire even if he won.

definition: Compensation paid (to someone) for damages or losses or money already spent etc.
example: He received reimbursement for his travel expenses.
etymology: From reimburse + -ment.

definition: Control and direct with or as if by reins.
example: Rein a horse.
etymology: From Middle English rein, reyne, from Anglo-Norman reyne, resne, from Early Medieval Latin retina, ultimately from Classical Latin retineō (“hold back”), from re- + teneō (“keep, hold”). Compare modern French rêne.

definition: Stop or slow up one's horse or oneself by or as if by pulling the reins.
example: They reined in in front of the post office.

definition: A military operation (often involving new supplies of men and materiel) to strengthen a military force or aid in the performance of its mission.
example: There's a website that can be a good learning reinforcement.
etymology: From reinforce + -ment.

definition: Feel happiness or joy.
etymology: From Middle English rejoicen, rejoisen, from Old French resjoir. Doublet of rejoy. Compare French réjouir; Spanish regocijar; Portuguese regozijar; Italian gioire

definition: Having a manner or nature that is easy to relate to.
example: The damage was relatable to the recent earthquake.
etymology: From relate + -able.

definition: (physics) the theory that space and time are relative concepts rather than absolute concepts.
An amplifier for restoring the strength of a transmitted signal.
In a faithful manner.
example: Genuine cowards follow the wicked and cannot reliably sustain any virtue.
etymology: From reliable + -ly.

definition: Relying on another for support.
etymology: From rely + -ant.

definition: An antiquity that has survived from the distant past.
etymology: From Middle English relik et al., from Old French relique, from Latin reliquiae (“remains, relics”), from relinquō (“to leave behind, abandon, relinquish”), from re- + linquō (“to leave, quit, forsake, depart from”).

definition: A trance induced by intense religious devotion; does not show reduced bodily functions that are typical of other trances.
Vigorous and enthusiastic enjoyment.
example: I have a relish for moderate praise, because it bids fair to be judicious.
etymology: The noun is a variant of release (“(obsolete) odour, scent”), from Middle English reles, relese (“odour, scent; taste;

definition: Load anew.
example: She reloaded the gun carefully.
etymology: From re- + load.

definition: Become established in a new location.
example: Our company relocated to the Midwest.
etymology: From re- + locate.

definition: Settled in a new location.
(physics) opposition to magnetic flux (analogous to electric resistance).
example: Our new dog shows reluctance to go on walks, preferring to be indoors.
etymology: From reluct + -ance. From Latin relū̆ctor (“to struggle against, oppose, resist”) + -ance, from re- (“back”) + luctor (“to struggle”).

definition: With reluctance.
etymology: From reluctant + -ly.

definition: (roentgen equivalent man) the dosage of ionizing radiation that will cause the same amount of injury to human tissue as 1 roentgen of X-rays.
etymology: Abbreviation of Roentgen equivalent in man.

definition: Something (especially a game) that is played again.
example: After being beaten in pool by Melanie, John asked for a rematch.
etymology: From re- + match.

definition: A small part or portion that remains after the main part no longer exists.
example: The remnants of the Neanderthal race mixed with members of Homo sapiens.
etymology: From Middle English, contraction of remenant, from Anglo-Norman remanant, present participle of remaindre, from Latin remaneō.

definition: Capable of being removed or taken away or dismissed.
example: A removable cord.
etymology: From remove + -able.

definition: Something that remunerates.
etymology: From Latin remūnerātiō.

definition: Of or relating to the kidneys.
example: Renal transplant.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin renalis, from Latin rēnēs (“kidneys”).

definition: A disease affecting the kidneys.
Inability of the kidneys to excrete wastes and to help maintain the electrolyte balance.
Veins that accompany renal arteries; open into the vena cava at the level of the 2nd lumbar vertebra.
A meeting planned at a certain time and place.
etymology: Borrowed from French rendez-vous (“appointment”), noun derived from second person plural imperative of se rendre (“to go to”), literally, “[you (imperative)] go to, get yourself to [a place]”.

definition: A performance of a musical composition or a dramatic role etc.
example: They heard a live rendition of three pieces by Schubert.
etymology: From obsolete French rendition, alteration (after rendre (“to render”)) of reddition (“reddition”). Many senses influenced by render.

definition: A rebate on rent given by a local government authority.
Open again or anew.
example: They reopened the theater.
etymology: From re- + open.

definition: The imposition of a new organization; organizing differently (often involving extensive and drastic changes).
example: A committee was appointed to oversee the reorganization of the curriculum.
etymology: From re- + organization.

definition: The act of returning money received previously.
etymology: From repay + -ment, also equivalent to re- + payment.

definition: The amount of money paid out per unit time.
Turn away from sin or do penitence.
example: Marry in haste, repent at leisure.
etymology: From Middle English repenten, from Old French repentir, from Vulgar Latin *repaenitīre, from Late Latin paenitīre, from Classical Latin paenitēre. Compare Modern French repentir.

definition: The entire range of skills or aptitudes or devices used in a particular field or occupation.
example: The repertory of the supposed feats of mesmerism.
etymology: Borrowed from French répertoire, from Middle French repertoire, from Late Latin repertōrium (“an inventory, list, repertory”). Doublet of repertory.

definition: An event that repeats.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin repetitionem (accusative singular of repetitio; cf. French répétition). Doublet of repetitio. By surface analysis, repeat + -ition.

definition: The act of making copies.
example: That painting is an almost exact replication of a famous Rembrandt painting.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English replicacioun, replicacion, from Anglo-Norman replicacioun and Old French replicacion (“reply, answer”), from Latin replicātiō, replicātiōnem. By surface analysis, replicate + -(at)ion.

definition: Characterized by or showing the suppression of impulses or emotions.
example: Repressed rage turned his face scarlet.
etymology: From repress + -ed.

definition: A publication (such as a book) that is reprinted without changes or editing and offered again for sale.
example: The reprint is much less expensive than a first edition.
etymology: From re- + print (verb).

definition: Having a good reputation.
example: A reputable business.
etymology: From repute + -able.

definition: The selling of something purchased.
example: They bought the contents of the locker for resale.
etymology: From re- + sale.

definition: Feel bitter or indignant about.
example: She resents being paid less than her co-workers.
etymology: From Middle French ressentir, resentir, from Old French resentir (Modern ressentir), from re- + sentir (“to feel”).

definition: The soil that is remaining after the soluble elements have been dissolved.
The soil that is remaining after the soluble elements have been dissolved.
In a respectful manner.
example: Might I respectfully suggest to the Town Council that they should adopt a policy of masterly inactivity?
etymology: From respectful + -ly.

definition: The passages through which air enters and leaves the body.
To close within bounds, or otherwise limit or deprive of free movement.
example: He was restrained by the straitjacket.
etymology: From Middle English restreinen, from Old French restreindre, from Latin rēstringere (“fasten, tighten”).

definition: Cool and formal in manner.
example: He greeted her for the first time in three years with a restrained embrace.

definition: Any of the enzymes that cut nucleic acid at specific restriction sites and produce restriction fragments; obtained from bacteria (where they cripple viral invaders); used in recombinant DNA technology.
The fragment of DNA that is produced by cleaving DNA with a restriction enzyme.
A subordinate clause that limits or restricts the meaning of the noun phrase it modifies.
A toilet that is available to the public.
example: Could you tell me where I can find the restroom?
etymology: From rest + room, from an earlier sense of "breakroom".

definition: Bringing again into activity and prominence.
etymology: From resurge + -ence.

definition: Take back by force, as after a battle.
example: The army tried repeatedly to retake the fort they had been driven from.
etymology: From re- + take.

definition: Thinking again about a choice previously made.
example: This business plan of yours looks risky. It needs a rethink.
etymology: From re- + think.

definition: The innermost light-sensitive membrane covering the back wall of the eyeball; it is continuous with the optic nerve.
etymology: From Middle English rethina, borrowing from Medieval Latin rētīna (“retina”, feminine noun), ellipsis of tunica rētīna (“net-like tunic”), used to describe the blood vessel system at the back of the eye.

definition: People who have retreated.
example: He had only contempt for the retreated.

definition: A justly deserved penalty.
etymology: PIE word *tréyes From Latin retribuere (“repay”).

definition: (computer science) the operation of accessing information from the computer's memory.
example: Search dogs assisted in the retrieval of survivors.

definition: Contemplation of things past.
example: In retrospect.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin retrōspectum, from retrōspicio (“to look back at”), equivalent to retro- + -spect. Compare review.

definition: Concerned with or related to the past.
example: Retrospective self-justification.
etymology: From retrospect + -ive. From Latin retrōspectus, perfect passive participle of retrōspiciō (“to look back at”).

definition: Have a reunion; unite again.
example: After ten years apart, the band will reunite.
etymology: From re- + unite.

definition: Use again after processing.
example: The students reused empty plastic bottles in their science experiment.
etymology: From re- + use.

definition: A tariff imposed to raise revenue.
Profoundly honored.
example: Revered holy men.

definition: Capable of reversing or being reversed.
example: Reversible hypertension.
etymology: Probably from Middle French, equivalent to reverse + -ible.

definition: Any process in which a system can be made to pass through the same states in the reverse order when the process is reversed.
Go back to a previous state.
example: We reverted to the old rules.
etymology: From Old French revertir, from Vulgar Latin *revertiō, variant of Latin revertō.

definition: Someone who reads manuscripts and judges their suitability for publication.
etymology: From review + -er.

definition: Make revisions in.
example: Revise a thesis.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French réviser, from Latin revīsō, from re- + vīsō (“examine”), frequentative of videō (“see”).

definition: Visit again.
example: We revisited Rome after 25 years.
etymology: From Middle English revisite, from Middle French revisiter and Latin revīsitāre. By surface analysis, re- + visit.

definition: Fail to follow suit when able and required to do so.
example: Your driver's license will be revoked.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French révoquer, from Latin revocare, from re- + voco, vocare. Doublet of revocate.

definition: A pistol with a revolving cylinder (usually having six chambers for bullets).
A consumer credit line that can be used up to a certain limit or paid down at any time.
An organization or institution with a high rate of turnover of personnel or membership.
A fund which, if borrowed or used, is intended to be replenished so it may be loaned or spent repeatedly.
Write differently; alter the writing of.
example: The editor asked me to rewrite my article for a non-technical audience.
etymology: From re- + write.

definition: A man who puts text into appropriate form for publication.
A woman who puts text into appropriate form for publication.
Of persons (or their blood) lacking the Rh factor present in their red blood cells.
Of persons (or their blood) having the Rh factor present in their red blood cells.
Of or relating to rhetoric.
example: Accepted two or three verbal and rhetorical changes I suggested.
etymology: From Middle English rethorycal, rethoricalle, rethorycall, from rethorik, rhetoric (noun) or Latin rēthoricus, rhētoricus, from Ancient Greek ῥητορικός (rhētorikós, “concerning public speaking”).

definition: Special emphasis placed exceptionally upon tones not subject to grammatical accent.
example: Rhetorical accent, or emphasis, is designed to give to a sentence distinctness and clearness.

definition: A use of language that creates a literary effect (but often without regard for literal significance).
Language designed to persuade or influence others.
example: Martin Luther King Jr. used rhetorical language to get his point across that everyone should be treated equal.

definition: A statement that is formulated as a question but that is not supposed to be answered.
example: He liked to make his points with rhetorical questions.

definition: Recurring with measured regularity.
example: The rhythmic chiming of church bells.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ῥυθμικός (rhuthmikós), from ῥυθμός (rhuthmós, “measured flow or movement, symmetry, rhythm”) + -ικός (-ikós, suffix forming adjectives), equivalent to rhythm + -ic.

definition: (prosody) a system of versification.
The bony enclosing wall of the chest.
A cut of meat (beef or venison) including more than one rib and the meat located along the outside of the ribs.
Soft unsegmented marine worms that have a threadlike proboscis and the ability to stretch and contract.
An automated kitchen appliance designed to boil or steam rice.
An automated kitchen appliance designed to boil or steam rice.
To an ample degree or in an ample manner.
example: We benefited richly.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English richely, from Old English rīċlīċe, from Proto-West Germanic *rīkīlīkō, from Proto-Germanic *rīkijalīkô; by surface analysis, rich + -ly (adverbial suffix).

definition: The property of being extremely abundant.
example: The idiomatic richness of English.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English richenesse; by surface analysis, rich + -ness.

definition: Pierce with many holes.
example: The bullets riddled his body.
etymology: From Middle English redel, redels, from Old English rǣdels, rǣdelse (“counsel, opinion, imagination, riddle”), from Proto-West Germanic *rādislī (“counsel, conjecture”). Analyzable as rede (“advice”) + -le.

definition: A canon in which the entrances of successive parts were indicated by cryptic symbols and devices (popular in the 15th and 16th centuries).
Ride on horseback.
Language or behavior intended to mock or humiliate.
etymology: The obsolete adjective is borrowed from French ridicule, from Latin rīdiculus (“laughable, comical, amusing, absurd, ridiculous”), from ridere (“to laugh”).

definition: A marine turtle.
etymology: Unknown origin.

definition: Look through a book or other written material.
etymology: Uncertain. Perhaps a clipping of riffle, or an alteration of refrain.

definition: Gear consisting of ropes etc. supporting a ship's masts and sails.
etymology: From Middle English riggyng, ryggyng, riggynge, equivalent to rig + -ing.

definition: A prism that has exactly two bases and whose other sides are all rectangles that are perpendicular to these bases.
example: The lateral area of a right prism is the sum of the areas of all the lateral faces.

definition: Forming a right angle or containing one or more right angles.
example: A right-angled bend.

definition: Adhering to moral principles.
example: Only for the righteousness of Christ imputed to us, and received by faith alone.
etymology: Corruption of earlier rightwiseness, from Middle English rightwisnes, from Old English rihtwīsnes (“justice”). By surface analysis, righteous + -ness.

definition: Legally valid.
example: A rightful inheritance.
etymology: From Middle English rightful, ryghtfull, riȝtful, from Old English *rihtfull (suggested by derivative unrihtfull (“unrightful”)), equivalent to right + -ful.

definition: A strategy of defense in cases of bioterrorism; vaccination only of people exposed and others who are in contact with them.
example: Ring containment is a proven method of halting a smallpox epidemic.

definition: Holds loose papers or magazines.
Building that contains a surface for ice skating or roller skating.
etymology: From Middle English rink, renk, from Old English rinc (“man, warrior, hero”), from Proto-Germanic *rankiz (“upright man”), from *rankaz (“straight, upright”), from Proto-Indo-European *reǵ- (“straight, direct”).

definition: A liquid preparation used on wet hair to give it a tint.
example: I'll just give this knife a quick rinse.
etymology: From Middle English rinsen, rincen, rencen (“to rinse”), from Old French rincier, reinser, Old Northern French raïncer (“to rinse, cleanse”). Of contested origin.

definition: Wash off soap or remaining dirt.
Uncontrollably noisy.
example: It was a rip-roaring bar fight, until the cops broke it up.
etymology: From rip + roaring.

definition: A small wave on the surface of a liquid.
example: I dropped a small stone into the pond and watched the ripples spread.
etymology: From an alteration of rimple.

definition: One of a series of small ridges produced in sand by water currents or by wind.
An Old World plantain with long narrow ribbed leaves widely established in temperate regions.
Birch of swamps and river bottoms throughout the eastern United States having reddish-brown bark.

Infestation with slender threadlike roundworms (filaria) deposited under the skin by the bite of black fleas; when the eyes are involved it can result in blindness; common in Africa and tropical America.
Sociable aquatic animal widely distributed along streams and lake borders in North America.
West Indian fruit resembling the mango; often pickled.
Edge of a way or road or path.
example: I pulled over to the roadside to check the map.
etymology: From road + -side.

definition: A road (especially that part of a road) over which vehicles travel.
etymology: From Middle English *rodeway, *radewey (attested in radewey-stile (literally “roadway-stile”)), equivalent to road + way;

definition: Move about aimlessly or without any destination, often in search of food or employment.
example: The gypsies roamed the woods.
etymology: From Middle English romen, from Old English rāmian, from Proto-Germanic *raimōną (“to wander”), from *raim- (“to move, raise”), from *h₃reyH- (“to move, lift, flow”).

definition: Cooking (meat) by dry heat in an oven (usually with fat added).
example: The slow roasting took several hours.
etymology: From Middle English rostynge; equivalent to roast + -ing.

definition: A thief who steals from someone by threatening violence.
etymology: Compare reaver (“robber, plunderer”), a native English word derived from Proto-Germanic *raubārijaz that is ultimately of more or less the same composition as robber.

definition: Swift predatory fly having a strong body like a bee with the proboscis hardened for sucking juices of other insects captured on the wing.
Of southwest United States and Mexico; call is like a dog's bark.
Mythical bird of prey having enormous size and strength.
etymology: From Spanish rocho, ruc, from Arabic رُخّ (ruḵḵ), from Classical Persian رُخ (rux).

definition: Tall widely distributed elm of eastern North America.
Found around rocky coasts or on reefs.
Small penguin of the Falkland Islands and New Zealand.
Slender long-legged Australian wallabies living in caves and rocky areas.
An attendant who rocks a child in a cradle.
example: "Girls & Boys" is […] also a tart, sneering rocker, full of ingenious musical gestures […].
etymology: From Middle English rokker, rockere, rokkere, equivalent to rock + -er.

definition: A lever pivoted at the center; used especially to push a valve down in an internal-combustion engine.
Armament in the form of a device capable of launching a rocket.
etymology: From rocket + launcher.

definition: Reaction propulsion using stored oxygen for combustion; used where there is insufficient atmospheric oxygen.
Propelled by (or as if propelled by) a rocket engine.
An exhibition of cowboy skills.
etymology: From Spanish rodeo, from rodear (“to surround”), which refers to a cattle roundup.

definition: A performer who gives exhibitions of riding and roping and bulldogging.
Fish eggs or egg-filled ovary; having a grainy texture.
etymology: From Middle English rowe, rowne, roun, rawne, from Old English *hrogn (“spawn, fish eggs, roe”), from Proto-Germanic *hrugnaz, *hrugną (“spawn, roe”), from Proto-Indo-European *krek- (“(frog) spawn”).

definition: Small graceful deer of Eurasian woodlands having small forked antlers.
etymology: From Middle English ro der, roadeor, from Old English rāhdēor (“roe deer”), corresponding to roe + deer. Cognate with Icelandic rádýr, Swedish rådjur, Norwegian and Danish rådyr.

definition: Biscuit made from dough rolled and cut.
Meal made from rolled or ground oats.
A hitch for fastening a line to a spar or another rope.
Grown for its thickened edible aromatic root.
The strands out of which ropes are made.
Handsome East Indian evergreen tree often planted as an ornamental for its fragrant white flowers that yield a perfume; source of very heavy hardwood used for railroad ties.
Of lavender tinged with rose.
Of a color tinged with rose.
Reflecting optimism.
example: A rosy future.
etymology: From Middle English rosy; equivalent to rose + -y.

definition: Turned in a circle around an axis.
example: This is a rotated view that shows the area of interest more clearly.

definition: The rotating armature of a motor or generator.
etymology: From an irregular clipping of rotator, originally in mathematics, coined by English mathematician and philosopher William Kingdon Clifford based on vector, see quotations. Doublet of rota and ruote.

definition: The long airfoil that rotates to provide the lift that supports a helicopter in the air.
The rotating armature of a motor or generator.
The axis around which the major rotor of a helicopter turns.
The axis around which the major rotor of a helicopter turns.
(biology) the process of decay caused by bacterial or fungal action.
etymology: From Middle English rotynge (“rotting”), from Old English rotung; equivalent to rot + -ing.

definition: A weak-stemmed winter annual native to Mediterranean region for long established in southern United States; cultivated as a cover and pasture crop.
A line generated by a point on one figure rolling around a second figure.
etymology: Borrowed from French roulette (“roulette, little wheel”). The sense "situation with a random chance of incurring serious harm" may be abstracted from Russian roulette.

definition: The ball used to play roulette.
Game equipment consisting of a wheel with slots that is used for gambling; the wheel rotates horizontally and players bet on which slot the roulette ball will stop in.
A roundabout road (especially one that is used temporarily while a main route is blocked).
A dissolute person; usually a man who is morally unrestrained.
etymology: From Middle English rounder, roundere, equivalent to round + -er (comparative suffix).

definition: (mathematics) a miscalculation that results from rounding off numbers to a convenient number of decimals.
example: The error in the calculation was attributable to rounding.
etymology: By surface analysis, round + -ing.

definition: (mathematics) a miscalculation that results from rounding off numbers to a convenient number of decimals.
example: The error in the calculation was attributable to rounding.

definition: The activity of gathering livestock together so that they can be counted or branded or sold.
etymology: Deverbal from round up.

definition: A woodworking plane with a narrow cutting head that will make grooves with smooth bottoms.
Eurasian tree with orange-red berrylike fruits.
etymology: Originally Scots and northern English, from Middle English ron, rone, compare also Northern English raan, ran. At first referring to its fruits, of North Germanic origin, from Old Norse reynir.

definition: Eurasian tree with orange-red berrylike fruits.
The act of rowing as a sport.
etymology: By surface analysis, row + -ing.

definition: A rowboat.
A club for rowers.
Large deeply rooted fern of worldwide distribution with upright bipinnate compound tufted fronds.
Rate of revolution of a motor.
An accumulation of refuse and discarded matter.
The remains of something that has been destroyed or broken up.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English rouble, rubel, robel, robeil, from Anglo-Norman *robel (“bits of broken stone”). Presumably related to rubbish, originally of same meaning (waste material, bits of stone, rubble).

definition: A baba soaked in rum.
A cocktail made with rum and lime or lemon juice.
Enlargement of the nose with dilation of follicles and redness and prominent vascularity of the skin; often associated with excessive consumption of alcohol.
A loud low dull continuous noise.
example: They heard the rumbling of thunder.
etymology: From Middle English rumblen, romblen, rummelyn, frequentative form of romen (“to roar”), equivalent to rome + -le.

definition: A folding outside seat in the back of some early cars.
Gossip (usually a mixture of truth and untruth) passed around by word of mouth.
etymology: From Middle English rumour, from Old French rumour, rumor, from Latin rūmor (“common talk”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *rewH- (“to shout, roar”).

definition: Trailing European aromatic plant of the mint family having rounded leaves and small purplish flowers often grown in hanging baskets; naturalized in North America; sometimes placed in genus Nepeta.
Any of various fungi causing rust disease in plants.
Australian tree resembling the banyan often planted for ornament; introduced into South Africa for brushwood.
A unit strength of a radioactive source equal to one million disintegrations per second.
etymology: After Ernest Rutherford.

definition: Any of various breads made entirely or partly with rye flour.
Flour made from ground rye grain.
example: Rye flour is used to bake the traditional sourdough breads of Germany, Austria, Switzerland, Russia, Czech Republic, Poland and Scandinavia.

definition: Any of several annual or perennial Eurasian grasses.
Vodka distilled from rye grains.
example: Among grain vodkas, rye and wheat vodkas are generally considered superior.

definition: Whiskey distilled from rye or rye and malt.
Whiskey distilled from rye or rye and malt.
Any of various ascomycetous fungi in which the spores are formed in a sac or ascus.
A long narrow feather on the back (saddle) of a domestic fowl.
Thin-shelled bivalve having the right valve deeply notched.
A decorative overcast or running stitch, especially in a contrasting color.
Droop, sink, or settle from or as if from pressure or loss of tautness.
example: A line or cable supported by its ends sags, even if it is tightly drawn.

definition: Cause to sag.
example: The children sagged their bottoms down even more comfortably.

definition: Large grouse of sagebrush regions of North America.
Willow shrub of dry places in the eastern United States having long narrow leaves canescent beneath.
A sodium salt of carbonic acid; used in making soap powders and glass and paper.
A solution of ammonium carbonate in ammonia water and alcohol.
etymology: From Latin sal volatile, literally "volatile salt".

definition: Containing salt.
example: A saline substance.
etymology: PIE word *sḗh₂l From Middle English salyne, from Medieval Latin salīna and Middle French salin, from Latin sal (“salt”).

definition: An isotonic solution of sodium chloride and distilled water.
A clear liquid secreted into the mouth by the salivary glands and mucous glands of the mouth; moistens the mouth and starts the digestion of starches.
etymology: A learned borrowing from Latin salīva (“spittle”), replacing or merging with Middle English salive, salve (“saliva”), from the same Latin source. Further origin uncertain.

definition: Fish loaf made with flaked salmon.
A room or establishment where alcoholic drinks are served over a counter.
example: A pint of beer in the saloon bar costs a penny more than in the public bar.
etymology: From Occitan salon, French salon, either augmentative of salle (“room”), or borrowed from Italian salone (“hall”), augmentative form of sala, salla (“room”);

definition: The proprietor of a saloon.
(used especially of meats) preserved in salt.
example: Salted peanuts.

definition: Formal and explicit approval.
example: The whalers had been operating in the contested waters off the island with sanction from the Japanese government.
etymology: From Middle French sanction, from Latin sānctiō.

definition: Southeast Asian badger with a snout like a pig.
The lean flesh of a small flounder from the Pacific coast of North America.
A ridge of sand created by the wind; found in deserts or near lakes and oceans.
Small amphipod crustaceans that hop like fleas; common on ocean beaches.
Small amphipod crustaceans that hop like fleas; common on ocean beaches.
etymology: From sand + hopper.

definition: Low-growing evergreen shrub of New Jersey to Florida grown for its many white star-shaped flowers and glossy foliage.
Highly venomous viper of northern Africa and southwestern Asia having a horny spine above each eye.
Free from filth and pathogens.
example: Sanitary conditions for preparing food.
etymology: 19th century, borrowed from French sanitaire, formed from Latin sanitas (“health”). Analysable as sanity + -ary.

definition: Set of standards established and enforced by government for health requirements as in plumbing etc.
A disposable absorbent pad (trade name Kotex); worn to absorb menstrual flow.
Normal or sound powers of mind.
example: Preserve one's sanity.
etymology: From Middle English sanite, sanyte, sanytee, from Middle French sanité, from Latin sānitās, from sānus (“healthy”) + -itās (“-ity”). By surface analysis, sane + -ity.

definition: A precious transparent stone of rich blue corundum valued as a gemstone.
Deciduous shrub of eastern Asia bearing decorative bright blue fruit.
Extremely evil or cruel; expressive of cruelty or befitting hell.
example: Satanic cruelty.
etymology: From satan + -ic.

definition: A smooth fabric of silk or rayon; has a glossy face and a dull back.
etymology: From French satin, which is derived from "Zaitun", the Arabic name for the Chinese city of Quanzhou, itself derived from Arabic زَيْتُون (zaytūn, “Zayton;

definition: Of southeast Australia; male is glossy violet blue; female is light grey-green.
Southeastern European plant cultivated for its fragrant purplish flowers and round flat papery silver-white seedpods that are used for indoor decoration.
Tropical American timber tree with dark hard heavy wood and small plumlike purple fruit.
Exposing human folly to ridicule.
