etymology: Borrowed from French tendon or Medieval Latin tendō, from Ancient Greek τένων (ténōn, “sinew, tendon”), modified by association with the verb tendō (“to stretch”). Compare Middle English thenoun.

definition: A racket used to play tennis.
Any of various drums with small heads.
The adult male singing voice above baritone.
The larvae of moths that build and live in communal silken webs in orchard and shade trees.
Flap consisting of a piece of canvas that can be drawn back to provide entrance to a tent.
A peg driven into the ground to hold a rope supporting a tent.
Under terms not final or fully worked out or agreed upon.
example: Just a tentative schedule.
etymology: From Medieval Latin tentātīvus (“trying, testing”), from tentō, past participle tentātus (“to try, test”); see tent, tempt.

definition: Mexican liquor made from fermented juices of an agave plant.
etymology: Borrowed from Mexican Spanish tequila, from Tequila, a town in Jalisco.

definition: Someone who exterminates (especially someone whose occupation is the extermination of troublesome rodents and insects).
etymology: * Partly from post-classical Latin terminator (5th century), from Latin terminō; partly from terminate + -or. * (android that kills humans): After the 1984 film The Terminator.

definition: Of or relating to or inhabiting the land as opposed to the sea or air.
example: A terrestrial plant.
etymology: From Middle English terrestrialle, from terrestre or Latin terrestris, from terra (“land, earth, ground”), with the suffix -al.

definition: A method of controlling the flight of a missile by devices that respond to the strength and direction of the earth's gravitational field.
A planet having a compact rocky surface like the Earth's; the four innermost planets in the solar system.
(astronomy) a measure of time defined by Earth's orbital motion; terrestrial time is mean solar time corrected for the irregularities of the Earth's motions.
A region marked off for administrative or other purposes.
Struck or filled with terror.
etymology: From terror + stricken.

definition: Of or relating to or based on a text.
example: Textual analysis.
etymology: From Middle English textewell, textueel, textuel, textuele, tixtuel (“learned in texts, bookish”), possibly from Latin textuālis; also compare Middle French textuele;

definition: Comparison of a particular text with related materials in order to establish authenticity.
The words of something written.
An umbrella term for disciplines that deal with describing, transcribing, editing or annotating texts and physical documents.
Someone skilled in making a roof from plant stalks or foliage.
etymology: From thatch + -er.

definition: Relating to or constituting a topic of discourse.
example: He had a thematic collection of postage stamps with flags on them (where (UK) thematic collection is equivalent to (US) topical collection).
etymology: From Ancient Greek θεματικός (thematikós), from θέμα (théma, “theme”). Equivalent to theme + -atic.

definition: (formal) in or into that thing or place.
example: They can read therein what our plans are.
etymology: From Middle English theryn, ther-inne, þer-in, from Old English þǣrin, þǣrinne, from Proto-West Germanic *þārin, *þārinna, from Proto-Germanic *þarin, *þarinna, equivalent to there + in.

definition: Having a thick body.
Insensitive to criticism.
Having a slim body.
Quick to take offense.
example: She's rather thin-skinned when it comes to comments about her work.

definition: An important intellectual.
example: HANK: The NRA is a Washington D.C. based organization. Are you telling me you support Washington D.C.? DALE: That's a thinker.
etymology: From Middle English thinkere, equivalent to think + -er. Compare West Frisian tinker (“thinker”), Dutch denker (“thinker”), German Denker (“thinker”), Danish tænker (“thinker”), Swedish tänkare (“thinker”).

definition: Without force or sincere effort.
example: Smiled thinly.
etymology: From Middle English þynnelich (“with thin material; thinly”); equivalent to thin + -ly.

definition: Coming next after the twelfth in position.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English thrittenthe, thrittethe, from Old English þrēottēoþa; equivalent to thirteen + -th (ordinal suffix).

definition: Something that causes irritation and annoyance.
example: He's a thorn in my flesh.
etymology: From Middle English thorn, þorn, from Old English þorn, from Proto-West Germanic *þorn, from Proto-Germanic *þurnaz, from Proto-Indo-European *tr̥nós, from *(s)ter- (“stiff”).

definition: Any of several plants of the genus Datura.
etymology: Cognate with Dutch doornappel and French pomme épineuse.

definition: Of a plant tipped with a thorn.
Stimulating interest or thought.
example: A thought-provoking book.

definition: Made with three slices of usually toasted bread.
Of or relating to vehicles having three wheels.
example: A three-wheel bike.

definition: The cardinal number that is the sum of one and one and one.
etymology: From three + -some.

definition: Any of numerous sun-loving low-growing evergreens of the genus Armeria having round heads of pink or white flowers.
example: His thrift can be seen in how little the trashman takes from his house.
etymology: From Middle English thrift, thryfte, þrift, from Old Norse þrift (“thriving condition, prosperity”). Equivalent to thrive + -t.

definition: A depository financial institution intended to encourage personal savings and home buying.
Place limits on (extent or amount or access).
etymology: From Middle English *throtel, diminutive of throte (“throat”), equivalent to throat + -le. Compare German Drossel (“throttle”). More at throat.

definition: A valve that regulates the supply of fuel to the engine.
Lose (something) or lose the right to (something) by some error, offense, or crime.
An aggressive and violent young criminal.
etymology: Borrowed from Hindustani ठग (ṭhag) / ٹھگ (ṭhag, “swindler, fraud, cheat”), further derived from Prakrit 𑀞𑀕 (ṭhaga), of uncertain origin. See there for more.

definition: A storm resulting from strong rising air currents; heavy rain or hail along with thunder and lightning.
etymology: From thunder + storm.

definition: Any of several closely related compounds that are produced by the thyroid gland and are active metabolically.
Any of several small veins draining blood from the thyroid area.
A metallic tapping sound.
etymology: From tick (“sheet, cover”) + -ing (“material, collection”).

definition: A problematic situation that will eventually become dangerous if not addressed.
example: The refugee camp is a ticking bomb waiting to go off.

California annual having flower heads with yellow rays tipped with white.
A pin used to hold the tie in place.
Active usually bright-colored beetle that preys on other insects.

definition: A young tiger.
Medium-sized moth with long richly colored and intricately patterned wings; larvae are called woolly bears.
example: Most tiger moths have broad, striped (hence the name) or spotted wings.

definition: Having stripes resembling those of a tiger.
Exaggeratedly proper.
The act of making something tighter.
example: The tightening of economic controls.

definition: Closely and firmly integrated.
example: A tight-knit organization.

definition: Skintight knit hose covering the body from the waist to the feet worn by acrobats and dancers and as stockings by women and girls.
etymology: From tight + -s.

definition: A cutter (tool for cutting) for floor tiles.
Departing or being caused to depart from the true vertical or horizontal.
example: The headstones were tilted.

definition: A hitch used to secure a rope to a log or spar; often supplemented by a half hitch.
A schedule listing events and the times at which they will take place.
example: The timetable has been changed several times since it was first announced.
etymology: From time + table.

definition: Showing fear and lack of confidence.
example: John's a very timid person. I doubt he'll be brave enough to face his brother.
etymology: From Middle French timide, from Latin timidus (“full of fear, fearful, timid”), from timeō (“to fear”).

definition: The transformation of ordinary white tin into powdery grey tin at very cold temperatures.
Cause to make a ting.
example: When the microwaved food was ready, the bell tinged.
etymology: Onomatopoeic.

definition: (used of noses) turned up at the end.
Producing exhaustion.
example: Carrying my bags up four flights of stairs is very tiring.

definition: A white powder used as a pigment for its high covering power and durability.
A white powder used as a pigment for its high covering power and durability.
A white powder used as a pigment for its high covering power and durability.
A floating or creeping Indian lettuce having terminal racemes of pale rose flowers; wet areas at high elevations of western North America.
Low-growing annual rush of damp low-lying ground; nearly cosmopolitan.
etymology: So named because of its tendency to grow in the same habitat where toads live.

definition: Browned over by exposure to heat.
example: He liked toasted marshmallows.

definition: Someone who who drinks to the health of someone or the success of some venture.
Kitchen appliance consisting of a small electric oven for toasting or warming food.
A plant disease causing discoloration of the leaves of tobacco plants.
example: RNA replaces DNA as the genetic material in many viruses (for example, tobacco mosaic, influenza, polio, certain RNA phages).

definition: Small moth whose larvae feed on tobacco and other dried plant products.
A pouch for carrying pipe tobacco.
Cheeselike food made of curdled soybean milk.
etymology: Borrowed from Japanese 豆(とう)腐(ふ) (tōfu), from Middle Chinese 豆腐 (duwᴴ bju^X, “curdled bean”). Doublet of dubu and doufu.

definition: Thick spicy sauce made from tomatoes.
Having or characterized or distinguished by tone or a specific tone; often used in combination.
example: Full-toned.

definition: Of or relating to or producing normal tone or tonus in muscles or tissue.
example: A tonic reflex.
etymology: From Ancient Greek τονικός (tonikós), from τόνος (tónos). 17th century writers believed health to be derived from firmly stretched muscles, thus tonic; the extension of tonic medicine appeared in the late 18th century.

definition: Emphasis that results from pitch rather than loudness.
The basic key in which a piece of music is written.
Lime- or lemon-flavored carbonated water containing quinine.
Hard white substance covering the crown of a tooth.
A fungus of the family Hydnaceae.
A bony socket in the alveolar ridge that holds a tooth.
Small brush; has long handle; used to clean teeth.
etymology: From tooth + brush.

definition: Glabrous or pubescent evergreen shrub or tree of the genus Salvadora; twigs are fibrous and in some parts of the world are bound together in clusters and used as a toothbrush; shoots are used as camel fodder; plant ash provides salt.
A dentifrice in the form of a paste.
example: Fluoride toothpaste.
etymology: From tooth + paste.

definition: A violent kind of alcoholic fermentation at a temperature high enough to carry the yeast cells to the top of the fermenting liquid; used in the production of ale.
example: Top fermentation uses a yeast that ferments at higher temperatures than that used for bottom fermentation.

definition: Pertaining to the surface of a body part.
example: A drug for topical (or local) application.
etymology: From topic + -al.

definition: Having no top.
example: A topless jar.
etymology: From top + -less.

definition: The configuration of a surface and the relations among its man-made and natural features.
etymology: First attested in 1432. From Middle English topographye, from Latin topographia, from Ancient Greek τοπογραφία (topographía), from τόπος (tópos, “place”) + γράφω (gráphō, “to write”).

definition: Unbearable physical pain.
example: I've gone through living torment.
etymology: From Middle English torment, from Old French torment, from Latin tormentum (“something operated by twisting”), from torquere (“to twist”). Compare native English bale (“suffering, woe, torment”) and English woe.

definition: An underground shelter where you can go until a storm passes.
An oil lamp with a glass chimney and perforated metal lid to protect the flame from high winds; candlestick with a glass chimney.
Small high-speed warship designed for torpedo attacks in coastal waters.
A tube near the waterline of a vessel through which a torpedo is fired.
A heavy rain.
example: Rain fell on the hills in torrents.
etymology: Borrowed from French torrent, from Italian torrente, from Latin torrentem, accusative of torrēns (“burning, seething, roaring”), from Latin torrēre (“to parch, scorch”).

definition: The body excluding the head and neck and limbs.
etymology: From Italian torso, from Late Latin tursus, from Latin thyrsus, from Ancient Greek θύρσος (thúrsos, “Bacchic staff”). Doublet of thyrse, thyrsus, and torse.

definition: Usually herbivorous land turtles having clawed elephant-like limbs; worldwide in arid areas except Australia and Antarctica.

definition: South African vine having a massive rootstock covered with deeply fissured bark.

definition: A capacious bag or basket.

definition: A capacious bag or basket.

Enduring strength and energy.

definition: Of imposing height; especially standing out above others.

definition: (nautical) a rope used in towing.

(nautical) a rope used in towing.

etymology: From Latin toxicum, equivalent to toxi- + -in.

definition: A government order imposing a trade barrier.

definition: The character flaw or error of a tragic hero that leads to their downfall.

definition: In a tragic manner; with tragic consequences.
example: The adventure ended tragically.

definition: Someone who is being trained.

definition: A conveyance that transports passengers or freight in carriers suspended from cables and supported by a series of towers.
etymology: From Spanish trama, or French trame (“weft”). Doublet of trama.

definition: A psychological state induced by (or as if induced by) a magical incantation.
etymology: From Middle English traunce, from Anglo-Norman transe (“fear of coming evil; passage from life to death”), from transir (“to be numb with fear; to die, pass on”), from Latin trānseō (“to cross over”).

definition: Of a mental act; causing effects outside the mind.
example: A transient pleasure.
etymology: From Late Latin transiēnt- (for classical transeunt-), stem of transiēns, present participle of trānsīre (“to go over, to pass”).

definition: A program that translates one programming language into another.
The act of sending a message; causing a message to be transmitted.
An electrical device that sends or receives radio or television signals.
Extending or lying across; in a crosswise direction; at right angles to the long axis.

etymology: Late Middle English, from Latin trānsversus (“turned across; going or lying across or crosswise”). Doublet of transversal.

definition: One of two processes that extend from each vertebra and provide the point of articulation for the ribs.
Stable gear consisting of a decorated covering for a horse, especially (formerly) for a warhorse.

definition: A convulsive epileptic state caused by a head injury.
A sum allowed for travel.
A person who changes location.
example: Ring traveller.
etymology: From Middle English traveler, travelour, travailere, travailour (“worker", also "traveller”), equivalent to travel + -er. Compare Anglo-Norman travailur, travailour, Old French travailleor, travelleeur, travelier.

definition: A horizontal beam that extends across something.
example: He will succeed, as long as there are no unlucky traverses not under his control.
etymology: From Middle English traversen, from Old French traverser, from Latin trans (“across”) + versus (“turned”), perfect passive participle of Latin vertere (“to turn”).

definition: Dangerously unstable and unpredictable.
example: Treacherous winding roads.
etymology: From Old French trecheros, tricheros (“deceitful”), equivalent to treacher + -ous. See treacher.

definition: A stinging herb of tropical America.
A mill that is powered by men or animals walking on a circular belt or climbing steps.
An exercise device consisting of an endless belt on which a person can walk or jog without changing place.
etymology: From tread + mill. Its figurative senses refer to the idea that running on a treadmill requires continued effort and motion to remain in the same place.

definition: A stress test in which the patient walks on a moving treadmill while the heart and breathing rates are monitored.
A formal exposition.
etymology: From Middle English tretys, from Anglo-Norman tretiz and Old French traitis (“treatise, account”), from traitier (“to deal with, treat”).

definition: Three times the amount that a court would normally find the injured party entitled to.
A clef that puts the G above middle C on the second line of a staff.

Any of numerous usually tropical ferns having a thick woody stem or caudex and a crown of large fronds; found especially in Australia and New Zealand; chiefly of the families Cyatheaceae and Marattiaceae but some from Polypodiaceae.
Arboreal wallabies of New Guinea and northern Australia having hind and forelegs of similar length.
Eurasian sparrow smaller than the house sparrow.
The base part of a tree that remains standing after the tree has been felled.
Arboreal amphibians usually having adhesive disks at the tip of each toe; of southeast Asia and Australia and America.
Vibrating slightly and irregularly; as e.g. with fear or cold or like the leaves of an aspen in a breeze.
example: Trembling hands.

definition: Vastly.
example: I enjoyed the performance tremendously.
etymology: From tremendous + -ly.

definition: In accord with the latest fad.
example: Trendy ideas.
etymology: From trend + -y.

definition: The cardinal number that is the sum of one and one and one.
etymology: PIE word *tréyes From Middle English trey, from Anglo-Norman trei or treis, from Old French treis (“three”). Doublet of three and tres.

definition: Having three angles; forming or shaped like a triangle.

etymology: From Middle English triangulare, trianguler, triangulere, from Old French triangulaire, triangulier and Latin triangulāris. By surface analysis, tri- + -angular.

definition: The leader of an Arab village or family.
Decorated in a particular way.
example: Tricked-out cupboards looking like Georgian cabinets.

definition: Flowing in drops; the formation and falling of drops of liquid.
example: The brook had shrunk to a mere trickle.
etymology: From Middle English triklen, likely a rebracketing (e.g. teres strikled > teerys trikled (“tears trickled”)) of Middle English striklen (“to trickle”), equivalent to strike + -le.

definition: A spear with three prongs.
example: Poseidon's trident.
etymology: PIE word *tréyes From Latin tridēns, from tri- (“three”) + dēns (“tooth”).

definition: Made neat and tidy by trimming.
example: His neatly trimmed hair.

Typing that leaves two lines blank between lines of typing.
A weathered and decomposed siliceous limestone; in powdered form it is used in polishing.

definition: Joyful and proud especially because of triumph or success.

definition: Something of small importance.

definition: A soldier in a motorized army unit.

definition: Causing difficulty or annoyance.

definition: A narrow depression (as in the earth or between ocean waves or in the ocean bed).
example: One of Harriet's chores was to slop the pigs' trough each morning and evening.

definition: Organization of performers and associated personnel (especially theatrical).
etymology: Attested 1825; Unadapted borrowing from French troupe, which see for more. Doublet of troop, and possibly also of thorp and dorp.

definition: The activity of transporting goods by truck.
etymology: From truck + -ing.

definition: A company that ships goods or possessions by truck.
An industry that provides transportation for commercial products.
The angular distance of a point in an orbit past the point of periapsis measured in degrees.
Any of various evergreen trees of the genus Abies; chiefly of upland areas.
Mahogany tree of West Indies.

Tailless amphibian similar to a frog but more terrestrial and having drier warty skin.

Expressing or given to expressing the truth.

definition: Adjustable wrench for gripping and turning a pipe; has two serrated jaws that are adjusted to grip the pipe.
Conduit consisting of a long hollow object (usually cylindrical) used to hold and conduct objects or liquids or gases.
etymology: From tube + -ing.

example: The tower of the World Trade Center tumbled after the plane hit it.

In deplorable condition.

definition: Slang for a paunch.

definition: An abnormal new mass of tissue that serves no purpose.
etymology: From Middle English tumour, from Old French tumour, from Latin tumor (“swelling”), from tumeō (“bulge, swell”, verb), from Proto-Indo-European *tewh₂- (“to swell”). Related to English thumb.

definition: Characterized by unrest or disorder or insubordination.

Stuffing for turkey.

A blue to grey green mineral consisting of copper aluminum phosphate.

definition: A small tower extending above a building.
example: Their Victorian house had three turrets and a large amount of gingerbread trim.
etymology: From Middle English touret, from Old French torete (French tourette), diminutive of tour (“tower”), from Latin turris. Doublet of tor, tourelle, and tower. See tower.

definition: A clock with more than one dial to show the time in all directions from a tower.
Two items of the same kind.
etymology: The word outlasted the breakdown of gender in Middle English and survived as a secondary form of two, then especially in the cases where the numeral follows a noun.

definition: Pinch or squeeze sharply.
example: To tweak the nose.

definition: Thick woolen fabric used for clothing; originated in Scotland.

etymology: From Middle English two-foted, equivalent to two + footed. Compare Old English twifēte (“two-footed”), Old Norse tvífættr (“two-footed”).

definition: Of or relating to vehicles with two wheels.
example: A two-wheeled cart.

definition: A strip of type metal used for spacing.

definition: Writing paper suitable for use in a typewriter.
A mistake in printed matter resulting from mechanical failures of some kind.
example: Sorry, I meant to say “buy a SODA”—“sofa” was a typo.

definition: A cruel and oppressive dictator.

definition: Having or employing wavelengths shorter than light but longer than X-rays; lying outside the visible spectrum at its violet end.

Radiation lying in the ultraviolet range; wave lengths shorter than light but longer than X rays.

definition: Lacking beauty or charm.
example: As unattractive as most mining regions.
etymology: From un- + attractive.

definition: Impossible to avoid or evade.
example: An unavoidable accident.

definition: Incapable of being tolerated or endured.
etymology: From Middle English unberable, equivalent to un- + bearable.

definition: Not conquered.

etymology: From Middle English on bete, unbeten, unibeten; equivalent to un- + beaten; compare Old English ungebeitne (“unhewn”).

definition: Not easy to believe.
example: He gestured unbelievably. Everyone knew he was faking his illness.
etymology: From unbelievable + -ly.

definition: Characterized by a lack of partiality.
example: An unbiased account of her family problems.
etymology: From un- + biased.

definition: Not yet brought into existence.
example: Unborn generations.
etymology: From Middle English unborn, from Old English unboren, from Proto-Germanic *unburanaz. Equivalent to un- + born.

definition: Suggesting the operation of supernatural influences.
example: Stumps … had uncanny shapes as of monstrous creatures.
etymology: From un- + canny; thus “beyond one's ken,” or outside one's familiar knowledge or perceptions. Compare Middle English unkanne (“unknown”).

definition: Not conditional.
example: Unconditional surrender.
etymology: From un- + conditional.

definition: Not conforming to accepted rules or standards.
example: Her unconventional dress and hair style.
etymology: From un- + conventional.

definition: Remove all or part of one's clothes to show one's body.
example: Uncover your belly.
etymology: From Middle English uncoveren, equivalent to un- + cover.

definition: Not trimmed.
etymology: From Middle English unkut, uncutte, unkyt, unkutt, equivalent to un- + cut.

definition: Not possible to deny.
example: Some believe that there is undeniable evidence of UFOs.
etymology: From un- + deny + -able, compare deniable.

definition: Not of legal age.
example: Underage drinking.
etymology: From under- + age.

definition: In an intelligible manner.
example: Understandably, he was too embarrassed to speak.
etymology: From understandable + -ly.

definition: A statement that is restrained in ironic contrast to what might have been said.
example: A master of understatement.
etymology: From under- + statement or understate + -ment.

definition: The archeology of underwater sites.
Someone who works underwater.
The brush (small trees and bushes and ferns etc.) growing beneath taller trees in a wood or forest.
etymology: From under- + wood.

definition: The criminal class.
example: In Hindu scriptures, the four-eyed dogs Śārvara and Śyāma guard the underworld's entrance.
etymology: From under- + world.

definition: Not wanted.
example: Undesirable impurities in steel.
etymology: From un- + desirable.

definition: Not made known.
example: An undisclosed location.
etymology: From un- + disclosed.

definition: Generally agreed upon; not subject to dispute.
example: The undisputed fact.
etymology: From un- + disputed.

definition: Lacking necessary documents (as for e.g. permission to live or work in a country).
example: Undocumented aliens.
etymology: From un- + documented.

definition: Not done.
example: The work could be done or undone and nobody cared.
etymology: From un- + done.

definition: Not yet payable.
example: An undue loan.
etymology: From un- + due.

definition: Lacking a sense of security or affording no ease or reassurance.
example: Farmers were uneasy until rain finally came.
etymology: From Middle English unesy, equivalent to un- + easy. Merged with Middle English unethe, uneathe (“difficult, not easy”). See uneath.

definition: Poorly balanced or matched in quantity or value or measure.
example: Unequal to the task.
etymology: From Middle English unequale, equivalent to un- + equal. Compare German unegal (“unlevel, uneven”).

definition: Not meeting requirements.
example: Unequal to the demands put upon him.

definition: Not conforming to approved standards of social or professional behavior.
example: Unethical business practices.
etymology: From un- + ethical.

definition: Not explained.
example: Accomplished by some unexplained process.
etymology: From un- + explained.

definition: In an unfair manner.
example: They dealt with him unfairly.
etymology: From unfair + -ly or un- + fairly.

definition: Develop or come to a promising stage.
example: To unfold a map; to unfold a tablecloth; She unpacks the new dress and unfolds it carefully.
etymology: From Middle English unfolden, from Old English unfealdan (“to unfold”), equivalent to un- + fold.

definition: A developmental process.
Impossible to forget.
example: The things he subjected me to were horrible and unforgettable.
etymology: From un- + forget + -able or un- + forgettable.

definition: Not feeling or showing gratitude.
example: Ungrateful heirs.
etymology: From un- + grateful.

definition: A person who shows no gratitude.
Not necessarily inaudible but not heard.
example: Her cries for help remained unheard.
etymology: From Middle English unherd, unherde, from Old English unġehīered (“unheard”), equivalent to un- + heard. Cognate with West Frisian ûnheard (“unheard”), Dutch ongehoord (“unheard”), German ungehört (“unheard”).

definition: Previously unknown.
example: A first novel by an unheard of writer.

definition: Any of several perennials of the genus Aletris having grasslike leaves and bitter roots reputed to cure colic.
An occurrence that involves the production of a union.
etymology: Either: * from unify + -ification (suffix forming nouns denoting acts or processes whereby subjects become something else); or * borrowed from French unification; or * borrowed from Italian unificazione.

definition: Involving only one part or side.
example: Unilateral paralysis.
etymology: A modern creation (circa 1802), from New Latin ūnilaterālis (“one-sided”), from Latin ūnus (“one”) + laterālis (“sided, lateral”), equivalent to uni- + lateral.

definition: A one-sided agreement whereby you promise to do (or refrain from doing) something in return for a performance (not a promise).
Line of descent traced through one side of the family.
Not deliberate.
etymology: From un- + intended.

definition: Having undisturbed continuity.
example: A convalescent needs uninterrupted sleep.
etymology: From un- + interrupted.

definition: A worker who belongs to a trade union.
etymology: From union + -ist.

definition: Corresponding exactly.
example: Marching in unison.
etymology: From Middle English unisoun, from Middle French unisson, from Medieval Latin ūnisonus (“having the same sound”), from ūni- + sonus (“sound”).

definition: The combination of two or more commercial companies.
Hypothetical universal solvent once sought by alchemists.
Suffrage for all adults who are not disqualified by the laws of the country.
example: On Dec. 5, 1934, women gained full universal suffrage in Turkey...

definition: Not fair; marked by injustice or partiality or deception.
example: The solution was very unjust.
etymology: From un- + just.

definition: Release or vent.
example: Unleash one's anger.
etymology: From un- + leash.

definition: Lacking a crew.
example: An unmanned satellite to Mars.
etymology: From un- + manned.

definition: Not married or related to the unmarried state.
example: Unmarried men and women.
etymology: From un- + married.

definition: A man who has never been married.
A woman who is not married.
In an unnecessary manner.
example: They were unnecessarily rude.
etymology: From unnecessary + -ly or un- + necessarily.

definition: Not noticed.
example: Hoped his departure had passed unnoticed.
etymology: From un- + noticed.

definition: Having an unpleasant smell.
Without preparation; not prepared for.

definition: Not characteristic of or befitting a profession or one engaged in a profession.
example: Described in unprofessional language so that high school students could understand it.
etymology: From un- + professional.

definition: Lacking protection or defense.
etymology: From un- + protected.

definition: Not published.
example: Unpublished letters and diaries.
etymology: From un- + published.

definition: Not solved.
example: Many problems remain unresolved.
etymology: From un- + resolved.

definition: Not subject to or subjected to restriction.
etymology: From un- + restricted.

definition: Not solved.
example: Many crimes remain unsolved.
etymology: From un- + solved.

definition: Not stated explicitly or in detail.
example: Threatened unspecified reprisals.
etymology: From un- + specified.

definition: Not capable of being stopped.
example: As unstoppable as the wind.
etymology: From un- + stoppable.

definition: Without success.
example: She tried unsuccessfully to persuade him to buy a new car.
etymology: From unsuccessful + -ly or un- + successfully.

definition: Not meant or adapted for a particular purpose.
example: A solvent unsuitable for use on wood surfaces.
etymology: From un- + suitable.

definition: Incapable of being conceived or considered.
etymology: From un- + think + -able.

definition: Too much to be measured.
example: Untold suffering.

definition: Still full.
example: An untouched cocktail in her hand.
etymology: From un- + touched.

definition: Not given medical care or treatment.
example: An untreated disease.
etymology: From un- + treated.

definition: Not according with the facts.
example: Unfortunately the statement was simply untrue.
etymology: From Middle English untrewe, from Old English untrīewe, from Proto-West Germanic *untriuwī, from Proto-Germanic *untriwwiz. Equivalent to un- + true.

definition: Properties acquired during a person's formative years.
example: Through her upbringing, Mildred's father had carefully programmed her to expect very little from life.
etymology: From Middle English upbringinge, equivalent to upbring + -ing.

definition: Frank and honest.
example: He was upfront about his intentions.

definition: Against difficulties.
example: She was talking uphill.
etymology: From up + hill.

definition: Fill with high spirits; fill with optimism.
example: Music can uplift your spirits.
etymology: From up- + lift.

definition: The rise of something.

etymology: From uplift + -ing.

definition: The higher of two berths.
Appropriate for people with good incomes.

etymology: From up + scale, 1966 (adjective), 1963 (verb).

definition: In or toward the northern parts of a state.
example: He lives upstate New York.
etymology: From up + state.

definition: The process of taking food into the body through the mouth (as by eating).
etymology: From Middle English uptaken (“to take up, lift”), partial calque of earlier Middle English upnimen (“to take up, lift”), equivalent to up- + take. Compare Swedish upptaga, uppta (“to take up”).

definition: Of or located in the upper part of a town.
example: Uptown residential areas.

definition: A guerrilla who fights only in cities and towns.
With great urgency.
example: Health care reform is needed urgently.
etymology: From urgent + -ly.

definition: An organ that separates waste substances from the blood and discharges them.
The quality of being of practical use.
example: The usefulness of his latest reorganisation has been disputed.
etymology: From useful + -ness.

definition: A hollow muscular organ in the pelvic cavity of females; contains the developing fetus.
Ideally perfect state; especially in its social and political and moral aspects.
Having been rendered unsusceptible to a disease.

definition: The parturition process in human beings; having a baby; the process of giving birth to a child.
In a vague way.

definition: Having or showing valor.

etymology: From Middle English vailaunt (“having or showing courage or valour, valiant; characterized by valour; powerful, strong; person of valour or strength; excellent, worthy; beneficial, useful; valuable;

definition: Declare or make legally valid.

definition: A lever pivoted at the center; used especially to push a valve down in an internal-combustion engine.
Willful wanton and malicious destruction of the property of others.

definition: Sweet vanilla flavored custard-like pudding usually thickened with flour rather than eggs.
Get lost, as without warning or explanation.

A cream used cosmetically (mostly by women) for softening and cleaning the skin.
The point beyond which something disappears or ceases to exist.
Place or situation affording some advantage (especially a comprehensive view or commanding perspective).

definition: A place from which something can be viewed.
example: From that vantage point he could survey the whole valley.

definition: The density of a gas relative to the density of hydrogen.
The quality of being subject to variation.

etymology: Derived form of variable, from Old French variable; see variable + -ity.

definition: An event that departs from expectations.
etymology: From Middle English variance, variaunce, equivalent to vary + -ance, from Old French variance or directly from Anglo-Latin variaunce, veriaunce, wariaunce; all from Latin variantia.

definition: The investigation of deviations in financial performance from the standards defined in organizational budgets.
A sock worn for athletic events.
Large large-footed North American hare; white in winter.
A unit strand of the vascular system in stems and leaves of higher plants consisting essentially of xylem and phloem.
Green plant having a vascular system: ferns, gymnosperms, angiosperms.
A sheet of vascular tissue separating the vascular bundles.
A dilation of superficial capillaries with a central red dot from which blood vessels radiate.
A unit strand of the vascular system in stems and leaves of higher plants consisting essentially of xylem and phloem.

Tissue that conducts water and nutrients through the plant body in higher plants.

Shaped in the form of a vase.

Edible seeds or roots or stems or leaves or bulbs or tubers or nonsweet fruits of any of numerous herbaceous plant.
example: Fruit and veg.
etymology: Clipping of various related words including vegetable, vegetarian, and vegetate.

definition: Engage in passive relaxation.
example: After a hard day's work, I vegetate in front of the television.
etymology: From veg + out, the former a clipping of vegetate.

definition: Any of various squash plants grown for their elongated fruit with smooth dark green skin and whitish flesh.
Mediterranean biennial herb with long-stemmed heads of purple ray flowers and milky sap and long edible root; naturalized throughout United States.
The loofah climber that has cylindrical fruit.
Edible seeds or roots or stems or leaves or bulbs or tubers or nonsweet fruits of any of numerous herbaceous plant.
etymology: Clipping of vegetable and/or vegetarian + -ie.

definition: Having or as if having a veil or concealing cover.
example: A veiled dancer.

definition: Any of numerous velvety-skinned wormlike carnivorous animals common in tropical forests having characteristics of both arthropods and annelid worms.
etymology: From velvet + worm. Named after their velvety skin texture and worm-like appearance.

definition: The act of selling goods for a living.
A slot machine for selling goods.
etymology: This name for such a machine is attested since 1889. The concept of such a machine is centuries older (for more, see Wikipedia at vending machine § History).

definition: Impressive by reason of age.
example: A venerable sage with white hair and beard.
etymology: From Middle French vénérable, from Old French, from Latin venerabilis.

definition: A shaft in a building; serves as an air passage for ventilation.
A noun that is derived from a verb.
As a verb.
example: He had a habit of using nouns verbally.
etymology: From verbal + -ly.

definition: Having a wide variety of skills.
etymology: From versatile + -ity.

definition: A tubular wind instrument with 8 finger holes and a fipple mouthpiece.
In a vertical direction.
example: A gallery quite often is added to make use of space vertically as well as horizontally.
etymology: From vertical + -ly.

definition: Fixed and absolute and without contingency.
example: A vested right.

definition: (law) an interest in which there is a fixed right to present or future enjoyment and that can be conveyed to another.
etymology: Popularized in sociology by Thorstein Veblen, The Vested Interests and the Common Man (1919). But used earlier, e.g.

definition: (of living things) capable of normal growth and development.
etymology: From viable + -ity.

A Roman Catholic priest who acts for another higher-ranking clergyman.
(Roman Catholic Church) an administrative deputy who assists a bishop.
A regent's deputy.
Compete for something; engage in a contest; measure oneself against others.

definition: Optical device that helps a user to find the target of interest.
Carefully observant or attentive; on the lookout for possible danger.
example: The vigilant eye of the town watch.
etymology: From French vigilant or its source, Latin vigilans, present participle of vigilare (“stay awake”), from vigil (“awake”). Doublet of vigilante, from Spanish. Displaced Old English wacor.

definition: Member of a vigilance committee.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish vigilante (“watchman, guard”), from Latin vigilans. Doublet of vigilant.

definition: Characterized by forceful and energetic action or activity.
example: A vigorous hiker.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman vigrus, from Old French vigoros (French vigoureux), from Medieval Latin vigorosus, from Latin vigor. Doublet of vigoroso.

definition: With vigor; in a vigorous manner.
example: He defended his ideas vigorously.

definition: Small maple of northwestern North America having prostrate stems that root freely and form dense thickets.

A thermoplastic derived by polymerization from compounds containing the vinyl group.
Venomous Old World snakes characterized by hollow venom-conducting fangs in the upper jaw.

definition: Hepatitis caused by a virus.
The condition or quality of being a virgin.
example: To lose one's virginity.
etymology: From Middle English virginite, from Old French virginite, from Latin virginitas. Equivalent to virgin + -ity. Displaced native Old English mæġeþhād (compare modern English maidhood), originally meaning “girlhood.”

definition: A natural and unavoidable catastrophe that interrupts the expected course of events.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin vīs maior.

definition: Relating to or affecting the viscera.
example: Visceral bleeding.
etymology: From Middle French viscéral (modern French viscéral), or from its etymon Medieval Latin viscerālis (“internal”) + English -al (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives).

definition: A system of functionally related neural structures in the brain that are involved in emotional behavior.
In a visible manner.
example: He was visibly upset.
etymology: From visible + -ly.

definition: A person given to fanciful speculations and enthusiasms with little regard for what is actually possible.
etymology: From vision + -ary.

definition: An annoying or frustrating or catastrophic event.
example: His mother-in-law's visits were a great trial for him.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman visitacioun, from Old French visitacion, from Latin vīsitātiō. By surface analysis, visit + -ation.

definition: The right granted by a court to a parent (or other relative) who is deprived of custody of a child to visit the child on a regular basis.
A mental image that is similar to a visual perception.
example: She used visualization techniques to prepare for the competition.
etymology: From visualize + -ation.

definition: Imagine; conceive of; see in one's mind.
example: To visualize data using a chart.
etymology: From visual + -ize (suffix forming verbs denoting the doing or making of what is denoted by the adjectives or nouns to which it is attached).

definition: Having greatly reduced vision.
An energetic style.
example: Youthful vitality.
etymology: From vital + -ity, from Middle French vitalité, from Latin vitalitas (“vital force, life”), from vitalis (“vital”); see vital.

definition: An examination conducted by spoken communication.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish viva and Italian viva.

definition: In a vivid manner.
example: He described his adventures vividly.
etymology: From vivid + -ly.

definition: A person who sings.

definition: A computerized system for answering and routing telephone calls; telephone messages can be recorded and stored and relayed.
example: Near-synonyms: voice mailbox, voicemailbox.

definition: The property of changing readily from a solid or liquid to a vapor.
etymology: From volatile + -ity.

The sudden occurrence of a violent discharge of steam and volcanic material.
A transformer whose voltage ratio of transformation can be adjusted.
The shape of something rotating rapidly.

Someone who vouches for another or for the correctness of a statement.
example: A voucher for a free kettle.

definition: A speech sound made with the vocal tract open.
etymology: From Middle English vowel, from Old French vouel, a variant of voyeul (whence French voyelle), from Latin vōcālis (“voiced”), itself a semantic loan of Koine Greek φωνῆεν (phōnêen). Doublet of vocal and vocalis.

definition: A mark placed below or near a consonant (as in Hebrew or Arabic) to indicate the spoken vowel.
A speech sound made with the vocal tract open.
The system of vowels used in a particular language.
A traveler to a distant land (especially one who travels by sea).
etymology: From voyage + -er.

definition: Ludicrous, foolish.
example: Some wacky plan for selling more books.
etymology: From whack (“someone who whacked his head onto something often, hence being weird”) + -y.

The act of gambling.

Mat-forming lithophytic or terrestrial fern with creeping rootstocks and large pinnatifid fronds found throughout North America and Europe and Africa and east Asia.
A decorative printed wallpaper usually placed on only one wall; the print can either be custom or chosen from a predefined set.
A silly and inept person; someone who is regarded as stupid.
An assured victory (especially in an election).
etymology: From German Walzer, from walzen (“to dance”), from Old High German walzan (“to turn”), from Proto-Germanic *walt- (“to turn”), from Proto-Indo-European *welH- (“to turn”). Doublet of valse. More at *waltaną.

definition: Dance a waltz.
A rod used by a magician or water diviner.
example: Curling wand.
etymology: From Middle English wand, wond, from Old Norse vǫndr (“switch, twig”), from Proto-Germanic *wanduz (“rod”), from Proto-Indo-European *wendʰ- (“to turn, twist, wind, braid”).

definition: Having warm blood (in animals whose body temperature is internally regulated).
etymology: From warm + blooded.

definition: Used of music.
Having been warmed up.
example: A cup of warmed milk.

definition: Used especially of timbers or boards; bent out of shape usually by moisture.
example: The floors were warped and cracked.
etymology: From warp + -ed.

definition: Someone who washes things for a living.
etymology: From Middle English wasshere, wassher, equivalent to wash + -er. Cognate with Dutch wasser, German Wäscher.

definition: Social or solitary hymenopterans typically having a slender body with the abdomen attached by a narrow stalk and having a formidable sting.
A very slender waist.
Inefficient in use of time and effort and materials.
example: A clumsy and wasteful process.
etymology: From Middle English wastful; equivalent to waste + -ful.

definition: Water mixed with waste matter.

A plant of the genus Trapa bearing spiny four-pronged edible nutlike fruits.
Water fern of Europe and Asia and the eastern United States distinguished by four leaflets resembling clover leaves.
Eurasian elm closely resembling the American elm; thrives in a moist environment.
Ferns that grow in water.
Forked stick that is said to dip down to indicate underground water or oil.

A jug that holds water.

An Asian buffalo that is often domesticated for use as a draft animal.

A deep blue cordierite often used as a gemstone.
